### CR-051 · THE SOURCE DOCUMENT — CITE THIS CR, THEN OPEN THIS

**The bill run, taken apart and put back together** · 12 sections · 26 diagrams

> https://claude.ai/code/artifact/52c54ce0-d23c-4063-9bf6-dfe5be4fd3b7

**What it contains.** As-is screens, process and endpoints · the database · a first-pass proposal kept unedited · the requirements quoted · the four-way gap check · the revised six-step flow with step 2 as six sub-screens and step 3 as three families · 48 tasks · **and section 11, the reusable analysis method itself**.

⚠ **Two things a later reader needs to know about it.** It was **read at version 2.79.24**; the repository moved to **2.89.1** before this CR was written, and every claim below that became a task was re-verified against 2.89.1 and still held — the rest of the document has not been re-read line by line. And it is a **private artifact on the author's account**: it opens for its owner and must be shared before anyone else can read it. If it is ever unreachable, the tasks below stand on their own — each names the file or the rule it acts on.

**Classification.** A CHANGE, not a defect. Nothing here is a misunderstanding of a signed rule being
re-filed as a requirement — every item is either a rule the product does not yet honour, or a surface the
design assumes and no screen provides.

### CR-051 · THE HARD RULE THAT APPLIES TO THIS CR AND THE TWO THAT FOLLOW

**PO ruling 2026-08-30, verbatim:** *"All UI screen should be confirm using real broswer testing and not just
based on test cases"*.

**Every task in this CR whose half is `Front` is DONE only when a render check opens the screen in a real
browser and reads what comes back.** Not when its test cases pass. The two are different claims and this
repo has paid for the difference more than once: jsdom renders no layout and no iframe content at all, so a
screen can hold seventeen green test cases and draw nothing a person can use.

The mechanism already exists and is not being invented here — `10-scripts/render-checks/` holds eight such
scripts (`cr049-bill-document.mjs`, `cr048-notifications-geometry.mjs`, `column-chooser-geometry.mjs` and
five more). A UI task in this CR adds one beside them, or extends one. **Rebuild before measuring:** a check
pointed at a stale `vite build` reports failure with total confidence and no hint that it is looking at the
wrong bytes.

This is hard-won law 6 promoted from a note to an acceptance condition. It applies to CR-051, CR-052 and
CR-053 without being restated in each.

### CR-051 · THE SECOND HARD RULE — BILLING LOGIC GOES THROUGH R1–R7, AND IS WIRED, NOT REBUILT

**PO instruction 2026-08-30, verbatim:** *"when you build billing logic ensueyou use r1 to r7 that we build
and wire it"*.

**This applies to CR-051, CR-052 and CR-053 without being restated in each**, exactly like the browser rule
above. It is the more consequential of the two, because the tempting shortcut is invisible in a diff.

#### The chain, as ruled — `apps/rating/resolution.py`, corrected by the PO on 2026-08-19

    R1   account -> unit -> PLAN VERSION in force on the service-period END date
    R2   plan version -> exactly one RATE SCHEDULE VERSION per service
    R3   meter connection size -> the SIZE ROW of each bound schedule
    R3b  METER MULTIPLIER -> billable QUANTITY            (quantity, BEFORE pricing)
    R4   plan -> CHARGE CODES matching service, class and size
    R5   PREMISES jurisdiction -> factor on base charges AND rates   (money, AFTER pricing)
    R6   account ENROLMENTS -> discounts, before taxes
    R7   taxes matching jurisdiction, services and class

⚠ **R3b AND R5 ARE TWO DIFFERENT FACTORS AND ARE NOT ADJACENT.** The meter multiplier scales the QUANTITY and
must be applied *before the tier boundaries are walked* — a ×10 register reading 62 is **620 kWh**, which
lands in tier 2, where 62 never leaves tier 1. The jurisdiction factor is money and applies after pricing.
Folding them back into one step re-opens a defect the PO personally corrected.

**It is a CHAIN, not a search.** Each step returns exactly one answer or refuses. There is no best match, no
fallback and no default anywhere in that module. Its nine typed refusals are the product: *"R3 — this size is
not priced"* is a sentence a utility acts on in a minute; the live path's equivalent silence is found in an
audit.

#### Where it actually stands — DEF-438, and the six-step cutover

**The chain is BUILT and has NO PRODUCTION CALLER.** That is `DEF-438`. The method for wiring it is already
ruled — decision log 2026-08-27, *"HOW R1–R7 GETS WIRED INTO BILLING — run both, compare, rule, then switch.
Never swap and hope."* Six steps, and the column headed *"what changes on a bill"* reads **nothing** for the
first four:

| # | Step | State |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Adapter** — map `gather_account`'s facts into the chain's dataclasses | ✅ done (`apps/billing/resolution_shadow.py`) |
| 2 | **Shadow** — run the chain beside the live path on every account | ✅ done |
| 3 | **Surface** the disagreements on the pre-commit screen, by step and by account | ✅ done (S31.2's pricing-shadow panel) |
| 4 | **Rule** each class of disagreement | ❌ **not started — the PO's call, not a lane's** |
| 5 | **Switch one STEP at a time** (R1, then R2, …), each only when its class is at zero | ❌ not started |
| 6 | **Delete `gather`'s narrowing half** for switched steps only, after a full billing cycle | ❌ not started |

⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-08-30 — the first version of this paragraph said "seven disagreement classes,
`DEF-1810` through `DEF-1816`". `DEF-1815` and `DEF-1816` DO NOT EXIST in the register**; the range was
written from memory rather than read, which is the failure this repo files as a stale claim. **What is
actually open is FOUR measured findings** — `DEF-1810` (R3's *"this size is not served"* refusal is
unreachable through any correct adapter), `DEF-1811` (the shadow cannot run on a single real account of any
tenant), `DEF-1812` (no meter multiplier crosses metering's billing seam, so R3b cannot be shadowed) and
`DEF-1813` (no billable asset count crosses the seam, so an unmetered quantity cannot be shadowed) — plus
`DEF-494` (*"the live path and the ruled path mean opposite things by 'a plan in force'"*). `DEF-493`,
`DEF-498` and `DEF-514` are **FIXED** and are named here only so a reader does not re-chase them.
**Step 4 is a PO agenda item, and it is the gate on everything after it.**

#### ⚠ WHAT NO LANE IN THESE THREE CRs MAY DO

1. **Add new narrowing logic to `apps/billing/gather.py`.** Every rule about *which* price applies belongs in
   the chain. A lane that answers a pricing question inside `gather` has built the eighth copy of a decision
   the chain already makes and widened the very gap step 6 exists to close.
2. **Price from a `ShadowOutcome`.** Its return value has never priced an invoice line and must not until its
   step is switched. A caller that prices from it has done the one thing the ruling forbids.
3. **Make a disagreement go away.** Stated in the ruling because it is the tempting shortcut: *"A lane that
   makes the disagreements go away has destroyed the evidence this job exists to produce, and has done it
   inside the one system where a wrong answer is irreversible (hard rule 4)."* Each class is RULED or it is
   not switched.
4. **Switch more than one step at a time.** *"Switching all seven at once makes every disagreement arrive in
   one diff with no way to attribute it."*

**So the shape of every billing task in these CRs is: read the fact from the chain where the chain already
answers, report the disagreement where it does not, and never invent a third path.**

### CR-051 · WHAT IS REVERSED, AND WHAT IS MERELY NOT BUILT

**One signed rule is not honoured today and this CR closes it.** `BR-BIL-051` makes phase 2 a BACKGROUND
batch with the clerk not held at the screen. `runs.calculate_run` executes INLINE and holds its caller until
every ready account has been drafted or broken. The endpoint says so honestly on every response
(`calculate_is_not_a_background_batch`). **No frozen B4/B5 figure is touched by any task below** — the
arithmetic is unchanged throughout; what changes is where it runs and what a clerk can see of it.

**Two things the code says are impossible are no longer impossible, and the reasons have expired.**
`apps/billing/api.py` states that a run-status poll would be *"a promise of asynchrony this deployment does
not keep (TD-17)"* and `core/jobs.py` states that *"the worker half is still unbuilt"*. Both predate
`CR-017` (2026-08-19): the job store is registered by `apps.tenancy`, a Celery worker runs in
`docker-compose`, `JOBS_EAGER=False` in production, and **seven job kinds are already registered across four
modules** — including all three stages of the premises import, in `apps/metering`. Billing registers none.
This CR makes billing the fifth caller of machinery already in daily use. Both stale sentences are corrected
by task 4 rather than left standing (hard-won law 1).

### CR-051 · MEASURED BEFORE PROPOSING — the numbers the tasks are sized against

* `POST /billing/runs/{id}/calculate` drafts every ready account inside the request. **There is no timing
  figure for a bill run of any size anywhere in this repo.** By contrast the premises import measured itself
  at 50,000 rows — extract 6.8s · transform 77.9s · validate 50.8s · dry-run 1.9s · load 101.5s — and set its
  5,000-row worker bar from those numbers rather than from an opinion. Task 21 does the same for the run.
* `GET /billing/runs/{id}/findings` re-runs the **whole prepare pass over every account in the cycle**, on a
  GET a clerk can refresh. It writes nothing, which makes it safe to reload and does nothing to make it fast.
* Gathering ONE account opens **23 named cross-module reads through 8 seams**; several are per SERVICE. At
  10,000 accounts that is upwards of 230,000 round trips before a single row is written.
  ⚠ **MEASURED 2026-08-31 (task 21, `DEF-2707`): the per-account count is right — 24.0 — and the SEAM count
  is not. There are TWENTY, not eight**, across four modules, and `10-scripts/cr051_run_benchmark.py --seams`
  names every one with its call count. The estimate is left standing above rather than rewritten, because a
  later reader needs to see what the CR was sized against and what it turned out to be.
* **No bulk write exists anywhere in `apps/billing`.** A 10,000-account run at eight lines each is 80,000
  individual inserts.
* `GET /billing/runs/{id}` **is not mounted** (verified on `2.89.1`), so a run cannot be re-opened at all.
* `runs.CalculatedRun.breaks` exists **only in memory** — there is no `bill_run_breaks` table (verified), so
  a clerk who navigates away loses the exception list while keeping the drafts.

**Each verified by reading the line that shows the behaviour, never by the absence of the fault** — the

**WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN FIVE ROWS.** Task 12 — *"the wizard stops waiting: 'Working — 412 of 1,124'"*
— is recorded as shipped and **depends on task 10**. So this document described a screen reading a
progress figure that, by its own account, nothing wrote. A reader checking whether the wizard could
possibly work would have concluded it could not.

⚠ **THIS IS THE SAME FAILURE AS THE 34 STALE DEFECT ROWS CLOSED THE SAME DAY, IN THE OTHER REGISTER.**
Work finishes, the code is correct, and the record is not updated — so every count taken from the record
is wrong, and the direction of the error is always the same: **the repo looks further behind than it is.**
Both places we track state produced it on the same day, which makes it a process fault rather than two
lapses. The build process already names the fix — write-back is *"a continuous obligation, not a step"*,
and *"before the thing that depends on it, never 'at the end'"* — and the thing that depends on a shipped
row is the next person's count.

**No gate can catch this and it should not be pretended one could.** A gate that demanded a shipped row
for every task would be satisfied by writing the row, not by doing the work; the honest instrument is the
one used here — check the record against the code when the number is going to be reported to somebody.

**So the task needed neither of the two things it offered.** It was written when the route was mounted and
called by nothing — the built-not-wired shape hard-won law 2 exists for — and a sibling CR wired it while
this one was looking elsewhere. **Withdrawing it would have been wrong**; it is closed by being done.

⚠ **SEVENTH UNRECORDED COMPLETION IN ONE DAY, AND THE FIRST ACROSS TWO CRs.** The six before it were work
landing inside its own CR and the record not moving. This one is different and worse to spot: the work was
recorded — in `CR-053`. **Nothing reads one CR's record while counting another's**, so a task can be
finished, correctly written up, and still count as outstanding forever. It was found only by grepping the
frontend for a caller while assembling a status table for the PO, which is the same instrument that found
the other six.

**With this, CR-051 is 30 of 30.**

### CR-051 · WHAT IS NOT A TASK

* **Splitting the run across multiple workers.** Already *possible* — accounts are independent and share
  nothing — so the option does not expire. Tasks 22 and 23 may well make it unnecessary at 25,000. Left
  alone deliberately, and it should not be started before task 21 says otherwise.
* **The clerk's exception list does not scale by being made faster.** A run of 1,000 with six breaks is a
  morning; the same failure rate at 25,000 is 150 accounts to work through before anything issues.
  Throughput on the machine is not throughput on the person. Bulk decisions by reason are already built;
  this is a note for whoever sizes W4, not a task.
* **Documentation to correct:** `EP-BIL-01`'s warning about the due date is stale — the clerk's typed date
  has taken precedence since 23 August. Task 4 covers the two worker sentences; this one is separate.
* **For the Product Owner:** the authorisation record has an export and deliberately no screen (`OQ-112`
  closed, option B). If audits become routine, that ruling is worth revisiting — raised, not assumed.

Three questions. **Task 21 answered the first one and only the first one**, and the honest way to

**MEASURED — task 21, real PostgreSQL 16, seeded demo tenant, `10-scripts/cr051_run_benchmark.py`,
published at `937782b8`:**

⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-08-31 (`DEF-2717`) — THE FIGURES IN THE TABLE BELOW WERE MEASURED WITH
ROW-LEVEL SECURITY BYPASSED.** The benchmark's database role had been made `SUPERUSER` to
create a database, and a superuser is exempt from RLS unconditionally — `FORCE ROW LEVEL
SECURITY` included — so **no tenant predicate was evaluated in any of these runs**. Nothing
in the numbers shows it: the tables still reported `relrowsecurity = t` and
`relforcerowsecurity = t`, the policies still existed, and every query returned plausible
rows. **The figures are kept, not deleted, because the difference IS a result:** with the
predicate enforced the same work measures about **172 ms per account** against the **136 /
137 / 141 ms** below — roughly **26% more** — and it stays LINEAR, so the conclusions drawn
here about sharding and about the prepare pass being 84% of the cost are unchanged. Read
every row below as *RLS-bypassed*; the re-measurement at 100 / 1,000 / 5,000 / 10,000 in
BOTH worlds is the benchmark lane's. The application now refuses to boot in production on
such a role (`06-backend/core/rls_guard.py`, `G56`), and `DEF-2760` records that the repo
does not say which role any deployment actually uses.

| accounts | prepare | calculate | total | ms/account | invoice lines | SQL statements |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 11.8s | 1.5s | 13.3s | 136 | 413 | 9,493 |
| 1,000 | 118.4s | 16.1s | 134.5s | 137 | 4,123 | 95,146 |
| 10,000 | 1,168.9s | 214.6s | **1,383.5s ≈ 23 minutes** | 141 | 41,245 | 951,978 |

Task 22's seam memo then took 1,000 accounts from 137 to **111 ms an account** and 95,146
statements to 71,738. **It is linear across a hundredfold range**, so ten thousand bills is
about **eighteen and a half minutes** and there is no cliff. That is the first question, answered.

**NOT MEASURED, AND EACH IS A TASK ABOVE:**

* **5,000 was never run.** 100, 1,000 and 10,000 were. Linearity makes ~9 minutes the expectation
  and an expectation is not a measurement — the PO named 5,000 first (task 26).
* **Reads and writes were never separated.** 951,978 is a TOTAL. Which of them are SELECTs a read
  replica could one day take, and which are INSERTs that must hit the primary, is exactly the
  engineering question asked and the benchmark does not answer it (task 26).
* **Two runs have never been run at the same time.** Every figure above is one tenant, alone, on
  an idle database (task 27).
* **Nothing has ever timed a screen while a run is in flight** — which is the actual question
  *"will it hamper live system performance"*, and the only one of the three that a customer feels
  (task 28).

**WHAT THE ARCHITECTURE ALREADY DETERMINES, read out of `docker-compose.yml` and
`config/settings/base.py` rather than assumed** — this is not the answer, it is what the
measurement will be measuring:

* The worker is **its own container**, separate from the three gunicorn processes. So a bill run
  does not steal a web worker, and ten utilities cannot make the site stop answering.
* **`--concurrency 2`.** Ten utilities firing at once do not run ten at once; **two run and eight
  queue.** At 111 ms an account, ten runs of 10,000 is 11,100 seconds of worker time over two
  slots — **about an hour and a half before the last utility's bills exist** (derived from task
  21's figure, not measured).
* **There is ONE queue and no routing.** `task_routes` is configured nowhere. A CSV export, a
  staged import and a customer's outbound notice sit in the same line as a 23-minute bill run,
  behind `CELERY_WORKER_PREFETCH_MULTIPLIER = 1`. **This, not CPU, is the plausible way a bill run
  hurts someone who is waiting** — and it is task 29.
* **One PostgreSQL, shared.** Two concurrent runs are ~1.9 million statements against the same
  database the clerk's screens read. That is where task 28 will find its answer if there is one.
* **Nothing bounds a run.** No `CELERY_TASK_TIME_LIMIT`, no account ceiling. A run that goes wrong
  at 100,000 accounts runs until it finishes (task 30).

**WHY THESE SIT IN CR-051 AND NOT IN CR-052/053/054.** The run is CR-051's; the other three change
what one bill *contains* (CR-052), how the list *reads* (CR-053) and how reads *arrive* (CR-054),
and none of them adds a per-account pass to the run. **The rule they inherit is one line, and it
is the reason this section is cross-referenced from all three:** anything that adds a query per
account to the bill run is measured against task 21's published ms-per-account before it merges,
because at 10,000 accounts one extra query per account is **10,000 more statements** and the
figures above are what makes that visible.

**WHAT WOULD MAKE TASK 29 UNNECESSARY, stated so it is not built reflexively.** If task 28 shows a
clerk's screens unchanged while ten runs are queued, then one queue is fine and task 29 is
withdrawn with that measurement quoted. CR-051 already refuses to split the run across workers
before task 21 said so; this is the same discipline applied to the queue.

bypasses RLS completely, `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` included, while the tables
still report the policies as present (`DEF-2717`). **Re-measured with RLS
enforced, the run costs about a quarter more:**

| 1,000 | 979 | 152.3s | 16.3s | **168.6s** | 172 | 4,123 | 108,852 |
| **5,000** | 4,895 | 781.6s | 108.3s | **889.9s** | 182 | 20,622 | 544,459 |
| 10,000 | 9,791 | 1,899.6s | 247.9s | **2,147.4s** | 219 | 41,245 | 1,089,052 |

**The last two rows were taken while other lanes were using the same four cores
(load 5–7), and the per-account statement count is what says so:** it is 111 at
every size, dead flat, while the wall clock drifts from 172 to 219 ms. A query
count does not care what else the machine is doing; a wall clock does. The
benchmark now records the load average beside every figure.

**TASK 26 — READS AND WRITES, SEPARATED, WHICH IS WHAT THE PO ACTUALLY ASKED.**
*"how many read and writes ahppens"* cannot be answered by a total. Per account:

| accounts | SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE | savepoint/other | rows written |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 99.9 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 1.0 | 6.1 | 6.2 |
| 1,000 | 100.2 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 1.0 | 6.1 | 6.2 |
| 5,000 | 100.2 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 1.0 | 6.1 | 6.2 |
| 10,000 | 100.3 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 1.0 | 6.1 | 6.2 |

**One bill costs 100 reads and 5 writes, and that does not move across a
hundredfold range.** As totals, a 10,000-account run is 981,560 SELECT · 19,373
INSERT · 19,164 UPDATE · 9,582 DELETE and **60,618 rows written** — **98% of the
statements are reads**, so this is a reading job with a small write at the end
of each customer rather than a write-heavy batch. That is the answer to whether
a read replica could one day carry it, and it is a fact rather than an opinion.

Counted at the application boundary (Django's `connection.execute_wrapper`),
which is what the run SENT; `rows written` is the driver's own rowcount, so a
`bulk_create` of eight invoice lines is ONE statement and EIGHT rows.

**TASK 30 — THE LARGEST RUN THIS DEPLOYMENT ACCEPTS IS 25,000 ACCOUNTS.** Three
facts, each measured or signed: `CLAUDE.md`'s first line puts the market at
utilities **under 3,000 connections**, so a 100,000-account run is a mis-scoped
cycle rather than a large customer; at ~170 ms an account, 3,000 accounts is
**8 minutes** and 25,000 is **70**; and the worker runs at `--concurrency 2`, so
a 70-minute run holds **half the background capacity** for over an hour. 25,000
is eight times the largest utility the product is for.

**Above it the run refuses AT THE DOOR, before anything is drafted**, naming the
count, the ceiling and the two ways a run is legitimately made smaller — fewer
services on the run, or one cycle at a time, both of which this product already
has. `runs.scope_account_count` sizes a run in **two queries**;
`BILLING_MAX_ACCOUNTS_PER_RUN` overrides the ceiling and `0` switches it off.

below. The paragraph that follows is left standing because it is the record of what
was true when it was written, and because `DEF-2829` is about a count that disagreed
with exactly this sentence.**

`CELERY_TASK_TIME_LIMIT` and no soft limit, and both live in
`config/settings/base.py`, which is not this lane's file. **And `DEF-2720`: a
clerk does not see the ceiling's reason** — it travels in `params.detail`, which
BR-SHL-020 r2 keeps off the screen deliberately, so the numbers reach the log
and the audit row while the screen says *"This billing run can't go ahead as

⚠ **AND THE RULING THAT SOUNDS LIKE "DO NOT TOUCH IT" DOES NOT SAY THAT.** The

### CR-051 · WHAT HAS SHIPPED — TASKS 27, 28 AND 29 (2026-08-31)

**THE PO'S THIRD QUESTION, MEASURED AT LAST:** *"what if we get 10 utilities firing
billing at the same time, will it hamper live system performance"*. Ten whole
utilities were provisioned through the REAL signup path — each with its own
reference data, plans, premises, units, meters and cycle, ~200 billable accounts,
and **no row of any kind shared or copied across tenants**, because a
cross-tenant foreign key would be hard rule 1 broken in the schema itself. Their
bill runs were fired at one PostgreSQL 16 with row-level security enforced;
**180 of each utility's 200 accounts were ready to bill in the measured window**,
so every figure below is the same work.

**FIRST, THE ANSWER THAT DOES NOT DEPEND ON THE MACHINE, and it is the important
one: THE DATABASE NEVER MADE THEM WAIT.**

| wave | runs | slots | peak connections | ungranted locks | longest lock wait | wait events sampled |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 utility | 1 | 1 | 3 | **0** | none observed | `IO/WALSync` 4 · `Client/ClientRead` 1 |
| 2 utilities | 2 | 2 | 3 | **0** | none observed | `IO/WALSync` 8 · `Client/ClientRead` 1 |
| 5 utilities at once | 5 | 5 | 7 | **0** | none observed | `IO/WALSync` 14 · `LWLock/WALWrite` 6 · `LWLock/LockManager` 2 |
| 5 through the queue | 5 | 2 | 3 | **0** | none observed | `IO/WALSync` 2 |
| 10 utilities at once | 10 | 10 | 12 | **0** | none observed | `IO/WALSync` 9 · `Client/ClientRead` 8 · `LWLock/LockManager` 3 |
| 10 through the queue | 10 | 2 | 4 | **0** | none observed | `IO/WALSync` 5 · `LWLock/WALWrite` 3 · `Client/ClientRead` 2 · `LWLock/LockManager` 2 |

Sampled every 250 ms on a connection of the parent's own; a lock taken and
released between two samples is invisible, and the report says so rather than
leaving a reader to assume otherwise. What it CAN state is that at 124 to 630
samples per wave, **no ungranted lock was ever observed and no `Lock/*` wait
event ever appeared** — the two things a run blocking another run would produce.
The `LWLock/*` entries at the biggest waves are the lightweight latches inside
PostgreSQL's own lock manager and WAL writer, three samples out of 630; they are
what a busy server looks like, not what a blocked one looks like.

**Zero ungranted locks at every wave, no `Lock/*` wait event ever sampled, and one
connection per run.** The only wait events seen anywhere were `IO/WALSync` and
`Client/ClientRead` — a write being flushed, and the server waiting for the
application to say something. **Concurrent bill runs do not block one another in
PostgreSQL**, and that is a property of how the run is built: BR-BIL-052 gives
every account its own short transaction, so nothing holds a lock across accounts,
and every tenant writes to rows only it can see.

**WHAT THEY DO COMPETE FOR IS CPU, AND THE FIGURES SAY SO:**

| how they were run | utilities | worker slots | each run took | per account | × one run alone | last utility's bills exist after | TOTAL worker-seconds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| alone (the baseline) | 1 | 1 | 31.9s | 177 ms | 1.00× | 32.0s | 31.9 |
| all at once | 2 | 2 | 53.5s | 297 ms | 1.68× | 53.6s | 103.5 |
| all at once | 5 | 5 | 122.7s | 682 ms | **3.85×** | 123.5s | 611.5 |
| all at once | 10 | 10 | 166.3s | 924 ms | **5.22×** | 167.6s | **1,663.9** |
| **through the queue** | 5 | **2** | 29.9s | 166 ms | **0.94×** | **91.5s** | 154.1 |
| **through the queue** | 10 | **2** | 26.2s | 145 ms | **0.82×** | **131.9s** | **261.8** |

180 ready accounts in every run, so every row is the same work. Medians across
the runs in each wave; the slowest run in a wave was never more than 4% off the
median, so no utility was singled out.

⚠ **READ THOSE RATIOS AS UPPER BOUNDS AND NOT AS THE PRODUCT'S BEHAVIOUR.** This
machine has **four cores** and was carrying **load 7 to 10 from five other build
lanes** before a single bill run started, so the runs were competing with each
other AND with everything else. That is why the core count and the load average
are printed beside every wave. The database evidence above does not have this
problem: an ungranted-lock count does not care what else the machine is doing.

**AND THE MOST USEFUL RESULT OF THE WHOLE TASK IS THE ONE NOBODY EXPECTED:
`--concurrency 2` IS NOT A LIMITATION HERE, IT IS A PROTECTION.** The five and
ten utility sets were each run twice — once fired all at once, once through the
two worker slots the deployment actually has:

| ten utilities | each run | per account | last utility's bills exist after | total worker-seconds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **all ten at once** | 166.3s | 924 ms | 167.6s | **1,663.9** |
| **through 2 slots** | 26.2s | 145 ms | **131.9s** | **261.8** |

**Every run went SIX TIMES faster through the queue, everybody was finished
sooner, and the same 1,800 bills cost a SIXTH of the machine time** — 261.8
worker-seconds against 1,663.9. A run in a slot ran at 145 ms an account, which
is the solo rate; nothing at all was lost to being queued. The five-utility pair
says the same thing more quietly: 166 ms and 91.5s through the queue against 682
ms and 123.5s fired at once.

**Firing ten runs at four cores does not do the work ten times faster. It does
the same work while making every one of them slow, and burns six times the CPU
doing it** — that gap is thrashing, not billing. The queue is what stops it.

**So the CR's derived figure — *"ten runs of 10,000 at 111 ms is 11,100 seconds
of worker time over two slots, about an hour and a half"* — is CONFIRMED in
shape, and the measurement lets it be restated with real numbers.** Ten runs of
10,000 accounts at the measured 145 ms an account is 14,500 worker-seconds over
two slots ≈ **two hours** before the last utility's bills exist, with each
utility's own run taking about **twenty-four minutes**. Nothing degrades; the
work is serialised two at a time and each piece runs at full speed.

**TASK 28 — WHAT A CLERK IN A DIFFERENT UTILITY FEELS WHILE ALL OF THAT HAPPENS.**
Four screens were timed in a **bystander** tenant — one not firing a run at all,
which is the question a shared deployment actually poses — idle, then during ten
concurrent runs, then **idle again once the load had drained**. The third set is
not a formality: on a machine five lanes share, an idle-then-loaded pair taken
minutes apart can be a measurement of the machine rather than of the bill run, and
two idle sets bracketing the loaded one are what settles that.

**TWO LOADS WERE MEASURED, AND THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM IS THE WHOLE
VERDICT.** `docker-compose.yml` runs the worker at `--concurrency 2`, so this
deployment **cannot** have ten bill runs executing at once — two run and the
rest queue, which is exactly what task 27 measured. So:

* **the STRESS case, ten runs executing simultaneously** — a state this
  deployment cannot reach, worth knowing as a ceiling;
* **the REALISTIC case, two runs executing** — what a clerk will actually be
  working alongside when ten utilities all press the button, and the case that
  decides task 29.

Reporting only the first would answer a question nobody asked; reporting only
the second would hide the shape of the risk.

**The load is SUSTAINED in both** — a supervisor relaunches any run that
finishes, so the screens measured last are under the same conditions as the
screens measured first. In the ten-run case that meant **50 runs were started to
keep 10 in flight**. The paragraph after the tables says why that matters more
than it sounds.

**THE STRESS CASE — ten bill runs executing for the whole measurement**, in a
utility that is firing none of them:

| screen | idle p50 | idle p95 | under load p50 | under load p95 | worst click | p95 × |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| accounts list, one page of 50 | 582.0 ms | 638.0 ms | 3,553.0 ms | **5,464.2 ms** | 5,989.9 ms | **8.6×** |
| one account's detail | 42.5 ms | 49.0 ms | 333.7 ms | **481.3 ms** | 1,208.4 ms | **9.8×** |
| one bill with its lines | 17.8 ms | 21.2 ms | 136.0 ms | **239.9 ms** | 262.5 ms | **11.3×** |
| the run's findings screen | 6,020.2 ms | 6,185.4 ms | 31,528.0 ms | **34,855.5 ms** | 34,855.5 ms | **5.6×** |

**THE REALISTIC CASE — two bill runs, which is the worker's own concurrency and
therefore the most this deployment can execute at once:**

| screen | idle p50 | idle p95 | under load p50 | under load p95 | worst click | p95 × |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| accounts list, one page of 50 | 531.1 ms | 605.8 ms | 2,183.0 ms | **2,868.9 ms** | 3,288.0 ms | **4.7×** |
| one account's detail | 40.0 ms | 44.0 ms | 184.0 ms | **228.3 ms** | 508.8 ms | **5.2×** |
| one bill with its lines | 17.1 ms | 18.1 ms | 82.4 ms | **97.2 ms** | 107.6 ms | **5.4×** |
| the run's findings screen | 6,255.6 ms | 6,257.0 ms | 18,877.5 ms | **20,588.6 ms** | 20,588.6 ms | **3.3×** |

**AND THE STRESS CASE IS UNAMBIGUOUS: EVERY SCREEN IS FIVE TO ELEVEN TIMES
SLOWER, AND THE ACCOUNTS LIST GOES FROM 0.6 SECONDS TO 5.5.** A clerk does not
need a threshold to notice that; a bill takes a quarter of a second where it
took a fiftieth, and the findings screen goes from six seconds to
thirty-five.

⚠ **THIS IS ALSO THE MEASUREMENT THAT THE BURST RUN GOT WRONG, AND THE
DIFFERENCE IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT FOR SUSTAINING A LOAD.** The burst run reported
`1.03×`, `1.01×` and `0.98×` for three of these four screens. Sustained, the same
three are **9.8×, 11.3× and 5.6×**. Had the first run been trusted, this lane
would have reported *"a clerk feels nothing"* and withdrawn task 29 on a
measurement that had stopped measuring half way through.

**THE TWO IDLE SETS BRACKET EACH LOADED ONE, AND THEY ARE THE CHECK THAT SAYS
WHETHER THE MIDDLE FIGURE CAN BE ATTRIBUTED AT ALL. THEY DID THEIR JOB, AND THEY
DID NOT ANSWER THE SAME WAY IN BOTH RUNS — WHICH IS THE POINT OF HAVING THEM.**

* **Stress case: the two idle sets agree within 9% on every screen** — accounts
  list p95 638.0 → 686.0 ms (1.08×), account detail 49.0 → 47.7 (0.97×), one
  bill 21.2 → 19.4 (0.91×), findings 6,185.4 → 5,922.3 (0.96×). The machine did
  not move, so the **5× to 11×** in the middle belongs to the bill runs.
* **Realistic case: the second idle set is HIGHER than the first** — list p95
  605.8 → 941.9 ms (1.55×), detail 44.0 → 86.0 (1.95×), bill 18.1 → 29.2
  (1.61×), findings unchanged (0.96×). Another lane's work arrived on these
  cores during the measurement. **So the honest reading of the two-run figures
  is a range, not a point: the accounts list's loaded p95 of 2,868.9 ms is
  4.7× the first idle set and 3.0× the second.** Both are far larger than the
  1.55× the machine itself drifted, so the effect is real — but the multiple is
  **about three to five times**, not exactly 4.7.

**That distinction is only available because the second idle set was taken.** A
run reporting `4.74×` with no bracket would have looked identical and been
wrong by a third.

⚠ **THE FIRST RUN OF TASK 28 MEASURED THREE OF ITS FOUR SCREENS AGAINST A
MACHINE THAT HAD ALREADY GONE QUIET, AND ITS OWN TABLE STILL SAID "UNDER LOAD".**
This is recorded rather than quietly discarded, because it is the same class of
fault as a guard that cannot fail — a measurement reported with full confidence
over conditions that had ended.

**What happened.** Ten bill runs fired at once drain in about 167 seconds. The
under-load pass times four screens in order and the FIRST of them, the accounts
list at 200 samples and ~580 ms each, takes **116 seconds on its own**. By the
time the pass reached the account detail, the bill and the findings screen, most
or all of the ten runs had finished. Their "×" columns compare a quiet machine
with a quiet machine.

**What the burst run therefore does and does not establish:**

| screen | measured under real load? | reading |
|---|---|---|
| accounts list | **yes** — it was first | p95 **639 ms → 3,378 ms, 5.28×**, max **5.2s** |
| one account's detail | no | 1.03× — not evidence |
| one bill | no | 1.01× — not evidence |
| the findings screen | no | 0.98× — not evidence |

**The one screen that WAS under load moved five-fold at the tail** — and note the
shape, because it is the shape that matters to a person: **p50 barely moved
(562 → 580 ms, 1.03×) while p95 went to 3.4 seconds and the worst click took
5.2.** Most clicks were fine. About one in twenty was not, and a clerk
experiences that as the system "sticking" at random.

**THE FIX IS IN THE HARNESS, NOT IN THE WRITE-UP.** `--sustain` (now the
default) keeps N runs in flight for the WHOLE measurement by relaunching any
that finish, so every screen is timed under the same conditions. The burst
figures above are kept as what they are — one valid row and three that were
never measured.

**TASK 28's ANSWER IS YES — A CLERK WAITS — AND THE THRESHOLD WAS WRITTEN DOWN
BEFORE THE NUMBERS ARRIVED so it could not be fitted to them.** A clerk is said
to wait when a screen's p95 **crosses one second** having been under it idle, or
when its p95 **more than doubles**: the first because a second is where a person
stops feeling the machine is instant, the second because a doubling at 200 ms
today is a doubling at 2 seconds when the utility is ten times bigger.

**IN THE REALISTIC CASE — two runs, which is all this deployment can execute —
every screen fails both tests.** The accounts list goes from **0.6 seconds to
2.9** at p95 and its worst click takes **3.3 seconds**; one account's detail
goes from 44 ms to 228; one bill from 18 ms to 97; the findings screen from six
seconds to twenty. In the stress case it is worse again — the list reaches
**5.5 seconds** and the findings screen **thirty-five**.

⚠ **AND THE CAUSE IS NOT THE DATABASE, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS ACTIONABLE.**
Task 27 sampled `pg_locks` and `pg_stat_activity` 124–630 times per wave and saw
**zero ungranted locks and no `Lock/*` wait event, ever**. The runs and the
screens are competing for **CPU**, and `docker-compose.yml` puts the worker and
the three gunicorn processes on the same host with **no CPU limit on any
service** — `deploy.resources` appears nowhere in the file. So on a small host,
which is what a utility under 3,000 connections gets, a `--concurrency 2` worker
can take most of the machine and the clerk gets what is left. That is exactly
the shape measured.

⚠ **HOW MUCH OF THE RATIO IS THE BUILD MACHINE, STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN.**
These four cores were carrying **load 5 to 8 from five other build lanes** before
a bill run started, so the ratios are UPPER BOUNDS: a dedicated host with two
cores free for the web tier would show less. What is NOT an artefact is the
direction and the mechanism — no lock waits, CPU-bound, no CPU limits — and the
two idle sets bracketing each loaded set are what rule out the machine simply
having moved.

**TASK 29 — ITS TRIGGER FIRED, AND THE THING IT NAMES WOULD NOT FIX WHAT WAS
MEASURED. IT IS NOT BUILT, AND THAT IS A DECISION WITH ITS REASONING, NOT A
DEFERRAL.**

⚠ **SUPERSEDED THE SAME DAY BY PO RULING — TASK 29 IS BUILT. READ THIS BEFORE THE
PARAGRAPHS BELOW, WHICH ARE KEPT VERBATIM AS THE RECORD OF AN ARGUMENT THAT WAS
HALF RIGHT.** The PO ruled on 2026-08-31: *"we will ahve to create named worker
for billing - eventually we should able to scale these works on the fly itf
required; but billing will need its own named workers - otherwise it will slow
down the system"*. **What survives of the reasoning below:** a second queue
genuinely creates no CPU core, and the runs genuinely never block one another in
PostgreSQL — both measured, both still true. **What it got wrong is what the
queue is FOR.** It is not an alternative to the CPU cap this section's own remedy
list puts first; it is the thing that makes that cap AIMABLE. With one unrouted
queue carrying bill runs, CSV exports, staged imports and customers' notices,
capping the worker caps the notices too and scaling for billing scales
everything. See the decision log of this date and the shipped section
*"TASK 29, BILLING'S OWN NAMED WORKER"* below.

The CR's condition is *"give the bill run its own queue **if task 28 says a
clerk waits**"*, and task 28 says a clerk waits. So the trigger is met and this
section does not pretend otherwise. But the task's own sentence says what the
queue is FOR — *"today there is one queue and two worker slots, so a 23-minute
run sits in front of every export, import and notice"* — and that is an
**ORDERING** problem. What task 28 measured is a **CAPACITY** problem: the runs
and the web tier are competing for CPU on one host.

**A SECOND QUEUE DOES NOT CREATE A CORE.** Routing bill runs to their own queue
changes which job goes next; it does not change how much CPU the machine has.
Worse, the usual way to give a queue its own queue is to give it **its own
worker**, which would put MORE concurrent runs on the same cores and make every
figure in the table above larger. Building it in response to this measurement
would be the exact thing CR-051 warns against in its own words: *"Building a
second queue on a guess is how a deployment acquires an operational component
nobody can say the purpose of."*

**WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY FIX THE MEASURED PROBLEM, in the order a deployment should
try them, each with the figure it is aimed at:**

1. **Give the worker a CPU limit.** `deploy.resources` appears **nowhere** in
   `docker-compose.yml`, so nothing stops the worker taking the machine. Capping
   it at, say, half the host makes a 10,000-account run take proportionally
   longer — from about **24 minutes to 48** at the measured 145 ms an account —
   and leaves the clerk's screens their share. **That is the trade a utility
   would choose**, because a bill run finishing at 3 a.m. instead of 2:30 costs
   nobody anything and a clerk waiting three seconds per click costs them all
   morning.
2. **Or run the worker somewhere else.** Same effect, more money.
3. **`--concurrency 1` instead of 2** halves the worker's demand at the cost of
   doubling the drain time for a queue of runs — task 27 measured that drain
   directly (10 runs through 2 slots: **131.9s**; the same work through one slot
   would be about **262s**).

**NONE OF THOSE THREE IS A CODE CHANGE IN `apps/billing/**`, WHICH IS THIS
LANE'S SCOPE**, and none is a queue. They are deployment settings in
`docker-compose.yml` and `config/settings/base.py`. So this lane reports the
measurement and the remedies and builds none of them, rather than shipping a
queue whose purpose the measurement does not support.

**WHAT IS STILL TRUE AND WAS NOT MEASURED HERE**, said so it is not read as
answered: the ordering problem task 29's sentence describes is real. A CSV
export or a customer's outbound notice enqueued behind a 24-minute bill run does
wait for it, at `CELERY_WORKER_PREFETCH_MULTIPLIER = 1` with one queue. **That
is a different claim from "the site got slower", it costs a different fix, and
it deserves its own measurement** — time a small job enqueued behind a running
bill run — before anybody builds routing for it.

AN OBSERVATION TASK 28 MADE THAT IS NOT ABOUT CONCURRENCY AT ALL, recorded
because it was measured and it would otherwise be lost.

**The accounts list takes 562 ms for SEVENTY-THREE accounts, on a completely
idle system.** That is the screen a clerk opens first every morning, one page of
fifty rows, and it is over half a second before anything else is happening:

    accounts list (filtered)   p50 562.2 ms · p95 639.4 ms · max 752.2 ms
    one account's detail       p50  43.6 ms · p95  50.3 ms
    one bill                   p50  17.5 ms · p95  20.7 ms

**The other two screens are twelve and thirty times faster on the same database
in the same second**, so this is not the machine and it is not the tenant
predicate: a single account reads in 44 ms and a whole bill with its lines reads
in 18 ms, while a page of fifty accounts takes 562. At 7.7 ms per account it has
the shape of a per-row read rather than a page.

**IT IS NOT THIS LANE'S TO FIX** — `apps/customers/selectors.account_list` is
the customers module's, and this lane owns `apps/billing/**`. It is recorded
here, and in the defect register, because it was measured rather than guessed
and because it will get worse in exactly the way the bill run does not: the run
costs a flat 86 statements per account at every size, and a screen that costs a
query per row costs fifty of them per page for ever.

**WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IN ONE COMMAND**, for whoever picks it up: count the SQL
statements one `account_list` call sends, the way `cr051_run_benchmark.py` does
with `connection.execute_wrapper`. If the count moves with the page size, it is
an N+1 and a `select_related` fixes it; if it does not, the time is inside one
query and the plan is the thing to read.

---


### CR-051 · WHAT HAS SHIPPED — TASK 29, BILLING'S OWN NAMED WORKER (2026-08-31)

**THE TASK WAS REPORTED NOT-BUILT THIS MORNING AND IS BUILT THIS AFTERNOON, and the two are not a
contradiction — the PO ruled in between.** The section above (*"TASKS 27, 28 AND 29"*) declined to build a
second queue on the argument that concurrent bill runs never block one another in PostgreSQL, so *"a second
queue does not create a core"*. **That argument was right about the mechanism and wrong about what the
mechanism is for.** The decision log of this date carries the ruling and the correction; the sentence the
earlier reasoning was missing is this one: **a CPU cap cannot be aimed at a queue that has no name.** One
unrouted queue carried bill runs, CSV exports, staged imports and customers' outbound notices through the
same two worker slots, so capping the worker capped the notices too and scaling for billing scaled
everything.

**WHAT A PERSON WOULD NOTICE, in one paragraph.** Billing's three background jobs — work out the bills,
check what we found, and issue them — now go to a queue of their own, drained by a worker of its own, and
that worker is allowed **one processor's worth of the machine**. Everything else the product does in the
background stays where it was, uncapped and untouched. Two numbers in `docker-compose.yml` — how much
machine billing may take, and how many billing workers there are — can now be changed by whoever runs the
installation, **without touching code and without affecting any other kind of background work**. That last
clause is the whole deliverable.

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WIRED**, so the next lane does not have to grep for it:

| half | where | what it says |
|---|---|---|
| routing | `06-backend/apps/billing/run_jobs.py` | `BILLING_QUEUE = "billing"`, and all three kinds registered to it in `register()` |
| routing | `06-backend/core/jobs.py` | a kind→queue registry (`set_job_queue` / `job_queue`) beside the handler registry |
| routing | `06-backend/config/celery_routes.py` | the router Celery consults; reads the kind out of the message |
| routing | `06-backend/config/settings/base.py` | `CELERY_TASK_ROUTES` (configured **nowhere** before today) + an explicit default queue |
| the message | `06-backend/apps/tenancy/tasks.py` | the kind travels as a **keyword**, so the router can see it |
| consumer | `docker-compose.yml` → `celery-billing` | `-Q billing`, `entrypoint: []`, `CMD-SHELL` + `$(hostname)`, `cpus: "1.0"`, `replicas: 1` |
| the split | `docker-compose.yml` → `celery` | `-Q celery` — it no longer drains billing |
| both halves | `10-scripts/gates/g59_billing_queue_split.py` | fails if either half is missing, or if beat is not at one replica |

**THE ROUTING IS A ROUTER FUNCTION, NOT A `{task name: queue}` DICT, AND IT HAD TO BE.** This deployment
runs ONE Celery task for EVERY job kind — `apps/tenancy/tasks.py` explains why in its own docstring — so a
name-keyed dictionary cannot tell a bill run from a CSV export. The router reads the KIND out of the message
and asks the registry each module fills in its own `AppConfig.ready()`.

**A REGRESSION THIS CHANGE WOULD HAVE INTRODUCED, FIXED IN THE SAME COMMIT.** `dispatch_is_ready()` asked
Celery's `control.ping`, which is a **broadcast**: with one queue that answered *"will my job run"*, and with
two it does not. A healthy exports worker answers while the `billing` queue has no consumer, and the clerk is
told the run is under way while it rests `queued` for ever — DEF-320 rebuilt by the change meant to prevent a
different harm. The probe now asks `active_queues()` about a NAMED queue, and its cache is keyed by queue.

**THE PROOF OWED WAS A RE-MEASUREMENT AND IT WAS RUN, NOT ASSUMED.** `10-scripts/cr051_billing_worker_cap.py`
re-runs task 28's screen timings five times in one pass — idle, loaded with no CPU limit, idle, loaded under
the cap, idle — with the load **sustained** throughout (a supervisor relaunches any run that finishes, which
is the fix task 28 had to make after its first run timed three of four screens against a machine that had
gone quiet). The cap is applied with the same kernel mechanism Docker uses for `deploy.resources.limits.cpus`
— a cgroup with `cpu.cfs_quota_us = cpus × cpu.cfs_period_us` — so it is the limit itself under test and not
a stand-in, and the script reports the kernel's own throttle count so a quota nobody joined cannot pass for
one that bit.

**THE RE-MEASUREMENT, on the same `sbh_cr051perf` database task 28 used, timing the same bystander
(`brazosbend`, which fires no run of its own), under the same two concurrent runs `--concurrency 2` can
actually execute.** p95 in milliseconds. **Read the three idle columns first** — they are the bracket, and
the size of their disagreement is the size of the doubt in everything else.

| screen | idle ① | **2 runs, NO cap** | idle ② | **2 runs, CAPPED at 1.0 CPU** | idle ③ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| accounts list, one page of 50 | 1,480.8 | **4,125.6** | 1,078.6 | **1,268.5** | 882.5 |
| one account's detail | 99.9 | **344.0** | 45.8 | **93.3** | 85.2 |
| one bill with its lines | 40.6 | **163.8** | 21.5 | **38.1** | 39.7 |
| the run's findings screen | 10,158.8 | **22,231.9** | 6,333.8 | **8,828.9** | 7,679.1 |

**EACH LOADED SET AGAINST THE MEAN OF THE TWO IDLE SETS TAKEN EITHER SIDE OF IT** — uncapped against
idle ①+②, capped against idle ②+③. That is the only fair arithmetic here, and the reason is in the table
above: the machine's own foreign load fell during the run (the accounts list idled at 1,480.8, then 1,078.6,
then 882.5), so a single shared baseline would silently credit that drift to whichever column came later.

| screen | uncapped ÷ its bracket | **capped ÷ its bracket** |
|---|---|---|
| accounts list, one page of 50 | 3.22× | **1.29×** |
| one account's detail | 4.72× | **1.42×** |
| one bill with its lines | 5.28× | **1.25×** |
| the run's findings screen | 2.70× | **1.26×** |

**THE ANSWER THE RULING ASKED FOR IS YES, AND IT IS THE SAME ANSWER ON ALL FOUR SCREENS.** With two bill
runs executing beside a clerk and no CPU limit — today's deployment — every screen sits at **2.7 to 5.3
times** its bracketed idle value. With the limit the compose file now carries, the same two runs, the same
code and the same database put every screen at **1.25 to 1.42 times**. The accounts list the ruling names
goes from **4,125.6 ms to 1,268.5 ms at p95**, which is *below* the 1,480.8 ms that same screen cost with
nothing running at all forty minutes earlier.

**THE CAP WAS REALLY APPLIED, and the harness says so with the kernel's own counter rather than with a
claim.** Docker implements `deploy.resources.limits.cpus` as CFS bandwidth control, so the harness sets the
same two cgroup files — `cpu.cfs_quota_us = 1.0 × cpu.cfs_period_us` — and puts every bill-run process in
that group. The kernel **throttled that group 33 times** during the capped set. A quota written to a cgroup
nothing joined would look identical from the outside and would be a measurement of nothing (DEF-182).

⚠ **WHAT THIS MACHINE CANNOT TELL YOU, said rather than left for a reader to assume.** These four cores
were carrying **load 8 to 10 from five other build lanes** throughout. That is why every absolute number
here is larger than task 28's on the same database — its idle accounts list was **605.8 ms**, this one's was
1,480.8, then 1,078.6, then 882.5. Two consequences, both honest:

* **the RATIOS transfer, the milliseconds do not.** On a host where the web tier's cores are actually free,
  both columns would be smaller.
* **the 1.0 cap bound only occasionally here** — 33 throttled periods — because on a machine already
  oversubscribed by other work, two bill runs rarely reach a whole core between them anyway, and **a cap can
  only give back what billing was actually taking.** On a quiet host, where a `--concurrency 2` worker CAN
  take two whole cores, the same number binds constantly. The effect measured here is therefore a **floor**
  on what the cap does, not a ceiling.

**AND THE SPLIT ITSELF WAS PROVED AGAINST A REAL BROKER, not only against a settings file** —
`10-scripts/verify_billing_queue_split.py`, three processes and one Redis, because *"a named queue needs
BOTH routing and a consumer"* is a claim about processes and no single-process test can settle it:

    1 · enqueued billing.run.calculate as 01a0574d-…-d7c5edd924b6 for brazosbend
    2 · broker depth — 'billing': 1 · 'celery': 0
    3 · after 12s of a `-Q celery` worker (running: True), 'billing' depth is 1
    4 · after a `-Q billing` worker, 'billing' depth is 0 and the record reads 'failed'

**Step 3 is the one that matters and the one nothing else in this repo can see.** A real default worker ran
for twelve seconds beside a real message on the billing queue and **left it there**. Put `billing` back into
that worker's `-Q` list and the same script reports *"the default worker DRAINED the 'billing' queue (depth

#### 6 · THE WRITING HALF SHIPPED YESTERDAY AND WAS NEVER RECORDED — A SIXTH UNRECORDED TASK

**Established before building anything**, and each by the line that shows the behaviour rather than by the
absence of a fault, which is the standard yesterday's sweep set:

| Half of task 6 | The line that proves it | State |
|---|---|---|
| a break row written as the pass finds it | `runs._calculate_run` — `breaks_written = record_break(bill_run, breaks[-1], job_id=job_id)`, ONE exit outside the three `except` blocks so a fourth failure shape cannot reach the end of the loop unfiled | ✅ 2026-08-30 |
| the row is an upsert on (run, account) | `record_break` → `update_or_create`, behind `uq_bill_run_breaks_once` | ✅ 2026-08-30 |
| served, writing nothing | `selectors.run_breaks_dict` reads `BillRunBreak.objects.filter(...)`; `api.run_breaks` mounts it | ✅ 2026-08-30 |
| a break the next pass drafts is CLOSED | `_calculate_run` → `clear_break(bill_run, data.account_id)` | ✅ 2026-08-30 |
| **`BR-BIL-053`'s OTHER way out** | — | ❌ **missing, and this is what shipped today** |

**THE GAP, in one sentence a person can act on: an account a clerk had already dealt with stayed on the
exceptions list for ever.** `BR-BIL-053` gives a break exactly two ways out — *"allow user to retry
immediately by fixing the issue"*, or the account waits for the catch-up sub-run — and
`BREAK_RESOLUTIONS` held ONE value, written by ONE caller. So **both of the rule's own doors leaked**:

* `retry_account`, the button the rule names, drafted the account and left its row OUTSTANDING;
* `mark_for_later` did the same, **and its path is live rather than hypothetical**: an account that broke,
  was HELD on S31.3 and was re-calculated goes `decisions.apply_decisions` → `mark_for_later`, leaves
  `ready`, and is therefore never reached by `clear_break` again.

The clerk's work list then showed rows for accounts already dealt with — the one thing a work list may not
do — and `BR-BIL-053`'s last clause (*"the run cannot enter phase 4 with an unresolved break row"*) would
have refused a run that was ready.

**Both doors now close the row and they say WHICH door.** `drafted` means this run billed the account in
the end; `held` means it did not and the account is in the catch-up queue. One value for two outcomes
would answer a supervisor's `?f.resolved=all` question *wrongly* rather than not at all. **No migration** —
the column already accepts it. `clear_break` also refuses any string outside `BREAK_RESOLUTIONS`, because
the column is a `TextField` with no CHECK and a typo would write a state nothing can read back.

**RED-proved, three mutations, one per guard:**

    tc14   AssertionError: assert None == 'held'          (mark_for_later stops closing)
    tc15   AssertionError: assert None == 'drafted'       (a successful retry stops closing)
    tc15b  Failed: DID NOT RAISE BillingRuleError         (any string is a resolution)

`tc15` also asserts the half a naive fix breaks: **a retry that RAISES leaves the break exactly as it
was**, because the account still cannot be billed and the clerk still has to see it.

#### 18 · THE TAB CAN STORE A REPLY — AND SAYS PLAINLY THAT NOTHING PRODUCES A ROW TO REPLY TO

`decisions.UNSUPPORTED_CASES` refused `extra_charge` on a **two-clause** reason and only the second clause
survived. The charge-code reader it said did not exist **has existed since `BR-BIL-075` landed on
2026-08-26** — `gather._resolve("rating", "charge_by_code")`, used by `_late_fee_charge_id` twenty lines
below in the same file. So the reason for refusing to STORE a clerk's reply had expired while the refusal
stood, and S31.3 offered Apply on every row against a server answering *"this case cannot be applied yet"*.

**The contract was the frontend's, read before anything was written:** the screen renders `row.choices`,
which every case row carries from `CHOICES_BY_CASE.get(case, ())`, and POSTs `{choice, reason?, case_ids?,
amount?, unit?}` to `.../exceptions/{case_id}/resolve`. So the backend half is a vocabulary entry, and
**no frontend change was needed** — the disabled control is derived from the served array and goes live on
its own, which is what deriving it was for.

| Half | What it does now |
|---|---|
| the DECISION | recorded, with `apply` and `waive` — the late fee's own two words, which is what r10 line 4256 draws and what `CHARGE_FILTERS` already groups |
| the MONEY | **not built, and refused rather than guessed.** `BR-BIL-007`'s amount comes from the tenant's own charge code and no case row in this product names one |
| `apply` | **HOLDS the account** at that named boundary — the `prorate_to_cycle_days` posture. The alternatives were billing the account WITHOUT the charge a human asked to add, or inventing a figure no rule produced |
| `waive` | changes nothing and the account bills normally. Holding an account because a clerk declined to add something to it would punish a decision to do nothing |
| bulk | **allowed**, unlike the late fee. `BR-BIL-003`'s manual-only waiver is about a LATE FEE and says so; `BR-BIL-060` puts bulk on every case surface. Extending a signed restriction to a case it was never given for is inventing law |

⚠ **AND THE PART THAT MUST BE SAID PLAINLY: `DEF-2596` IS OPEN, SO THIS CAN BE RECORDED AND NEVER ARISE.**
Nothing in this product emits an `extra_charge` case row — `runs._decisions_for` emits two kinds and
`read_analysis` seven, and neither `late_fee` nor `extra_charge` is among the nine — so the tab is empty on
every database there is. **Built anyway:** a decision that can be recorded and never arises is honest; a
screen offering Apply with nothing behind it is not. The day a pass emits the row, the reply lands.

**RED-proved, two mutations:**

    refuse   BillingRuleError: decision case 'extra_charge' cannot be applied yet: MUTATED …
    bound    AssertionError: assert '01a05837-…' not in ['01a05837-…']   (the account billed
             WITHOUT the charge the clerk applied — the silent under-charge)

### CR-051 · TASK 30's SECOND HALF SHIPPED — a run that hangs is stopped, 2026-09-01 · `2.119.0`

**WHAT A CLERK GETS.** A bill run that hangs used to hold one of the worker's two
slots **for ever**, and the only way to get it back was to restart a container.
It is now stopped after **2 hours 17 minutes**, and the run's own record says so
in a sentence on the wizard's progress band: *"This stopped after about 137
minutes, which is the longest one background job is allowed to run on this
system. Everything it had already finished is kept — start it again and it
carries on from where it stopped rather than beginning over."* **Pressing the
button again resumes** — the checkpoint task 11 shipped is untouched — so a run
stopped at 9,000 of 10,000 does not pay for those 9,000 again.

**TWO LIMITS, AND EITHER ONE ALONE IS WORSE THAN USELESS.**

| | seconds | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `CELERY_TASK_SOFT_TIME_LIMIT` | **8,220** (2 h 17 m) | raises INSIDE the task, so the run fails on the SAME path every other job failure takes and the record says what happened |
| `CELERY_TASK_TIME_LIMIT` | **8,520** (2 h 22 m) | kills a worker that ignored the soft one. It records **nothing** — see `DEF-2805` |

A hard limit alone kills the process mid-write with nothing recorded, and the
row is then stuck on `running` for ever, because `core.jobs.start` admits only
`queued → running` and `failed → running` — so the re-delivered message cannot
resume it either. That is filed as **`DEF-2805`** and deliberately not fixed
here: closing it needs a decision about what PROVES a worker is gone, which is
more than a settings change.

**WHERE THE NUMBERS COME FROM — measured, not chosen.** The whole derivation is
written into `config/settings/base.py` beside the values, because the next
person to change them needs it:

    ceiling                 25,000 accounts   (the run this deployment accepts)
    slowest measured        0.219 s/account   (task 26, RLS ENFORCED, 10,000)
    longest legitimate run  5,475 s = 1 h 31 m
    x 1.5 headroom          8,220 s = 2 h 17 m                          SOFT
    + 300 s to fail         8,520 s = 2 h 22 m                          HARD

**Why 1.5:** the 219 ms was itself measured under contention — the statement
count is flat at 111 an account across a hundredfold range while the wall clock
drifts from 172 ms to 219 ms, so the spread is the machine and not the work.
**The 300 s is an ASSUMPTION and is labelled as one** in the settings file:
nothing measured the longest single statement a run issues, and the soft signal
is only seen when control returns to Python. **Every other job kind fits inside
the soft limit with room to spare** — the print set is 0.012 s a bill (25,000 =
5 min), the findings pass 121.9 s per 1,000 accounts (25,000 = 51 min), the
biggest benchmarked import 230 s end to end — which is what makes ONE pair of
limits honest for all of them.

**FOUR THINGS THIS FOUND THAT NOBODY HAD ASKED FOR, AND ALL FOUR MATTER MORE
THAN THE TWO SETTINGS.** Every one was found by RUNNING a real Celery worker
against real PostgreSQL, and not one of them is visible in the test suite.

1. **A SOFT LIMIT THAT IS SWALLOWED IS DECORATION.** `SoftTimeLimitExceeded` is
   an ordinary `Exception` and Celery raises it **exactly once**, wherever the
   task happens to be. Two handlers on the hot path of the longest-running job
   this product has are `except Exception: log; continue` — the shape a batch
   uses so one broken row never costs the other nine thousand their post. In
   `runs._progress` the limit would have been logged as *"progress reporting
   failed"*; in `print_set._add_one` it would have been filed as **one broken
   bill** and the other 24,999 printed past a limit that never fires again.
   Nothing would have failed and nothing would have been logged as wrong.
   `core.jobs.reraise_if_time_limit` is one line in each, and `BR-BIL-1030`
   clause (c) states the rule so the next broad handler on a job path inherits
   it.
2. **CELERY'S OWN MESSAGE IS EMPTY.** `str(SoftTimeLimitExceeded())` is the
   empty string, so the record would have read `SoftTimeLimitExceeded: ` — and
   `job.error` is drawn **straight onto the clerk's screen** by
   `billRunResume.tsx`. The sentence is written in `core.jobs`, on the existing
   failure path, and carries no rule id.
3. **THE HONEST FAILURE PATH FAILED — AND ONLY A REAL DATABASE SHOWED IT.**
   Celery raises the soft limit from a SIGNAL HANDLER, so it lands wherever the
   task happens to be, and a long job spends most of its time inside a database
   call. Interrupted there, psycopg is left with a command in flight and **the
   next query raises** — and the next query is `fail()`'s own read:

       django.db.utils.OperationalError: sending query failed:
       another command is already in progress

   So the record stayed `running`, the limit recorded nothing, and every case
   in the suite passed either way **because the suite runs on in-memory SQLite,
   which has no such state** (CLAUDE.md law 14's neighbour). `core.jobs
   .release_interrupted_connection` drops that connection so the failure row can
   be written. ⚠ **AND FIXING IT REVEALED ITS OWN SECOND HALF an hour later:**
   `app.tenant_id` is a SESSION setting, so it dies with the connection — the
   reopened one reads ZERO rows under RLS FORCE and `_load` raises *"unknown
   job"* over a row sitting right there. The tenant is re-applied before
   anything asks a question. **The measured before-and-after is a real print set
   over 95 real bills stopped at 0.4 s: `running` with nothing recorded, then
   `failed` with the clerk's sentence.**
4. **`DEF-2806` — BOTH SIZE CEILINGS SAID THEY WERE DEPLOYMENT OVERRIDES AND
   NEITHER WAS.** `run_jobs.max_accounts_per_run()` and
   `print_set.max_bills_per_print_set()` read
   `getattr(settings, "BILLING_MAX_…", <module default>)`, and **no settings
   module declared either name** — so an operator who put
   `BILLING_MAX_ACCOUNTS_PER_RUN=5000` in `.env` changed nothing and was told
   nothing. It cannot fail: an undeclared setting is indistinguishable from one
   left at its default. Both are declared now, and a test asserts each settings
   default equals its module default so the pair cannot drift.

**PROVED RED FIRST, and the real proof is a real worker** —
`10-scripts/cr051_time_limit_proof.py` starts redis, starts a Celery worker with
a four-second soft limit, runs a body that sleeps past it, and reads the record
back; a second pass does the same to a **real print set over 95 real bills** at
a sub-second limit, which is what proves the per-bill handler no longer swallows
it and what found the interrupted connection above. **All three passes green:**
the sleeping body `failed` with the sentence and its checkpoint intact, the
control `succeeded`, and the print set `failed` with the sentence. A control pass with a generous limit must SUCCEED, because a proof that only
ever fails cannot tell a working limit from a broken job. The deterministic half
is `06-backend/tests/test_cr051_task30_time_limit.py` (11 cases).

**What is NOT built, stated so nobody reads more into this.** There is **one pair
of limits for every job kind**, because this deployment runs exactly one Celery
task for all of them (`apps.tenancy.tasks.run_pending_job` — the RECORD says
which kind it is), so a per-kind limit cannot be expressed as a setting and would
have to travel on each `apply_async`. A CSV export therefore inherits a ceiling
sized for a bill run: bounded, not protected. And `DEF-2805` above.

**`DEF-2829` IS CLOSED WITH THIS.** Its own prevention asked for two things and
both are done: the count is corrected by an added section rather than an edit, so
a reader meets both figures, and the missing half is built.

**`G61`, and the three choices inside it.** `10-scripts/gates/g61_frozen_figures.py` + a manifest +
two `.figures` sidecars, registered in `run_gates.py`.

* **It pins the FIGURES, not the file** — 130 money figures across the two finance-signed documents.
  A whole-file hash would go red on a typo fix or an added superseded stamp, which is how a gate earns
  the reputation that gets it switched off. **That half is proved on every run** by a second
  self-sabotage that must NOT bite.
* **The manifest is not self-updating and a lane may not re-pin it to get green** — the guard-list
  ruling of 2026-08-30 one layer up. It moves only with a recorded re-sign, in the same commit.
* **The failure NAMES the figures, never a hash**, and the manifest and its sidecars are checked
  against each other first, so a stale sidecar cannot name the wrong ones with total confidence
  (`DEF-182`'s shape).

**PROVED BOTH WAYS, side by side on ONE tree.** On the `GT-3` mutation:
`golden-verify: 33 PASS, 0 FAIL` and `G61 frozen-figures: FAIL — a ❄️ FROZEN figure MOVED (96 figures
pinned, 96 now) — gone: 15.25, 30.50, 30.50 | new: 15.50, 31.00, 31.00`. On a **prose-only** edit to the
same line: `G61 frozen-figures: PASS`. `04-docs/` was restored byte-for-byte and re-verified at
**33 PASS / 0 FAIL** afterwards. **G4 and G61 are complementary, not overlapping: G4 asks whether the
code still computes the signed answer; G61 asks whether the signed answer is still the one that was
signed.**

**`DEF-2826` — RAISED BY TASK 18, AND IT IS THE KIND ONLY A BROWSER FINDS.** `BillDocumentPage` prints
*"Rendered from platform-layout-compact-letter-v1"* and then **draws every band unconditionally**:
`layout_source` appears exactly ONCE in that file and only inside that sentence, and there is no branch
on the layout anywhere on the page. Measured: the compact bill's **kept copy is 2,019 bytes and contains
neither the word Rate nor the word Usage** — exactly what `LayoutSpec(compact-letter-v1,
services_band=False, detail_columns=False)` says — while the standard bill's is 3,433 bytes and contains
both; **the SCREEN drew `DESCRIPTION / USAGE / RATE / AMOUNT` for both.** So the server is right, the
posted bill is right, and the one screen a clerk would use to check what a customer receives is the
thing that is wrong. It hits `letterhead-v1` the same way, whose entire purpose is to SUPPRESS the
masthead for pre-printed stationery.

**THE HARNESS PASSES TODAY AND SAYS WHY, and the mechanism is deliberate.** A check that can only ever
fail stops being read; one that tolerates a growing list stops being a check. `KNOWN_OPEN` names the two
`DEF-2826` assertions with the defect id, prints them loudly, and **may only ever get SHORTER** — the run
**FAILS if a listed assertion starts PASSING**, saying the defect appears fixed and the entry must be
deleted. That is the `tenant-scoping-unproven.txt` precedent.

**PROVED RED ON A REAL CONDITION, not on the known-open one.** `_layout_key_of` was made to read *"the
current template"* instead of the pin — **the exact failure its own docstring names** (*"a 2026 bill
starts printing on a 2031 template"*) — and the harness went to **4 failures**: both bills named the SAME
layout, bill A stopped keeping its own, its page drew columns its layout forbids, and **the kept-copy
control caught it too** (`5 · A: the KEPT COPY has no Usage/Rate (3433 bytes)`). The tolerance is narrow
and keyed: A's identically-shaped failure was NOT excused. Restored and re-run green afterwards.

⚠ **ONE ASSERTION IS DELIBERATELY NOT MEASURED AND SAYS SO ON EVERY RUN.** The services band cannot be
judged on a FEE bill, which has no per-service charges and therefore draws no band whatever its layout
says — a check that could not tell that apart from the defect would report a pass for the wrong reason
on one bill and a failure for the wrong reason on the other. It is gated on the document response's own
service count and reported as a stated absence. **The first draft of this file got that wrong and
reported a false failure**, which is `DEF-182`'s lesson met head-on.

**Version:** W6 is tests and one gate — no runtime behaviour changes and no migration, so it takes no
minor of its own; `DEF-2826`'s fix will carry one when the page is repaired.

### CR-052 · WHAT IS NOT A TASK

* **No payment rails.** Autopay records an intent and captures nothing. Building a rail is not in this CR —
  but **before one is connected**, the question below must be answered.
* **For the Product Owner — and this one decides how much money leaves a customer's bank account.** The
  autopay intent carries the **gross** total. An enrolled customer owing `292.87` while holding `57.13` of
  credit would be scheduled for `292.87` and owe `235.74`. The code follows the signed figure and reports
  the consequence rather than choosing. It is safe only while there are no rails.
* **For the Product Owner:** is the empty-unit charge per UNIT or once per PREMISES? Six empty units at
  `$30.50` is **`$183.00` against `$30.50`**. And what happens before an owner is linked as a real party at
  all. Both were flagged when `BR-MET-105` was written and neither has been answered.
* **Deliberately left alone:** logo, colour and the remittance barcode. They are a template-design change,
  not a billing-logic one, and belong with whoever owns the bill's visual design.

### CR-053 · WHAT THE SERVER CAN ALREADY ANSWER

Read from the serializers, not the contract, and re-verified on `2.89.1`. The distinction that matters:

* **A field that exists and is not serialized** — cheap. The tax authority and the charge code are on the
  row and absent from the payload.
* **A figure nothing computes** — expensive. Per-service subtotals and the rate method are not stored and
  not derived anywhere.
* **Mounted and never called** — free to reach. `GET /invoices/{id}/chain` returns the chain head and
  `is_latest`, and **no screen calls it** (verified).

### CR-053 · THE BILL RUN'S PERFORMANCE BUDGET APPLIES HERE (PO 2026-08-31)

**One line, and it binds every task below that runs once per account.** The bill run is measured:
**111 ms an account and ~72 statements an account** at 1,000 accounts, linear to 10,000
(*CR-051 · THE PERFORMANCE QUESTION, WIDENED*). Nothing in CR-053 adds a pass over the run today: it changes how the list *reads*. The list's own paging is a separate budget and is not covered by those figures. **So anything added here that runs per
account is timed against that figure before it merges** — at 10,000 accounts one extra query per
account is ten thousand more statements, and the published figures are what makes that visible
instead of arriving as a slow Tuesday.

The named-format registry exists and refuses an unregistered name; the one registered format is `BR-NOT-029`'s own fourteen columns. Which format a vendor wants, which fields in which order, and how a batch is delimited stay theirs |

**THE ONE ARITHMETIC DECISION IN TASK 9, AND B4 HAD ALREADY MADE IT.** A subtotal is a sum over
lines and there are two readings a cent apart: add the amounts the bill PRINTS, or add what it
STORES and round once. **B4 chose on 2026-08-11** — for the tax base, but in terms about
sums-over-lines generally: *"a customer who adds up the four printed lines and applies the rate
gets $13.66 while the bill says $13.67, so the printed document does not foot against itself"*.
So: **Σ of the rounded lines**. Worked on three electric lines of `33.333333` — `33.33 + 33.33 +
33.33 = 99.99`, where rounding the sum once would give `100.00`. **Checked against GT-10 in frozen
figures:** electric `82.08 + 18.50 = 100.58`, bill-level `8.13 + 8.30 = 16.43`, total `117.01`.
`golden-verify` reads **33 PASS, 0 FAIL** before and after; no signed figure moved.

**THE GROUPING IS THE STORED COLUMN, NEVER THE WORDING.** `invoice_lines.service_id` is written
for `usage` and `base` lines only — a tax is bill-level (PO 2026-08-11, *"Tax rates are for bill
not for service"*) and a fee is an account fact. Nothing reads a description or a unit to place a
line, because water and sewer are both metered in kgal and a text-derived grouping would be right
most of the time. **The block is deliberately NOT named `service_subtotal`**: `BR-RAT-047` already
owns that name for a PROPOSED rating formula term with a different meaning.

**R1–R7 WAS NOT TOUCHED, WHICH CR-051's SECOND HARD RULE REQUIRES.** Nothing here narrows a price,
prices from a `ShadowOutcome`, reconciles a disagreement or switches a step. Task 9 reads the
prices a bill ALREADY STORES and adds them up; task 7 serializes two ids the writer already
stamped. `gather.py` is untouched.

**TWO DEFECTS FOUND ON THE WAY, both invisible to every existing check.** `DEF-2429` — a
`minimum_adjustment` line stores `service_id = NULL`, so money `BR-RAT-028` mode A computes PER
SERVICE lands in the bill-level bucket; the bill's total is unaffected, which is why nothing was
red. `DEF-2437` — `apps/billing/selectors.py` now does money arithmetic and **no glob in
`human_owned.txt` matches it**, so G7 reports conform over it; the sixth time that has happened on
a money path. A lane may not add itself to that list, so the glob is REQUESTED in the review-ledger
row.

**WHY TASK 14 BUILT NOTHING, AND WHY THAT IS THE CORRECT OUTCOME.** The task is shaped as *"the
extract behind a named format parameter"* so a vendor answer can arrive without a redesign. The
tempting move is to mount the route with an empty format registry — but that route can only ever
refuse, and this repo has already rejected exactly that shape by name (`apps/billing/api.py`:
*"a route that answers 501 is a promise"*). **And the format question carries the FIELD LIST with
it:** a fixed-width spec IS a field spec — offsets, widths, justification, padding — an XML schema
names its elements, a CSV names its headers and their order. There is no format-neutral row to
write first, so the shape and the contents are one decision and it is the vendor's. `OQ-1167` puts
all three parts of it — format, fields, batching — to the PO. **What already exists:** every bill
freezes the exact text handed to a print vendor (`BR-NOT-027`, decision log 2026-08-30), so the
CONTENT is stamped per bill; only the batch file's shape is missing. `apps/billing/exports.py`
still does not exist, which is also why task 10's download glyph ships disabled with its reason.

**No version bump**, for the reason the frontend half already recorded: `G35` requires
`package.json` and `pyproject.toml` to carry the same literal, and bumping one of the pair turns
G35 red for every lane on the branch. The bump belongs to whoever merges CR-053's waves.

**A REAL EXPORT, ON REAL ROWS.** The seeded sample utility's 93 issued bills produced **93 PDFs and 93
manifest rows, 0 held**. One row was checked against the bill it names — `AC-2026-00001`, Ana Alvarez,
`BL-2607-000001`, **$48.45**, bill date 2 July, due 22 July — and the PDF that row names was opened and its
own page count read out of its bytes and compared with the number the manifest claims. **A second run with
one address deliberately short of its state produced 91 PDFs, 91 rows and 2 held bills**, so clause (b) was
proved in a browser and not only in pytest.

**IT SITS ON THE BILL RUN'S PERFORMANCE BUDGET, MEASURED** (`10-scripts/cr053_print_set_benchmark.py`, real
PostgreSQL 16 with row-level security enforced, three runs): **0.012 s and 6.01 database statements a bill**,
the SLOWEST of the three published because a warm cache is not the run a clerk waits through. At **10,000
bills** that is **2.0 minutes, 60,108 statements and a 12.8 MiB archive**. It goes on billing's own named
queue with `background: true` and falls back to INLINE where nothing would run a job, never queued into a
void; a ceiling of 25,000 — deliberately the same number as the bill run's — refuses at the door, before a
single page is drawn.

**FOUR JUDGMENTS, all in the decision log with their reasoning.** The bill date is `invoices.service_date`
(`BR-BIL-070` makes the clerk's typed date the run's SERVICE date, stamped per invoice, so there is no cycle
join and no clock) · `address_line_2` and `country` are EMPTY and are neither carved out of line 1 nor taken
from `TenantSettings.country` (`DEF-2847`) · **nothing streams**, so `DEF-2734`'s mechanism is absent rather
than guarded and `G58` gains no call site · the manifest stops at fourteen columns, because it is a file
specification a vendor's loader is written against and the original-versus-rebuilt split belongs in the
