### CR-053 · TASK 15 CLOSED — the tie-out nobody had ever drawn, 2026-09-01

**W5's task 15 is on `claude/confirm-app-version-310jd3`** as
`10-scripts/render-checks/cr053-charges-tie-out.mjs` — **44 assertions, all green, proved RED
first.** No product file was touched: this is a `Test` task and it adds a check, not a screen.

**FOUR SATISFACTION ROWS IN THIS CR DISAGREED WITH EACH OTHER ABOUT TASK 15, AND READING THE CODE
SETTLED IT DIFFERENTLY FROM ALL FOUR.** For the next reader, because a status is taken out of these
rows:

| Where | What it said | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| *WHAT HAS LANDED*, 2026-08-30 | *"covers tasks 1–5 and 10–12; tasks 6–13 are not covered because they are not built"* | **true on the day, stale since.** 6, 7, 8, 9 and 13 all shipped after it |
| *THE W2 FRONTEND HALF*, 2026-08-31 | *"task 15's render checks now cover 1–8 and 10–12"* | **stale** — task 13 shipped hours later. This CR already flags it |
| *TASK 13 DONE*, 2026-08-31 | *"`cr053-print-bills.mjs` covers task 13; `cr053-bill-surface.mjs` covers 1–8 and 10–12"* | **stale the same way**, and it is the row this lane was pointed at |
| *WHERE THIS STANDS*, 2026-09-01 | *"task 9 is a `Back` task with no screen to open"* | **WRONG, not merely stale.** Task 9's figures ARE a screen — the *"What each service cost"* panel task 6 built over them — and `cr053-bill-surface.mjs` assertions 11 and 12 were already comparing every one of them against `GET /invoices/{id}` fetched in the same run |

**SO THE REAL GAP WAS NARROWER AND WORSE THAN ANY OF THEM SAID.** `cr053-bill-surface.mjs`'s tie-out
assertion is `String(cbs.tie_out.ties_out) === charges.tiesOut` — the server's verdict against the
screen's, which is the right assertion — and **every bill it has ever opened ties out**, so it has
only ever evaluated `true === "true"`. A screen that hard-coded `data-ties-out="true"` and deleted
the disagreement branch would pass it every time. **The branch a clerk actually needs — *these lines
add up to $258.28 and the bill says $260.00* — had never been drawn in a browser at all**, and
neither had three of its neighbours.

**THE FIVE STATES THE NEW CHECK DRAWS**, on the shipped `vite build` bundle in a real browser:

| Bill | What it proves |
|---|---|
| `ties` | the control — Water **238.60** + bill-level **19.68** = **258.28** = the bill's total, drawn as the server's own 2dp strings with the 4dp stored scale ABSENT |
| `drift` | **the one nothing had ever drawn** — the same rows against a bill claiming **260.00** |
| `noservice` | `services: []` — no zero-valued row is invented for a service the bill never touched |
| `minimum` | `DEF-2429`'s misfiled minimum-bill note. Seeded bills carry `tax` and nothing else, so this had never been on a screen either |
| `noblock` | the server omits `charges_by_service` — the page states the absence rather than white-screening |

**THE ASSERTION THAT MATTERS IS ARITHMETIC, NOT PRESENCE.** Two figures being on the page proves
nothing; a screen could print any two. So: the difference between the two figures a PERSON reads
must equal the server's own stated `delta` (**1.72**); the per-service and bill-level cells on the
drifted bill must be **byte-identical** to the control's, which is `BR-BIL-032`'s evidence still on
the page, unreconciled; the bill's own total must not appear in a subtotal cell; and **the two bills
must produce DIFFERENT tie-out text**, which is the one thing a hard-coded verdict cannot pass
(`DEF-182` — a check whose output cannot distinguish pass from fail is worse than no check). The
disagreement is also `role="alert"` and **measurably** painted in the danger tier — a different
computed `background-color` and `border-left-color` from the control — which no jsdom test can see
and which B14 rule 21's per-file migration clause makes unsafe to assert from a class name.

**PROVED RED FIRST (law 7), on the defect the file is written for.** Making the tie-out
unconditional in `BillDetailPage.tsx` — `data-ties-out="true"` with no branch, which IS *"a tie-out
that is present, green, and cannot fail"* — and rebuilding gave **9 failures, exactly the drift
half, with every other assertion still green**:

```
FAIL drift: the verdict on screen is the server's — "false" — true
FAIL drift: the sentence names what the ROWS add to — $258.28 — These add up to the bill's total.
FAIL drift: the sentence names what the BILL says — $260.00 — These add up to the bill's total.
FAIL drift: a disagreement is ANNOUNCED — role=alert, so it is not a quiet hint — null
FAIL drift: the two figures a person reads differ by the SERVER's own delta (1.72) — drawn=[] serverDelta=1.72
FAIL drift: the line is PAINTED differently from the control — rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) vs rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)
FAIL the tie-out is CONDITIONAL — the two bills produce different verdicts
```

`BillDetailPage.tsx` was restored byte-identical, rebuilt, and all 44 went green again.

**WHY IT USES A STUB API AND NO DATABASE, AND WHAT THAT COSTS.** A drifted bill is not a state the
product can be driven into — `invoice_lines` is immutable (hard rule 4) and the engine writes lines
that foot — so reaching one end to end means corrupting a bill in a throwaway database, and **there
is no bill to corrupt: all 35 databases on this box hold ZERO invoices**, re-measured 2026-09-01
(`DEF-2901`). ⚠ **PostgreSQL itself is UP** — the note this lane was handed said it was down, and
`pg_isready` answers on 5432. The file's own header names four things it therefore does not prove:
nothing about the server, nothing about whether a real bill can drift, not the join, and not the
rest of the Charges tab — all of which stay `cr053-bill-surface.mjs`'s and
`test_cr053_charges_tab_backend.py`'s. It follows `def2826-bill-layout.mjs`'s pattern for the same
reason that file gives.

**NO VERSION BUMP, and the reasoning rather than an omission.** Step 7 asks for one per wave, and
`G35` needs `package.json` and `pyproject.toml` to carry the same literal plus a `CHANGELOG.md`
entry for it. This task adds a check and changes nothing a person sees, so there is no product
change to describe in a changelog written for people; bumping both literals would touch three
shared files under five live lanes for zero user-visible change. The repo stands at **`2.110.2`**
and G35 is green on it.

### CR-053 · TASK 14 — THE MECHANISM, WITH ONE HONEST DEFAULT, 2026-09-01 · `2.119.0`

⚠ **READ THIS FIRST: `OQ-1167` IS STILL OPEN AND NOTHING BELOW CLOSES IT.** No
print vendor has told us which file format they want, which fields in which
order with which address form, or how a period's bills are delimited. All three
are facts only they hold, and **not one of them is guessed here.**

**WHAT CHANGED, AND WHY IT IS NOW THE RIGHT MOVE WHEN IT WAS NOT ON 2026-08-30.**
The task's own text says how to proceed — *"build the PDF set first and the
extract behind a named format parameter"* — and on 30 August the PDF set did not
exist, so the only thing a route could have done was refuse. The decision log
recorded that reasoning and it was correct: *"that route can only ever refuse,
and this repo has already rejected exactly that shape by name — a route that
answers 501 is a promise"*. **Task 13 then shipped the PDF set, the manifest and
the held-back list on 2026-08-31**, so the first half of the sentence is done and
the second half is buildable. A registry with one real, already-ratified,
already-shipping format in it is not a promise.

**WHAT A PRINT VENDOR RECEIVES TODAY.** Exactly what they received yesterday: one
print-ready PDF per bill, plus **one list with a row for every bill and fourteen
columns** — account number · bill number · customer name · address line 1 ·
address line 2 · city · state · postal code · country · page count · bill date ·
due date · amount due · the PDF filename. That is `BR-NOT-029`'s ratified list,
**reused exactly and not restated**: the registry takes the columns from
`print_set.MANIFEST_HEADER`, so one place in the repository says what a vendor
gets. The file is still called `manifest.csv` and an archive nobody asks a
question of is byte-for-byte what task 13 shipped.

**WHAT IS NEW IS THE DOOR.** `apps/billing/print_formats.py` holds a registry of
named formats. `POST /billing/print-sets` takes `format`; `GET` publishes the
list. Adding a vendor's shape is a REGISTRATION — a name, a filename, an encoder
and, when they state one, their own field list — and nothing in `print_set.py`
or `print_api.py` changes to accept it. That is the *"without a redesign"* the
task asked for, and the suite exercises it with a pipe-separated file that has
its own two columns and no header row.

**ASKING FOR A FORMAT NOBODY HAS REGISTERED REFUSES BY NAME AND SAYS WHICH EXIST.**
Verbatim, as a clerk sees it: *"there is no print file format called 'xml', so
nothing has been produced. The formats this system can write are: manifest-csv (a
comma-separated list, one row for every bill, with the column names on the first
line). If your printer needs a different one, tell us what it looks like and we
will add it — we will not guess at it."* **There is no silent fallback to the
default, and that is the whole rule** (`BR-NOT-1030`): a vendor's loader handed a
shape it did not expect either stops — a bad day — or **reads the wrong field
into the wrong place**, which is bills posted to the wrong people and money
chased from the wrong customers. A refusal costs a clerk one attempt.

**THE FORMAT IS PART OF THE IDEMPOTENCY KEY** (`billing:print-set:<format>:<the
filters>`, hard rule 6). Two requests over the same bills in two shapes are two
files and two intentions; folded onto one key the second caller would be handed
the FIRST one's archive and told it succeeded. That would have had no symptom at
all.

**NO SCREEN CHANGED, DELIBERATELY.** There is one format, so a picker would be a
control with a single option — content a clerk reads for no decision (B14 rule
32, the PO's *"too much content"*). The list is on the `GET`, so the picker is a
screen change and not a server change on the day a second shape is registered.
The route's `unavailable` list still says out loud, in plain words, that only one
shape exists and that a printer's own shape is theirs to state — so a working
default cannot be read as the question being answered.

**PROVED RED FIRST.** `get()` made to return the default for an unknown name →
*tc4 DID NOT RAISE*; the format dropped from the scope key → tc8 red. Ten cases
in `06-backend/tests/test_cr053_task14_print_formats.py`, and task 13's own suite
runs unchanged and green beside them.

  and then **scales its tier boundaries by the period's calendar days (B4.4)**, so a wrong read date
  reprices every tier invisibly — task 25. Seasonal is the opposite: a period crossing a boundary splits
  pro-rata automatically *unless* a real read is dated on the boundary, which beats the split, so a boundary
  read is worth taking.

  the bill *refuse* was right, and this CR's claim that it makes the bill *wrong* was not.

### CR-054 · THE BILL RUN'S PERFORMANCE BUDGET APPLIES HERE (PO 2026-08-31)

**One line, and it binds every task below that runs once per account.** The bill run is measured:
**111 ms an account and ~72 statements an account** at 1,000 accounts, linear to 10,000
(*CR-051 · THE PERFORMANCE QUESTION, WIDENED*). CR-054 is the reads upload rather than the run, and its own large-batch figures are the import's, not the run's — but a read that arrives here is a read the run then prices, so the same budget governs anything this CR adds to the per-account path. **So anything added here that runs per
account is timed against that figure before it merges** — at 10,000 accounts one extra query per
account is ten thousand more statements, and the published figures are what makes that visible
instead of arriving as a slow Tuesday.

⚠ **`postSplit()` IS A DERIVATION, NOT A SERVED FIGURE, AND IT IS DECLARED AS ONE (`OQ-1200`).**
`commit_read_batch` publishes `held_reads` and `unresolved_errors`; `validate_read_batch`
publishes neither, and `read_batch_counts` cannot be summed into them — it has no bucket for
*"an error row nobody has decided"*, which is the term the split turns on. So the pre-post
figure is a **literal port of `read_rejects.would_hold`**, its three clauses in its order, over
the server's own stored `severity` and `disposition`; it re-judges nothing, and it is a
**ceiling** for the two reasons that function names (a head billed since stage 3, a write the
database refuses — both make MORE holds, never fewer). The receipt prints the server's own
count, so the forecast never stands as the record. Proved across a real commit: the button said
**5** and the post created **5**.

Both rejects routes wrap a LAZY generator in a `StreamingHttpResponse`, and

rejects file too**, and those two are the only `StreamingHttpResponse` call sites in

every lazily-evaluated response body in `06-backend`: **2 affected** (these two), **1 safe**
(`tenancy/api.py::export_file`, whose `FileResponse` streams an already-open file handle and

3. **The alternative is worse, and that is the real argument.** Putting `On-peak` in the key
   would make the key LOCALISED: the labels are transcribed from the locale catalogue and
   there are eleven catalogues. A key whose text changes with a copy edit or with the clerk's
   language cannot round-trip, and a key that cannot round-trip reports *"was the meter
   replaced?"* against a meter nobody touched.

### CR-054 · WHAT ONLY THE PRODUCT OWNER CAN DECIDE

* **The meter-factor tolerance.** `factor_flag` is named in `BR-MET-021`'s vocabulary and has **no signed
  threshold anywhere in the corpus**, so it reports instead of firing — the reading detail page says so in
  as many words. The meter factor is the multiplier that turns a register difference into billable
  consumption, and a wrong one bills a clean multiple of the right number. A figure closes it; the
  implementation behind it is one seeded value and letting the rule fire.
* **Whether a clerk may post a meter whose bill is already certain to refuse.** ⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-08-30,
  after reading the `Meter Reads Blueprint` (below). The first version of this bullet said the billing
  consequence was unruled and that the bills would be silently wrong. BOTH HALVES WERE WRONG**, and the
  correction is in the pricing engines' own words: `apps/rating/pricing/models/demand.py` — *"An absent read
  REFUSES by name — a month with no demand read is not a month with no peak"* — and
  `apps/rating/pricing/models/tou.py` refuses a priced window that nothing measured, because billing it at
  another window's rate or dropping it *"are both wrong in ways"* it names. **So an incomplete meter produces
  NO bill, not a wrong one, and the account breaks in the run.** What is genuinely open is narrower and is a
  workflow question, not a pricing one: today the clerk may post such a meter with a reason, and the
  alternative is holding those rows at import where the fix is cheap rather than at the bill run where it is
  20 broken accounts. `plan_register_completeness` stays a WARNING either way — a hard error there would
  close this question at a call site, which the prime directive forbids.
* **Partial posting, three details.** One rejects file or two, errors and warnings kept apart? Offered at
  validation, at the end, or both? Do failed rows stay staged to be fixed in place, or is the file
  re-uploaded? CR-047 answered these one way for accounts; reads may want another.
* **The rail vocabulary.** Four of the five stage headings are already plain English. The ETL words live in
  the page title, the five chips, the stage kicker and the forward buttons. Renaming them for reads buys
  plainness in one importer and costs consistency across seven. Task 19 puts the mechanism in place either
  way; whether to use it for the chips is a naming call across all seven and is not taken here.

### CR-054 · WHAT IS NOT A TASK

* **A hand-held collector integration.** A utility whose meters are read by a device gets a file in that
  device's shape and cannot use a generated sheet. That is served by task 11's panel — the shortfall stated
  the moment the file is staged — not by an integration, which is a per-vendor project and is not folded in
  here.
* **Teaching the clerk the register model.** Explicitly rejected. The document's finding is that the system
  already knows everything the clerk is being asked to work out, and the fix is to stop asking.
* **The cost of pre-filling, stated and accepted.** Showing the previous reading invites confirming rather
  than reading. The `zero` and `low` rules turn a copied column into a wall of flags at stage 3, and the
  printed route sheet already shows the last read to the field crew. It is a real trade and it is being
  taken deliberately.

## CR-055 — a premises upload never rejects a row because of the owner's name

**HOW IT ARRIVED, verbatim, with the requester's own spelling** (2026-08-31, from a screenshot of the
premises-upload flowchart, box 2.6):

> *"We ahve prepare this logic for premises upload - we need to allow 2.6 - owner can have multiple
> premises ownership- how you will ahndle this please confirm you make any cahnges"*

### CR-055 · CLASSIFY — HALF DEFECT, HALF CHANGE, AND SEPARATING THEM IS THE WHOLE OF THIS CR

The reason given — *"owner can have multiple premises ownership"* — describes something **already built
and already ruled**, and box 2.6 is not the box that would stop it. So by the change process's own step 1
(*"when it is ambiguous it is a DEFECT, not a change"*) the first half is **ours**: the picture said
something we did not mean.

**WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, measured in the code before anything was written:**

* `Premises.owner` is an ordinary FK — one owner, many premises, no cap. Its own comment: *"deleting an
  owner that twelve addresses point at must refuse, never silently untype twelve premises."*
* `resolve_owner_name`'s `exact` branch **reuses the party that exists**, with the comment *"this is the
  branch that stops twelve addresses becoming twelve landlords."*
* `owner_selectors.owner_detail_dict` serves **`premises_count`**, and cites the PO's own ruling as its
  reason: *"the same landlord across twelve addresses is one party."*
* `premises_ids_owned_by_account` returns a **list**.

So 500 upload rows naming one landlord resolve to **one** owner. That is box **2.7 (one exact match)** and
it loads. **Box 2.6 was never about multiple ownership**, and the branch label *"several look alike"* is
what made it read that way — filed as a documentation defect against the flowchart, since it reads
naturally as *"several premises name this owner"* when it means *"the name matches two or more EXISTING
OWNER RECORDS."*

### CR-055 · THE ACTUAL CHANGE, AND WHAT IT REVERSES

Raising 2.6 surfaced a genuine question, and the PO answered it: **an uploaded owner name that matches no
owner exactly but resembles two or more existing owners now LOADS THE PREMISES WITH NO OWNER, flagged for
someone to fill in later — exactly as a blank owner column already does. The row is no longer rejected.**

**WHAT IS SUPERSEDED, quoted, with its scope stated so the supersession is not read wider than it is.**
`import_runs.KIND_OWNER_REF` records the current behaviour as *"a NEAR name is REJECTED for a person to
settle (PO decision 3 — 'offer the match, clerk decides', so the import may not pick)"*. **Decision 3 is
NOT reversed.** It says the import may not PICK, and this change does not let it pick — it still refuses
to choose between two parties. What changes is the CONSEQUENCE of refusing to choose: the row loads
ownerless instead of being thrown out. **The create screen is untouched**, where `BR-MET-401` still
refuses a premises with no owner, because a clerk filling in a form knows the answer or can find it.

**THE PRECEDENT THIS FOLLOWS IS THE PO's OWN, FROM 2026-08-27:** *"what if owner column is empty - in such
case we create the premises and keep owner name empty - we cna edit and updaste it later"*. The reasoning
recorded with it applies here word for word — a migration is thousands of rows, half the owner answers are
in a filing cabinet, and *"the addresses it cannot load are the ones its meters and accounts then cannot
name either."* A near-match is the same situation with a spelling instead of a blank.

**THE CONSEQUENCE, STATED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER.** No owner means **no master account**, so the
premises has **nobody to charge**. It is a real premises — it holds units, it holds meters, it can be read
— and **it cannot be billed until the owner is filled in**. That is already true of the blank case; this
change adds near-matches to the same pool. `unmatched_premises_qs()` lists them and the import receipt
counts them as `premises_with_no_owner`, so they are never silently indistinguishable from complete rows —
and **that count is what stops this being a quiet way to lose revenue.**

**WHAT IT BUYS:** after this the premises upload **cannot reject a row on owner grounds at all.** Blank
loads, exact reuses, near loads ownerless, unknown creates the party. Owner spelling can no longer stall a
migration.

### CR-055 · THE OPTIONS AS PUT, so the signature covers what was shown

Three, in plain English with the cost of each: **load it with no owner** (recommended, chosen) · **keep
rejecting the row** — safest, but *"a big migration can stall on spelling"* · **pick the closest match
automatically** — explicitly recommended against, because the owner carries the master account, so a wrong
pick eventually sends somebody else's bill to the wrong party, and it would reverse decision 3 outright.

## CR-056 — the owner becomes a person, and his account hangs off the address

**Raised:** 2026-08-31, from the Product Owner reading *Who Gets Billed, and Under What Number* (the analysis
artifact, read from the code at `v2.97.0`). **Requester:** Product Owner. **Classification:** CHANGE, not a
defect — it reverses signed rules deliberately rather than correcting our misunderstanding of them.

### 0 · WHAT ARRIVED, AND WHY IT IS A CR AND NOT A DEFECT ROW

**Five rulings were made in that session and NOT ONE of them reached the repository.** The session was
instructed *analysis only, no repository writes*, so the lane was right at the time — and the artifact says so
in its own closing words: *"None of this is in the repository yet … Say the word and I will capture all of it
properly."* Nobody said the word, and a week of work has been planned around rules that exist only on a web
page. **This CR is that capture, plus the build it implies.**

⚠ **ONE RULING IS VERBATIM AND FOUR ARE RECONSTRUCTED, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS STAMPED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED.**
Only the first is quoted from the PO's own typing; the other four are stated as the artifact describes them
and **must be confirmed before anything in W1–W6 is built on them.** Recording a paraphrase as if it were a
quotation is precisely how two contradictory rules end up in one repo.

| # | The ruling | Form |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | *"Duplex should be linked to master account of Ajinkya → link this account to customer # that already exist"* | **VERBATIM** |
| R2 | A Master Account attaches to the PREMISES itself, not to a unit inside it | reconstructed |
| R3 | The Customer # is keyed on IDENTITY (SSN · phone · driving licence) and reused — never allocated twice to one person | reconstructed |
| R4 | A common area gets no account of its own | reconstructed |
| R5 | A premises row with a blank owner column is still created; the owner is flagged, not invented | reconstructed |

### 1 · WHAT SIGNED STATEMENT IS BEING REVERSED

**`BR-CUS-068` and the PO ruling of 2026-08-27 closing `OQ-500`** — *master-ness is derived from occupancy:
owner-billed vs tenant-billed*, and is **explicitly never chosen at creation**. An owner-occupier gets one
Regular Account and no master shape at all.

**R1 and R2 replace that.** Every address gets its owner an account whether or not anything is shared, and
that account hangs off the address. The supersession is the whole reason this is a CR: **both rules cannot
be true at once**, and under both together an owner-occupier holds two accounts and receives two bills for
one house.

**THE SHIFT, IN ONE LINE — and it is a better idea than it looks:**

> **FROM:** a Master Account is the bill for shared space.
> **TO:** a Master Account is the owner's account at an address.

Everything that was awkward falls into place once that is the definition. The empty-flat charge has somewhere
to post. A departing tenant's shortfall has somewhere to post. *Is there a common area?* stops being the gate
that decides whether the owner exists in the product at all.

### 2 · THE MONEY THAT MUST NOT MOVE

**`1408 Elm Street` must still bill `$69.60`** — `$41.20` hallway and exterior lighting plus `$28.40` shared
irrigation, asserted in `tests/test_br_cus_068_master_bill.py` tc1, with tc2 asserting the anchor-only
behaviour gives `$41.20` and is NOT `$69.60`. Under R2 the account hangs off the address and those two spaces
become things it is CHARGED FOR rather than the thing it hangs off. **Same figure, different plumbing** — and
a signed number that changes quietly is the failure this line exists to prevent. **No B4/B5 frozen figure is
touched.**

### 3 · THE QUESTION THAT BLOCKS THE REST

⚠ **AN OWNER WHO LIVES IN HIS OWN HOUSE — ONE ACCOUNT OR TWO?** R1 gives every address a Master Account for
its owner; the 27 August ruling gives an owner-occupier one Regular Account and no master shape. **Under both
at once he holds two accounts and gets two bills for one house, and for a small utility that is most of the
book.** Every customer would see it on day one.

**The recommendation, ours to propose and the PO's to rule:** keep both accounts and send ONE bill, because
**an account with no charges produces no document**. He occupies the only unit, so nothing falls to his
Master Account and it stays silent. It changes nothing structural, costs no bill-assembly machinery, answers
a second open question for free (*does a premises-level Master Account produce a `$0.00` bill every month?* —
no), is the general rule rather than an exception carved out for one case, and **degrades correctly**: the day
he lets the house out his Regular Account closes, the unit falls to the Master Account that already exists,
and there is no migration and no clerk step. That transition is the whole point of the model.

**Eight more are raised as OPEN and none is guessed:** an owner name nobody on file has · is the empty-unit
charge per UNIT or once per PREMISES (`six flats at $30.50` is `$183.00` against `$30.50`) · does a tenant
move-out reassign automatically or on approval · what happens to the account when he sells · two shared spaces
taking the same service, standing charge once or twice · addresses already on file with only a typed-in owner
name · whether the owner record may point at a tenant's account (today it is silent and accepts it) ·
unallocated usage, where three readings of the question give three answers and none is ruled.

### 4 · WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT AND IS NOW WRONG

* **A Master Account hangs off a common-area unit and refuses to exist without one.** The `accounts` table has
  **no premises column** and its unit column **cannot be empty**, so the account anchors on the first common
  area and reaches the rest through service agreements. **This is the largest single item in the CR** — schema,
  plus every screen and query that assumes an account has a unit.
* **`ensure_owner_master_account()` refuses by design**, raising `NotImplementedError("OQ-790")`, because at
  the moment a premises is created nobody occupies anything yet and the system cannot tell which kind of
  account the owner needs. R2 removes that ambiguity and the refusal becomes unnecessary.
* **Exactly one function writes a customer-to-account link and it runs only inside an import.** Every Master
  Account in the product has a blank customer column, and an account opened at the counter shows a dash where
  its number should be.
* **Identity is not on the customer at all** — no SSN, no phone, no licence, no date of birth. What exists is
  an encrypted SSN on the SERVICE REQUEST and a date of birth plus the last four of an id on the CONTACT,
  which belongs to one account.
* **What makes an owner one person today is his NAME**, unique per utility, case-insensitive. *A. Kulkarni*
  and *Ajinkya Kulkarni* are two landlords and nothing objects.
* **The owner-occupier breaks on the day he lets the house out.** His Regular Account closes, the empty unit's
  standing charge has no posting target, and the settlement refuses rather than post to a name. The workaround
  in the code — pointing the owner record at his Regular Account — **dies on the day it is needed**, because
  that account is closed by the very event that creates the charge.

index beside it so a randomised ciphertext can be MATCHED without being readable (migration
`customers 0036`, 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING). `apps/customers/identity_match.py` computes
`BR-CUS-089`'s signed criteria — **name AND date of birth AND one government identifier**, the PO's
own words of 2026-08-25 — and nothing else. Task 12 RECONCILES rather than duplicates: the request's
encrypted SSN and the contact's date of birth are lifted into the one row that spans a person's whole
relationship with the utility, `gov_id_last4` is copied nowhere (four digits cannot identify), and
neither source is moved or deleted. Task 14: the carry-forward now works from the counter and refuses
a weak match **showing no figure at all** — `$150.00` stays where it is.

**W3 · the link nothing wrote (tasks 15–18).** `link_customer` stays the ONE writer and every door
reaches it: the S18 wizard, the S19 move-in and the master-account door. `customer_accounts` carries
`BR-CUS-089`'s four match columns, which gives `discounts._stored_match` a second store — the hole
that meant *"a move-in that did not come from a service request has no stored tier at all"*. Task 18
rules the owner→customer shortcut out (`BR-MET-1020`): the write door refuses it by name and the read
reaches the party through the master account. **The column is not dropped** — `BR-MET-150` asked for
it in the PO's own words, so its removal is `OQ-1240` rather than a lane's to take.

**W5 · task 25.** The customers list, its search and one person's accounts. Tasks 23 and 24 belong to
another lane and are untouched.

where this work made their stated absences false. **Open:** `OQ-1240`. **Filed:** `DEF-2920` (this
lane's own renumber rewrote nine of the W0/W1 lane's rule citations; found by law 11's hunk check and
fixed one commit later).

⚠ **WHAT W2 DID NOT DO, AND IT IS THE ONE THING FOR THE PO.** The database does **not** refuse a
second customer carrying a Social Security number already on file. R3 — the ruling that would license
that constraint — is RECONSTRUCTED, and §0 above says a reconstructed ruling must be confirmed before
anything is built on it. A unique index is a one-way door: it refuses a save at the counter on digits
a clerk may have mistyped and cannot be relaxed without a migration. R3's BEHAVIOUR is built in the
service layer, where it is reversible; the constraint is not. Named in the review-ledger row in plain
English as the single thing that needs a ruling.

### 9 · WAVE W2b — LANDED 2026-09-01 · v2.111.0 · the COMPANY half of W2: identity is per kind

⚠ **THIS IS `W2b`, NOT `W6`, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS.** §5's table already gives `W6` to
tasks 26-28 — the tenant move-out that drops a unit onto the owner's account — and §6 holds those
until the owner-occupier answer is ruled. **This wave is the COMPANY HALF OF W2**, which the decision
log of 2026-09-01 names in as many words: *"A task for the company half belongs in the CR before
anyone reads W2 as finished."* It touches nothing in W4 or W6. **THREE TASKS JOIN §5's TABLE:**

| # | Wave | Task | Kind | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | W2b | A company's Tax ID on the customer, encrypted, with its blind index | Back | 11 |
| 33 | W2b | The matcher branches on the kind, and capture follows it | Back | 32 |
| 34 | W2b | The kind is an explicit input at every door that can create a customer | Back | 33 |

**A COMPANY COULD NOT BE RECOGNISED AT ALL, AND THE SIGNED RULE IS WHY.** The PO's ruling of
2026-09-01 — *"Customer can be person or company - in case of person , if we have SSN, or DL or
Phone number, we create the Customer ID and attached these to custoemr ID ; if it is Company then we
ask for Tax ID"* — collided with `BR-CUS-089`, which is signed and verbatim and asks for **name AND
date of birth AND one government identifier**. A company has no date of birth, so read literally the
signed rule made every business permanently unmatchable and the **$150.00** deposit it gates could
never follow one to a new account. **`BR-CUS-089` is NARROWED onto persons, not reversed**
(`BR-CUS-1022`), and the narrowing is DIRECTIONAL: it removes a clause a company cannot satisfy and
adds nothing to a person's test.

**WHAT A COMPANY NEEDS:** its name and its **Tax ID**. `customers.tax_id` is a new
app-layer-encrypted column with a keyed blind index beside it — migration `customers 0038`, 🔒
HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING, exactly the shape `0036` built for a person's SSN and licence. ⚠
**`tenancy.ein` IS NOT REUSED**: that is the UTILITY's own tax number on another module's table, and
it is the counter-example rather than the precedent, because it holds nine plaintext digits against
`OQ-016`, which is CLOSED.

**WHAT A PERSON NEEDS:** unchanged — name, date of birth and an SSN or a driving licence.

**CAPTURE FOLLOWS THE KIND.** A company is never asked for a driving licence and a person is never
asked for a Tax ID; a borrowed field is refused BY NAME rather than dropped, because a dropped key
means a clerk believes an identifier was stored when it was not (`DEF-632`'s shape one level up).
`set_identifier` is the second lock, for in-process callers that never meet the door's validator.

**NO UNIQUE INDEX ON THE TAX ID**, and this time it is a PO ruling rather than a reconstruction: *a
duplicate identifier refuses to LINK and never refuses to SAVE.* Two customers may carry the same
Tax ID; the LINK is refused by name and the screen shows **no figure at all**.

**THE KIND STOPS BEING A SILENT DEFAULT, and the line is drawn at the harm.** Identity presented
with NO kind is REFUSED by name — a government identifier filed under a party nobody classified sits
in a column the other kind's matcher never reads. A door presenting NO identity still OPENS the
account and keeps the `person` fallback, which is now WRITTEN by the service and recorded as
`kind_defaulted` on the audit row rather than arriving invisibly from the model's column default.
Refusing the save would have been the same one-way door §7's ruling 10 declined.

**Rules written:** `BR-CUS-1022`; `BR-CUS-089` carries its narrowing beneath it.
**Open:** `OQ-1241` (does a company get an incorporation date?) and `OQ-1242` (is a sole trader a
person or a company?) — both stubbed with `raise NotImplementedError`, neither guessed anywhere.
**Filed and fixed:** `DEF-2873` — the master-account refusal `BR-CUS-1011` raises had no sentence in
any of the eleven catalogues, so it arrived on screen empty; `G32` was already red on it at the tip.

**Measured:** `test_cr056_w2b_company_identity.py` **19 passed**, `test_cr056_w2_customer_identity.py`
**21 passed**, golden-verify **33 PASS / 0 FAIL** and `G61` **PASS (130 frozen figures)** both sides,
`makemigrations --check` **No changes detected**, `npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `G32` **0 unresolved**,
`G33` **no new or changed refusal over 6 words**. **RED FIRST (law 7):** the kind requirement was run
against the existing person suite before anything was adapted — **14 of 21 cases went red**, every
one on `customers.customer.kind_required_for_identity`.

**ROLLBACK, stated before shipping (step 8).** Revert the commit and run `migrate customers 0037`.
Every operation in `0038` is an `AddField` of a nullable column plus one `AddIndex`, so a rollback
drops ciphertext and index tokens and loses no fact that existed before it ran — nothing else reads
either column. The behaviour reverts with it: the matcher returns to the person-only test, and
`link_customer` stops refusing an identity with no kind. **Nothing a customer receives moves either
way** — no bill, no document and no posted amount touches these columns.

**BROWSER PROOF (PO hard rule 2026-08-30), PROVED RED FIRST.**
`10-scripts/render-checks/cr056-company-identity.mjs` opens the customers list in a real Chromium
against a real Django and PostgreSQL and reads the COMPANY row: it draws **`•••• 1234`** where every
business in the product used to read *"Nothing on file"*, the search prompt names the Tax ID, typing
the whole number leaves exactly that one row and typing half of it leaves none — which is a property
of the encryption (an equality probe over an HMAC) and not a bug in the box — and no spelling of the
number appears in any `/customers` response body or anywhere in the rendered page. **The RED:** the
defect was put back by making `selectors.customer_row` serve `tax_id_held: False`, and the check
failed with *"a company draws its Tax ID mark ending 1234 — identity cells read ['Nothing on
file']"*, the exact sentence the old behaviour showed. ⚠ **And proving it red found a flaw in the
CHECK, which is what law 7 is for:** the page carries two `input[type="search"]` and a bare
`querySelector` took the app shell's global box, so three assertions were reading the wrong control
and reported failures that were not screen defects.

⚠ **`DEF-2870` — THE DEMO FIXTURE WOULD NOT LOAD, AND THAT IS FILED RATHER THAN WORKED AROUND
QUIETLY.** On a database created today, `migrate` → `seed_demo` → `load_sample_data --tenant
brazosbend` refuses metering's premises block with `VAL-002 metering.cycle.code_duplicate`; ten
further blocks report `SD-PRECONDITION` waiting on it and the tenant ends with **0 accounts and 0
customers**, so every customers screen is empty on a freshly seeded box. **Not diagnosed and not
guessed** — the reproduction is what is recorded. The two rows the browser proof reads were opened
through `customers.services.create_account` instead, which is the door a clerk uses and is stronger
evidence than a fixture row: it exercises the validator, the encryptor, the blind index and the link
write, where an ORM insert would have proved the column and skipped every rule.

# 10 · WAVE W6 — LANDED 2026-09-01 · `v2.113.0` · a customer number needs a name **and one ID**

**PO verbatim, 2026-09-01:** *"Customer ID - minimum name and one ID - minimum - please make this rule and
apply"*. Signed into **`BR-CUS-1023`**; the ruling and this lane's judgments are in the decision log of the
same date under **A CUSTOMER # NEEDS A NAME AND ONE IDENTIFIER** and **THE MINIMUM-IDENTITY RULE IS BUILT**.

**What a person and a business each need now:** a person, a name plus a Social Security number, a driving
licence **or** a phone; a business, a name plus its Tax ID. **A name alone no longer creates a customer
number, and the account still opens either way.**

collects the right ID (and now SENDS the block at all — `DEF-2818`, built-not-wired since W3); the owner's

### 11 · WAVE W6 — LANDED 2026-09-01 · `v2.116.0` · the move-out story, and NONE of it was waiting on a ruling

⚠ **THIS IS THE `W6` OF §5's TABLE — TASKS 26, 27 AND 28 — AND NOT §10's.** Section 10 above is
headed *"WAVE W6"* and is the minimum-identity rule (`BR-CUS-1023`, `2.113.0`); it took the label
from the wave it shipped in and touches nothing here. The two are told apart by their tasks.

**THE HEADLINE, IN PLAIN WORDS: the day a tenant moves out owing money now has an answer end to
end.** The unit falls to the owner's account, the screen says so before the clerk commits, and the
shortfall has somewhere to be posted. What still does not happen is the BOOKS moving, and that is
`OQ-1250` rather than a silence.

**THE FIRST FINDING WAS THAT NOTHING WAS BLOCKED (`DEF-2952`).** This wave was dispatched on this
CR's own sentence — *"the one piece genuinely waiting on a ruling"*. It is not: every one of the
nine questions was ruled by 2026-09-01, three of them on 2026-08-31 in the very session that
unblocked W4 and W6. Both stale paragraphs are corrected above. **Nothing was put to the Product
Owner by this lane** (law 13), and the only new question raised is one no ruling could have
pre-empted.

**TASK 26 — the unit falls to the owner, and there is ONE mechanism.** A move-out sets the terminal
status, `BR-MET-036` derives the unit back to vacant, and `base_charge_only_coverage` puts every
unit with no occupying account onto the owner's bill. **A cut reaches the identical state through
the identical function**, which is why `$69.60` of common areas becomes `$81.60` whichever event
emptied the unit — measured, because the dispatch said that two paths to one state would be a
defect. **No second mechanism was written.** What WAS missing is the sentence the PO ruled must be
explicit (`BR-CUS-1040`), plus four of the six impact fields `moveShared.tsx` has drawn as blanks
since 2026-08-24 — `units_occupied_after`, `owner_on_record`, `owner_is_free_text` and
`common_area_account_no`, all mapped to `null` by the port under a comment naming who owed them
(hard-won law 2). The ruled sentence rides the ADVISORY rail rather than a panel row, because a
panel folds away and a money movement a clerk must expand a panel to find is still a surprise.
**`vacant_base_charge` stays `null` on purpose:** one total is a PRICE and pricing is the engine's;
the plan's own per-service base charges are served VERBATIM instead, no minimum added (`OQ-1166`).

**TASK 27 — the settlement stops refusing, and it found two defects on the money path.**
**`DEF-2951`:** `transfer_target_for` still walked the premises' COMMON AREAS and took whoever paid
for the hallway — the derivation the PO retired on 2026-08-27 with the reason *"a fallback that

moved that day; this second copy in another file was not, and **it was blind to every single-family
address**, which is task 28's whole case. Replaced by two DECLARED rungs — the owner's own

### 12 · WAVES W4 AND W5 — LANDED 2026-09-01 · `v2.117.0` · no lines, no document

**Tasks 19, 20, 21, 22 and 23. Task 25 was found ALREADY BUILT and is ticked with its evidence rather

**WHAT A CLERK SEES, in one paragraph.** When an owner's account has nothing to bill — he lives in his
own house, so nothing falls to it — the run produces **no bill at all**, and the run screen says
*"Nothing to bill this period"* beside his account number instead of an empty table or a red
exception. A new figure counts those accounts beside *ready to bill* and *cannot be billed*, and the
list of who was quiet opens with one click and stays closed until somebody asks for it.

**TASK 19 — the document decision moved to the END, where the lines are known.** `BR-BIL-1024`.
`apps/billing/stages/assemble_document.py` — the last stage, and the only one that writes the row —
answers `None` instead of creating an `invoices` row when the priced bill carries no lines. **The test
is `len(lines) == 0` and never `total == 0`**, and that is the judgment worth reading: `OQ-670` (PO
2026-08-27, *"(b) Bill $0.00"*) puts a `$0.00` line on a real document, so a suppression keyed on the
TOTAL would delete the very bill that ruling exists to produce, silently, for 48 trash accounts.
`BR-BIL-023`'s draft replacement still runs FIRST, so a re-run that now prices nothing leaves no
document rather than last pass's. ⚠ **IN SINGLE MODE IT IS A REFUSAL, NOT SILENCE.** A cycle run has
nobody waiting on one account; a rebill, a final bill and an interim bill are all asked for BY NAME, so
`calculate_single_bill` raises with the sentence — which also stops `corrections` writing a credit note
against a rebill that does not exist.

**TASKS 20 AND 22 — the two are opposites and the difference is the build.** `BR-BIL-1025`. **One
classifier and one list, never two exclusion paths.** `gather.nothing_to_bill` asks the same two seams
the bill itself would ask — the units the account covers, and the unoccupied units `BR-CUS-170` puts on
it — and both empty means the account is SILENT. `PreparedRun.silent` and `CalculatedRun.silent` carry
them; `blocked` and the break rows go on meaning *a human must act*. **`account_count` counts silent
accounts**, so *"480 of 500"* still counts everybody the run touched. **A coverage read that REFUSES is
never turned into silence** — an unreadable master goes on blocking the run exactly as it does today.

**Task 22's own half is `DEF-2960`, and it was live.** The run's billed set was built from
`covered_units` alone, which answers a master's COMMON AREAS; `BR-CUS-170`'s empty units are disjoint
from that set by construction, so **every unoccupied unit the owner IS charged for was reported as
*"in this cycle but has no billable account"*** — a false alarm about a billed unit, on the tab a clerk
is meant to act on, since 2026-08-27. Fixed by building the set from both halves. An unoccupied unit
that reaches NOBODY goes on being reported exactly as before, which is the task's own sentence.

**TASK 21 — in words, never an empty table.** `billRunStep23.tsx` gains a **Nothing to bill** tile

**WHAT WENT RED FIRST.** `tc19b` — *a `$0.00` LINE is still a document* — failed on a priced-line stub

**WHAT IS LEFT:** task 24 — the premises IMPORT creating the master account — and W7's 29, 30 and 31.

⚠ **AND ONE CORRECTION TO §12 ITSELF, WRITTEN THE SAME HOUR AND BEFORE ANY REPORT WAS GIVEN — WHICH
HALF OF THIS IS LIVE TODAY AND WHICH IS A SAFETY NET.** Traced through the scope read rather than
assumed: **a silent owner account cannot reach a CYCLE run at all.** `accounts_for_bill_run` puts an
account in scope only when its unit is in the cycle or its `covered_unit_ids` intersects the cycle —
and an account that covers nothing satisfies neither. So on a whole-cycle run, `PreparedRun.silent` is
**empty by construction**, and the *"Nothing to bill this period"* tile and list read **0**.

**WHERE IT IS LIVE TODAY:** the single-account path — a clerk asking for that one bill BY NAME
(`single.prepare_single_bill`, asserted by `tc20`). That clerk used to be told the account *"has no
unit and covers none"*, a configuration problem that does not exist; they are now told there was
nothing to bill. **And `DEF-2960`'s fix is live on every cycle run**, because it is about UNITS rather
than about silent accounts.

**WHAT IS THEREFORE A SAFETY NET RATHER THAN A LIVE PATH:** the `assemble_document` guard and
`CalculatedRun.silent`. Both are correct, both are tested, and neither can fire until the scope hole
above is closed — at which point the run already does the right thing instead of needing the rule
built under time pressure on the day it first matters.

⚠ **AND THE DURABLE RECORD IS THE HONEST GAP, STATED RATHER THAN FAKED.** A silent account has no ROW
anywhere — no draft, no break — so the only place a cycle run's *who was quiet* could come from today
is the POST response that produced it. `BillRunWizard.tsx` records at length why that is a defect and
not a shortcut (`CR-051` task 7: *"the only copy of the exception list was the response to the POST
that produced it, so a refresh emptied it, a logout emptied it, and a second clerk never had it at
all"*). **So it was not wired that way.** Closing this properly means a row for a silent account, and
it belongs with the scope fix rather than ahead of it.

⚠ **AND A HOLE MEASURED HERE AND DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT.** A master account that covers NO common area
is **invisible to a cycle run**: `accounts_for_bill_run` resolves a unit-less master through
`covered_unit_ids` only, so an owner's account whose only reason to be billed is an unoccupied unit is
never in scope — and `gather_account` would refuse it anyway, for want of a unit to take a plan from.
That is the ordinary shape of a house or a duplex. Building it means choosing which unit supplies the
plan and the geography for a bill made only of empty-unit base charges, which is a money decision, and
`W6` has just landed the move-out story next door — so it belongs beside that work rather than being
answered by a call site here.

**Rollback:** three independent edits. Remove the `if not tuple(getattr(priced, "lines", ()))` guard in
`assemble_document` and every account gets a document again; remove the `gather.nothing_to_bill` branch
in `runs._prepare_run` and `single.prepare_single_bill` and a silent account is a blocked one again;
remove the `premises` branch in `create_connection` and New Connect demands an address again. No column
was added, no migration was taken, and every new key in the eleven catalogues is additive.

**Version:** `2.117.0` — `07-frontend/package.json`, `07-frontend/package-lock.json` (two literals),
`06-backend/pyproject.toml` and a `CHANGELOG.md` entry. `G35` PASS.

## CR-057 — the charge code says which connection sizes are priced, and R3's release condition becomes readable

**Raised:** 2026-09-01, in one sentence in the working chat. **Requester:** Product Owner, verbatim:
*"rate schedule will not provdie the size, charge code will provide"* — said in the same message as
*"What can actually release R3 — The refusal. Where a rate schedule doesn't price a connection's size at
all"*. **Classification:** CHANGE. It reverses a signed clause deliberately; it is not our
misunderstanding of one. **Version:** `2.112.0`. **Status:** DONE.

### 0 · WHAT ARRIVED

The lane measuring the pricing cutover reported that the connection-size step (R3) could not be released
by the comparison the release condition names, because that comparison asked one seam the same question
twice and reported the echo as agreement (`DEF-2878`). Its recommendation was that R3's REFUSAL is the
only independent evidence. **The PO agreed and corrected where the refusal must look.**

### 1 · WHAT SIGNED STATEMENT IS BEING REVERSED

`BR-RAT-088` (PO ruling 2026-08-20, CONFIRMED), at ONE clause: *"R3's refusal semantics are unchanged — a
size absent from the **schedule** still means not served"*. Supersession chain: `BR-RAT-012`/`BR-RAT-027`
→ `BR-RAT-088` (2026-08-20) → **`BR-RAT-1010` (2026-09-01), at that word only.** Everything else in
`BR-RAT-088` stands, and all of `BR-RAT-120` stands including its sequencing clause.

**No ❄️ FROZEN B4/B5 figure is touched.** This changes which OBJECT states a size, never any amount, any
rounding or any tax treatment — `golden-verify 33 PASS / 0 FAIL` and `G61`'s 130 frozen figures are
unchanged either side of the build.

### 2 · IMPACT

| Surface | What moved |
|---|---|
| Business rules | `BR-RAT-1010` added; `BR-RAT-088` stamped SUPERSEDED at one clause |
| Decision log | the ruling, its narrowing order, and why the strict reading is not taken |
| Rating engine | `resolution_catalogue.base_code_sizes_for` (new) · `configured_sizes_for` asks it first · `ScheduleVersion.size_axis_source` · `resolve_served_size`'s sentence names its object |
| Measurement | `10-scripts/cr052_r1r7_shadow_measure.py` — the carry report becomes R3's per-utility release verdict, plus `--sabotage R3-coverage` to prove it can fail |
| Tests | `06-backend/tests/test_br_rat_1010_charge_code_states_the_size.py`, TC1–TC8 |
| Open questions | none opened, none closed. `OQ-560`/`OQ-561` (thermal steam and battery bands) are deliberately still raising |
| Demo fixture | untouched — `BASE-W` stays flat at `$8.00`, which is why no tenant changes axis |

### 3 · WHAT WAS ALREADY BUILT AND IS NOW WRONG

**Nothing, and that is measured rather than asserted.** `charge_code_amounts` is empty on every tenant of
this database, so every service falls to the schedule exactly as before. The whole cutover chain has no
production caller (`SERVED_BY_CHAIN_DEFAULT` is empty), so no invoice, no ledger row and no screen figure
moves. Three lanes were building in `apps/rating` and `apps/billing` when this landed; none touches
`configured_sizes_for`.

### 4 · SIZE, AND THE PLAIN-ENGLISH CONFIRMATION

Small — one function, one field, one sentence, one report. Put to the PO as: *"where a utility prices its
base charge per connection size, that table is what says which sizes exist; a size missing from it stops
the bill instead of being charged at another size's rate. Nothing changes for a utility charging one base
for every size, which is all of them today."*

### 5 · ROLLBACK

Delete the four-line `from_code` branch in `configured_sizes_for`. The axis returns to the schedule's
configuration and every other change (the source field, the sentence, the report) is inert without it.


### CR-057 · WHERE THIS STANDS — 2026-09-01, read from the code

**FINISHED.** This CR has no numbered task table — it is one function, one field, one sentence and one
report — so there is nothing to tick and nothing to miscount. Verified rather than taken from the

## CR-058 — who gets an account and a customer number, corrected at every door

**Raised:** 2026-09-01, in the working chat, as a set of corrections to a door-by-door table we put to
the Product Owner. **Requester:** Product Owner. **Classification:** CHANGE. One ruling reverses
shipped behaviour deliberately (transfer); one adds a creation the product has never done (premises
import); three confirm current behaviour. **Version:** `2.118.0` for tasks 10–19 (W3 + W4 + W5). **Status:** OPEN — tasks 1–9 are a sibling lane's.

Every ruling is quoted verbatim in `12-governance/02-decision-log.md`, 2026-09-01, *"SEVEN CORRECTIONS
TO WHO GETS AN ACCOUNT AND A CUSTOMER NUMBER"*. **Read it before starting any task below** — the
reasoning, the supersessions and the three unruled questions are all there and are not repeated here.

### THE ONE RULE UNDERNEATH ALL OF IT

*"During regular and master account creation process - we check whether we ahve mathicng customer ID,
if yes, we use it if no we create it, given we have identify atleast 1"* — **match first, create only
on no match, and only where an identifier is present.** Every task below is an application of it.

### WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE AND MUST NOT BE REBUILT

* The customer writer, the identity evidence types and the returning-customer matcher exist.
* `POST /accounts` and `POST /accounts/{id}/move-in` **already accept the whole customer block**; the
  two wizards do not send it. Much of W1 is WIRING, not new backend.
* The company Tax ID shipped 2026-09-01 (encrypted, last four on screen).
* The master account already hangs off the ADDRESS (`premises_id`, `unit_id` NULL).

### TASKS 3–9 — BUILT, v2.122.0 (`BR-CUS-1024` · `DEF-2587`)

**THE FIGURE THAT MOVED, AND IT IS BIGGER THAN THIS CR EXPECTED.** The CR says the master door mints
a new Customer # from a free-text owner name *"every single time"*. **Half of that had already closed
hours earlier** — `BR-CUS-1023` landed the same morning, so a free-text owner name with no kind now
creates NOTHING, and running the door three times produces **zero** customer numbers, not three.

**The half that was still open is worse and is the case ruling 0 is actually about.** Give the same
landlord a name, the kind and a real Social Security number — an identifier, exactly what the ruling
asks for — at three buildings, and the product wrote **`C-00001`, `C-00002` and `C-00003`: three
customers over one Social Security number**, having recognised him each time and said so. Filed as
`DEF-2587`; **after task 5 the same landlord has ONE number at all three.**

## CR-059 — Payments, end to end: thirty-seven specified changes, ten rulings that never reached the repository, and three defects that reach the customer

**Raised:** 2026-09-01, Product Owner, in the working chat session.

### CR-059 · 5 · SIZE, AND THE PLAIN-ENGLISH CONFIRMATION

For reading aloud: *"Money coming in works. A clerk takes a payment, it meets the right bills in the
right order, it reaches the books, and the bank ties out — that whole path is finished. What is
missing is almost everything that happens when something goes wrong afterwards. A cheque that bounces
is a weekly event and there is no button for it anywhere, even though the machinery behind it is
written and tested. A customer who overpays cannot be given their money back from a screen. A clerk
who types 1,000.00 instead of 100.00 has no way to undo it, and the account then carries 900.00 of
credit the customer never paid, which quietly gets spent on their next bill. And three things are
actively wrong today: a customer paying their payment plan perfectly on time is still chased for it
and their plan never closes; a bill corrected after it was paid tells the customer they owe money they
have already paid; and when we decide to give somebody 25.00 off their bill, we write and tell them so
— and then the account still shows the full amount and we chase them for it."*

**The three figures to quote.**
1. A bounced **$292.87** cheque leaves the customer owing **$292.87** where it should be **$322.87**
   once the utility's $30.00 returned-cheque fee is charged — the reversal is exact and the missing
   $30.00 is a charge line billing must write.
2. Ajinkya's corrected bill: he paid **$100.00**, the bill was corrected to **$80.00**, and his account
   says he owes **$80.00** and is **six days late**, while the ledger says the utility owes **him
   $20.00** — a **$100.00** gap between the subledger and the ledger that nothing anywhere reports.
3. **A 25.00 goodwill credit on a 247.30 bill.** The signed answer is that the customer owes
   **222.30**. The books record it correctly. The account screen says **247.30**, the next bill is
   calculated without it, and the collection ladder chases them for it — **after a letter has gone out
   telling them they were given the 25.00.**

### CR-059 · 6 · THE TEN RULINGS OF 2026-09-01 — VERBATIM, WITH THE OPTIONS THAT WERE ON THE TABLE

**THIS SECTION IS THE MOST PERISHABLE THING IN THIS CR AND IS THEREFORE FIRST IN THE TASK LIST.**
These answers live in the source document and nowhere else in the repository. **The options matter as
much as the answers** — a signature covers only what was shown (`CLAUDE.md`, PO ruling 2026-08-11) —
so the declined options are recorded, not just the chosen one.

**Q1 · When someone moves in and owes a deposit, what may the clerk do?**
(a) **CHOSEN** — all three: take it now · add it to the first bill · waive it with a reason.
(b) declined — take it now, or waive it; no adding to the bill.
(c) declined — take it now only; no waiving.
*Reason recorded:* adding it to the first bill is how somebody who cannot find $150 at the counter
still gets connected, and a waiver with a stated reason is what an auditor asks to see.

**Q1b · If waiving is allowed, what reasons may they pick?**
(a) **CHOSEN** — a short fixed list the utility sets: *good payment history · landlord guarantee ·
assistance programme · manager's discretion*.
(b) declined — free text, with the approving manager named.
(c) declined — one reason only: manager's discretion.
*Reason recorded:* a list is the only version you can later report on — how much deposit did we waive
last year, and why. It is a reference list, so it is a card on the settings grid and mints no new
screen ID.

**Q2 · A customer closes one account and opens another, and you already hold their $150.**
(a) declined — refund the old one, collect a new one.
(b) **CHOSEN** — offer it forward: the move-in screen says the deposit is held on the old account and
the clerk accepts it.
(c) declined — carry forward only when the two accounts are close in time, say within 60 days.
*Cost recorded:* money has to move between two accounts, which nothing in the product does today.

**Q3 · Someone leaves. You hold $153.50, they owe $88.00, so $65.50 is left over.**
(a) declined — refund it, a cheque goes out.
(b) declined — hold it as a credit on the closed account until they ask.
(c) **CHOSEN** — move it to their new account if they have one; refund it if they do not.
*Reason recorded:* (b) would leave real money sitting on a closed account nobody looks at again.

**Q4a · May a landlord pay a tenant's bill when the tenant hasn't agreed?**
(a) **CHOSEN** — yes, always. Anyone may pay any bill.
(b) declined — only when the tenant's account is marked landlord-paid.
(c) declined — yes, but the tenant is told it happened.
*Consequence recorded:* the authority check becomes a **RELATIONSHIP** check — is this unit on this
master's building? — rather than a consent check, which is simpler than first drawn.

**Q4b · Does paying a tenant's bill let the landlord see it?**
(a) declined — no; they see what they paid, per unit, as an amount and nothing else.
(b) **CHOSEN** — yes, the whole bill, including usage.
(c) declined — the amount and the due date only.
*Consequence recorded, and it is owed to a person:* **a tenant's consumption becomes visible to their
landlord.** Worth telling the tenant at sign-up or on the bill, so it reads as policy rather than as
something discovered by accident.

**Q5a · A tenant leaves owing $500 and there is no landlord account at all.**
(a) **CHOSEN** — the debt stays on the closed tenant account and is chased there.
(b) declined — it is written off.
(c) declined — the clerk must name some account to move it to before they can close.
*Reason recorded:* this is already how a closed account carrying a balance behaves, so nothing new has
to be invented.

**Q5b · May a landlord refuse a residue moved to them?**
(a) declined — no; if the clerk ties it back, it moves.
(b) declined — yes, they can dispute it and it returns to the tenant's account.
(c) **CHOSEN** — it moves only if they agreed in advance, as a standing arrangement recorded on the
building.
*Consequence recorded:* **this needs a fact the product does not hold** — who agreed, when, and
whether it still stands — plus a place to set it and a check at move-out. Without that record the
ruling cannot be honoured however carefully the transfer is built.

**Q6 · A customer overpaid $40.00 in June and $17.13 in July and wants the $57.13 back.**
(a) **CHOSEN** — the refund belongs to the ACCOUNT, not to one payment.
(b) declined — two refund rows, oldest first; but then one cheque appears on two rows and the bank
reconciliation has to un-pick it.
(c) declined — a child table listing which payments funded the refund; exact, but a new concept for a
two-person office.
*Cost recorded:* it changes a schema that was signed off, so it goes through the contracts side.

**Q7 · A bounced cheque is presented again by the bank and clears.**
(a) **CHOSEN** — the same cheque, with a history: presented → returned → re-presented → cleared.
(b) declined — a new payment, linked back to the bounce.
(c) declined — a new payment with no link.
*Reason recorded:* it is how the bank thinks about it and how the customer asks about it — *did my
cheque go through in the end?* — and the only version where that question has a single answer.
Lateness was settled separately: it reads the day the money actually arrived.

**THE FOUR THAT WERE ALREADY RULED AND WERE CORRECTED IN PLACE RATHER THAN RE-ASKED** (law 13 — never
ask the PO the same thing twice): the posting date of an imported payment (ruled 2026-08-11 —
lateness is judged by the actual date the money arrived, never by the posting or import date, and an
imported row takes its date from the file; the no-date fallback to the recorded date was ruled the
following day) · many-to-one bank matching (ruled 2026-08-12 **to BUILD it**, on a worked case of two
deposits posted as one bank credit) · a grace period after a missed instalment (ruled 2026-08-12 the
other way — **no grace period**) · who is chased once a tenant's residue moves to the master (ruled
2026-08-27 — the sub-account is closed the moment the debt transfers, so the ladder follows the
master). **Two more are v2 scope by the 2026-08-08 ruling, not open questions: card rails and the
customer portal.** **And a fifth, found with the credit-note section: whether a goodwill credit debits
a separate write-off account — ruled 2026-08-12, implemented, and still described as undecided on
three screens.**

**⚠ ONE QUESTION REMAINS GENUINELY OPEN — THE OTHER WAS RULED ON 2026-09-01, BEFORE IT WAS EVER RAISED.**

1. ~~**When a landlord's cheque bounces, what happens to the tenant?**~~ **RULED 2026-09-01**, PO
   verbatim: *"If acocunt is will Utility , utility will chase it and apply penalty"*. **Reading:** the
   account is the TENANT's and is held with the utility, so the utility chases THAT account and the
   returned-cheque penalty applies to it. **The tenant IS chased; the landlord's failure does not
   shield them.** ⚠ **This went the way the question was written to guard against, so the cost is named
   rather than discovered:** a tenant who paid nothing wrong gets a collection notice and an NSF charge
   because their landlord's cheque bounced — **so the bounce letter must make plain WHOSE payment
   failed.** Almost free to build: a bounce already re-opens the bills at their ORIGINAL due date and
   the fee is already a charge code billing writes. **⚠ And it SUPERSEDES half of CS-27's third
   proposed rule** — see CS-27, which must be rewritten before it is built.
2. **The identifier that names a residue transfer's target is recorded as ambiguous**, and a transfer
   cannot be built against an ambiguous target. *(CS-28. This is now the ONLY one.)*

*(Three more are named against their own specs and are **ours to decide and write down** rather than
ask: whether the offset may apply automatically when a refund is raised or always needs a person
(CS-8) · whether a payment that does not match an instalment exactly meets the earliest one anyway,
and whether an overpayment rolls onto the next (CS-23) · and which of the two postings owns a goodwill
concession once payments records the credit row (CS-38).)*

### CR-059 · 7 · HOW THE MODULE WORKS TODAY — the facts every task below depends on

Reproduced so the tasks are buildable without the source page.

**Intake — one live channel, four reserved.** Staff entry (`POST /accounts/{id}/payments`, Admin or
Billing Clerk, dedupe namespace `entry|<form token>`) is the only path that creates a payment outside
demo seeding. Gateway webhook, lockbox/CSV import, autopay drafting and customer self-service are
named and reserved in code and none is wired. The dedupe namespaces (`webhook|…`, `import|…`) and the
`UNIQUE (tenant, webhook_key)` index already exist and wait.

**Tender.** A per-utility lookup list, not a fixed enum — seven seeded: Cash · Check · ACH · Card ·
Wire · Money order · Lockbox (`apps/tenancy/fixtures/lookup_defaults.json`, table `payment_methods`).
Each may carry its own clearing GL account; one mapped to a dead account refuses the payment **by
name**. A tender freezes once used. It is nullable — a credit or adjustment row carries no instrument,
and such a payment is skipped when the day's takings are batched and **named in the result rather than
dropped**. *The tender is the instrument; lockbox and webhook are channels.*

**Purpose — four, all with working write paths.** Every payment names exactly ONE account; there is no
bill-first entry point anywhere.
* **bill** (default) — meets open bills in the ratified order; the remainder carries as account credit.
* **prepay** — identical treatment; on an account with no open bills the whole amount carries.
* **plan down** — meets the arrears the plan spreads AND attaches to the plan (`payments.plan_id`), or
  the customer pays the down payment and still owes the full schedule.
* **deposit** — meets no bill and becomes no credit. **Deliberately excluded from the credit
  position**, because a deposit read as credit would auto-apply to the next bill and the utility would
  spend money it is only holding.

**The recording workflow — one service, one transaction** (`services.py:636 record_payment` →
`:837 _allocate_and_post`). The form mints its own idempotency token (the server refuses a request
without one and **will not invent it**, because a key generated server-side would differ on the second
submit and dedupe nothing while looking as if it had). Linkage is proved before anything is written. A
float is refused outright, never converted. The posting date is required and is the user's date — **no
clock is read anywhere on this path, and a guard enforces it**. A double-clicked Record finds the
original and returns it with `created: false` and **HTTP 200** — deliberately not a 409, because a red
error for a button that worked is a wrong answer a clerk would act on. The `PMT-` number is allocated
inside the transaction under the payment's own posting date, so a backdated entry numbers under its
date and a rollback rolls the counter back. No clearing date → status `processing`: it meets no bill
and posts nothing, **and its posting date still protects the customer from being late**. The allocator
is a **pure calculation** — no database, no clock, no writes — which is what keeps its frozen finance
figure meaningful. The ledger is asked for one balanced entry and stamps its id back write-once; a
posting refusal rolls the whole payment back rather than landing it unbooked. The audit row is written
**inside** the transaction, so money recorded with no record of who took it is impossible; the receipt
is queued inside it too, but a failure there returns a problem code rather than raising, **because
money handed over is recorded whatever happens to its paperwork**.

**THE TWO DATES, WHICH ARE THE CARDINAL RULE OF THIS MODULE.** `posted_at` (required) — when the record
entered the system, user-entered, never the system clock; it decides on-time-ness and it is the day the
takings are batched on. `cleared_at` (null = processing) — when the money was actually received; the
books, bank reconciliation and every bounce hang off it. **A single "payment date" field does not exist
anywhere in this product, and the two are never derived from each other.**

**Allocation — two orders at once, both per-utility settings with shipped defaults.**
Across bills: *oldest first* (default) · *carry credit* · *newest first* (API only) · *a specific bill*
(disabled on the form) · *split across bills* (disabled on the form). The two disabled ones render with
their reason printed on screen: picking one bill needs a list of the account's open bills with what
each still owes, and **no endpoint serves that position**.
Inside one bill: **usage + base → taxes → the class the utility defines → fees last**. A permutation
stored on the Billing defaults page, so a regulator that wants tax first has somewhere to say so. The
reason the breakdown is computed at all is tax remittance.

> **❄️ FROZEN — `GT-7`, finance-signed 2026-08-08.** Open `BL-A` 100.00 (oldest) and `BL-B` 147.30;
> pay 120.00 oldest-first → `BL-A` settled 100.00 → `BL-B` part-paid 20.00 → **still owed 127.30**.
>
> **`PE-4`** — open bills 292.87, cheque 350.00 → applied 292.87, **credit 57.13** carried.
> Overpayment is not a sixth mode; it is a property of all of them.

**Five states, and a utility cannot invent a sixth:** `processing` → `cleared`; `reversed` carried by
the new reversing row; `posted` and `failed` are reserved by the schema and nothing writes them. A
payment past `processing` accepts **no UPDATE and no DELETE, ever**; while still `processing` only its
status and clearing date may move; an allocations row accepts no UPDATE or DELETE **in any state**.
These are database triggers, not application checks, and **no route declares PUT, PATCH or DELETE on a
payment**, so a forged verb is rejected before any handler runs. *"Has this payment been reversed?" is
a question about the existence of another row, never about a flag on this one.*

**The bounce, when the service is called** (`reversal.py:673 reverse_payment` — complete, tested,
unreachable): it refuses if the money sits in a reconciled batch (unreconcile first, a deliberate
recorded act) · writes a NEW negative payment row with its own `PMT-` number, the original's tender and
purpose, status `reversed`, a link to the original and one of four reasons (`nsf`, bank chargeback,
data-entry error, customer dispute), **both dates being the bank's return date** · writes one negative
allocation row per row the original wrote, hung off the REVERSING payment because the original's rows
are untouchable — and those negative rows re-open the bills **at their ORIGINAL due date, so the
late-fee clock never resets and a bounce buys no grace** · hands the ledger the original entry id to
**mirror inverted** rather than composing a correction here · increments the NSF count and evaluates
the cash-only flag against the utility's threshold, reporting by name when the threshold cannot be read
rather than assuming two · posts the bank's own fee as a separate entry to bank fees if given
(**explicitly not** the customer's NSF fee, which is a charge code billing writes) · queues a
returned-payment letter **for NSF only**. One reversal per payment, enforced by a unique index.

> **`PE-7`** — a 292.87 cheque bounces at a utility whose NSF fee is 30.00. Before: bill 292.87 paid,
> balance 0.00. After, today: bill re-opened, balance **292.87**. After, correct: **322.87**. The
> reversal is exact; the missing 30.00 is a charge line billing must write.

**Refunds — five states, one of which moves money** (`refunds.py`, `refunds_api.py`): `requested` →
`approved` (Admin only) → `issued` (**the money moves here**) → `cleared` or `void`. The credit is
tested **twice** — at request and again at issue — because a credit real on Tuesday can be spent by
Thursday's bill, and the money moves on Thursday. Refusals say which case it is: a credit of 57.13
refunded at 80.00 refuses; a zero credit refuses; a **negative** credit refuses by saying the account
owes that money, not that the credit is insufficient. Cheque and ACH only — card is not a value the
column can hold. One person may both raise and approve in this version, and both acts are recorded
separately in **four columns, not an approved flag**; the audit trail is the separation-of-duties
control today. A void is a status move **plus a reversing posting**, never a deletion, and the row
carries both entry ids. **Only `approve`, `void` and the queue are routed.**

> **`PE-9`** — credit on `ACC-1042` of 57.13 from ONE 350.00 cheque, refunded by cheque #10241 at
> 57.13 → credit 0.00.

**Write-offs — three modules, three verbs; the split IS the control.** Payments initiates, the ledger
posts, finance approves and reports. Request: raised from Outstandings against ONE account, at that
account's own **computed** balance — never a typed figure; one row and one audit entry, the ledger
asked for nothing and no balance moved. A write-off spanning four accounts could not post four balanced
entries or close four plans, so it is one request per account, in a loop. Reason is a closed set of
four enforced by a database check: *uncollectible after 120 days · customer bankruptcy · deceased with
no estate · below the write-off threshold* — which is why the prototype's *send to a collections
agency* cannot be written as a reason. Threshold seeded at 0.00 and a request must exceed zero, so
**every write-off needs an approver until a utility deliberately types a number and is seen doing it**.
Approve posts `DR write-off / CR accounts receivable`, the outstanding falls to zero, and the GL
account comes from finance's designation, never a picker on the clerk's screen. **The approval closes
an active payment plan — from the approval, not the request**, or the account could take a second plan
on a debt it still owes.

> **`US-PAY-012 TC-2`** — DR write-off 948.20 / CR accounts receivable 948.20 → outstanding 0.00.

**Overpayment credit — three verbs.** *Visible* (built): a signed position plus the payments behind it,
deposit-purpose money excluded. *Auto-applied at issue* (built and wired): billing's issue path applies
the smaller of what the bill still owes and what the account still holds, recomputing both sides from
the rows every time — so a retried bill run applies the residual, or nothing, and **can never
over-apply**. *Refundable* (partly): the cross-account offset is computed and the transfer is another
module's single writer. **It can go NEGATIVE by ruling, and negative is a real debt the utility
pursues — nothing calls `max(0, …)` on that figure.**

**Autopay — the absence is the feature.** When a bill is issued to an enrolled account, ONE capture
intent is written carrying the bill's total dated the bill's own due date. The row carries exactly one
status, `awaiting_rails` — no `captured`, no `failed`, no `retrying`, because *a status set that can
express a charge is one some path eventually gets written against*. The amount and date are stored, not
recomputed, so what the customer was told would be drafted survives a later correction to the bill.
"Fulfilled" is computed from whether the invoice settled, never stored. One intent per invoice, unique
index. An unenrolled account gets no intent, and that is the ordinary case — a run issuing four hundred
bills must not fail because three hundred accounts are not on autopay. **There is no "retry autopay"
action anywhere** — the prototype's button is permanently superseded.

> **`PE-12`** — intent 292.87, scheduled 22 Aug 2026, status `awaiting_rails`.

**Banking and reconciliation — the most complete workflow in the module.** Two records deliberately say
different things: the payment says cash was received, because that is what the clerk saw; the ledger
says a holding account, because that is what the bank has confirmed — which is nothing yet. Cut one
batch per **day × tender** over cleared, positive, not-yet-banked payments; the day is the **drawer day
(posting date)**, never the day the bank credits it. Codes read `DEP-260808-CHK` and the code is a
LABEL — the banking date is a real typed field nobody parses back out of the string. A second cut on
the same day is a no-op and membership is stamped write-once. Statement identity is a SHA-256 of the
exact bytes **plus** a fingerprint of two tags (bank account, statement period), so a corrected
statement imports normally and the same file re-uploaded is blocked, naming who imported it first and
when. Auto-match links a line to a batch only on **equal amounts within the utility's ± day
tolerance**, and refuses to guess in three ways: two candidates leaves both alone · a non-equal amount
is never auto-linked · a bank's own prose (`CARD SETTLEMENT STRIPE`) is never parsed for a tender.
**There is no "force match anyway"** and no code path reconciles an unexplained residual. Every
difference carries a reason AND a GL account — **that pairing is the whole control**. Reconcile posts
`DR cash + DR fees / CR exactly what each member receipt debited`, read from the ledger entries
themselves rather than from today's tender mapping, **so re-pointing a tender never strands money in
the old account** — and the batch then locks by database trigger. Unreconcile is the only way back, and
both events are attempt-numbered so a corrected second reconcile is not swallowed as a replay.
**Known limit: matching is strictly one-to-one.**

> **`PE-10` — ❄️ frozen.** `DEP-260808-CHK` 292.87 + 142.30 + 36.22 = **471.39**;
> `DEP-260808-CSH` 105.36 + 16.42 = **121.78**.
> A card day: DR 1000 Cash **4,972.90** + DR 6800 Bank fees **147.50** / CR 1010 Undeposited funds
> **5,120.40** — the fee as its own line, never netted into cash, and **a difference in the WRONG
> direction is refused**, since a bank crediting more than we recorded has not charged us a fee.
