**Collections.** Outstandings computes every figure from bills minus allocations, **never from the
account's cached balance** — a collections list driven off a cache chases people who have already paid,
and the customer receives the letter. Ageing buckets 1–30 / 31–60 / 61–90 / 90+; an account not yet
past due sits in none of them. The ladder: rung 0 friendly reminder (due + N days) · late fee
(billing's, cited only) · rung 1 ten-day disconnect notice · rung 2 five-day · rung 3 forty-eight-hour
certified final. **Five things stop it and all five are recorded, never silent:** a balance floor
(seeded **$25.00**, per utility — chasing $2.40 with an $8.00 certified letter costs more than it
recovers) · an active and current payment plan · a partial payment above a per-utility percentage · a
medical hold · a manual pause. **One step per account per pass** — an account 58 days overdue must not
receive four notices in one afternoon. Nothing here SENDS anything; every notice goes to the platform's
outbound queue. **Nothing runs this nightly** — every result carries the words `no_scheduled_caller`,
and the Outstandings bulk action is the only thing that advances the ladder. **Returned mail** is
recorded as an event, flags the address as bad, banners the account, feeds an attention queue and can
suppress further paper — a real input into whether a notice goes out at all.

**Payment plans.** Proposed by the wizard, activated on the customer's e-signature alone, one live plan
per account by index, paid down by ordinary payments judged on their POSTING date. The arithmetic lives
in one place and payments only re-checks that instalments plus down payment equal the total, to the
cent — *a second implementation would eventually disagree and tell a customer two different figures.*
**Nobody is dropped off a plan:** no void, no defaulted state, no miss counter. A missed instalment
lifts the pause the next day and ends nothing. **The pause has a scope** — it covers the arrears the
plan spreads, not the current month's bill.

> **`PE-13` / `GT-47` — ❄️ frozen.** 267.30 − 50.00 down, over 6 → **5 × 36.22 + 36.20**, the remainder
> on the LAST instalment. A customer on a 36.22 instalment who also has a 184.20 October bill owes
> **220.42** in October.

**What the books get.** Payments never writes a journal line; it composes a request under a ratified
contract, resolves accounts **by designation rather than by number**, and hands it to the ledger.
Payment cleared: DR the tender's clearing account (or **1010 Undeposited funds** when unmapped) for the
full amount / CR **1200 Accounts receivable** for what met bills and **2400 Customer credit** for the
remainder. Deposit taken: DR 1010 / CR **2000 Deposit liability**. Batch reconciled: DR **1000 Cash**
for what the bank gave and **6800 Bank fees** as its own line / CR exactly what each member receipt
debited. Payment reversed: the ledger's own mirror, linked not netted, refused a second time by a
unique index. Bank's return charge: DR 6800 / CR 1000. Refund issued: DR 2400 / CR 1000. Refund voided:
a mirror of the issue entry, the row keeping both ids. Write-off approved: DR **6900 Write-off** /
CR 1200. **The entry is dated the CLEARING date** — cash in the books must agree with cash at the bank
on a given day — while the posting moment is the payment's own. **Nothing on this path reads a clock.**

**The guarantees, and none of them is a comment promising something:** tenant isolation (RLS FORCE on
every table plus explicit filters; a cross-tenant account id resolves to no bills, not to somebody
else's) · immutability (trigger pairs in the migrations) · money precision (decimal columns, stored to
4, displayed at 2, always beside a 3-character currency; a float refused at the API boundary, never
converted; **nothing re-rounded on the way out**) · one currency per utility, never converted ·
**six separate idempotency keys**, each catching a different fact — the payment's `entry|token`, one
reversal per payment, one refund per submit token, one bank import per file + tags, one autopay intent
per invoice, one batch per day × tender · audit inside the money transaction · one ledger writer ·
module boundaries (**the account's cached balance is NOT updated here, and every record result says so
out loud**).

**Twenty-one live endpoints**, roles enforced on the server: `POST /accounts/{id}/payments`
(Admin·Clerk) · `GET /payments` · `GET /payments/summary` · `GET /outstandings` ·
`GET /autopay-intents` · `GET`·`POST /write-offs` (Admin·Clerk) · `POST /write-offs/{id}/approve`
(Admin, in service) · `GET /refunds` (Admin·Clerk) · `POST /refunds/{id}/approve`·`/void` (Admin only)
· `POST /collections/run` (Admin·Clerk) · `GET /collections/ladder` and
`GET /accounts/{id}/collections` · `GET`·`POST /deposit-batches` and `POST /deposit-batches/cut`
(Admin·Executive) · `POST /deposit-batches/{id}/match`·`/reconcile`·`/unreconcile` ·
`GET /bank-accounts`, `GET`·`POST /bank-statements` · `POST /accounts/{id}/payment-plans`, `/preview`,
`/{id}/activate`. **There is deliberately no `GET /payments/{id}` and no payment detail page** — the
only thing a detail view would add over the row is what the payment paid, and that is already on the
row.

**CREDIT NOTES — created correctly, and then barely used.** *(§33 of the source document, added by the
PO after the first reading of this CR.)* They are real rows in their own table with their own
constraints, they do **exactly one piece of work — the ledger posting** — and after that almost nothing
looks at them.

* **Two writers, and both live inside the bill-correction workflow. Nothing else in the product creates
  a credit note.** A **restatement** credits the original bill in full — Ajinkya's 100.00 bill produces
  a credit note for −100.00 and a rebill stands in its place; *the credit note is the reversal half of
  a correction, not a gift.* A **goodwill concession** credits an amount the clerk chooses **and the
  bill is deliberately left alone** — the ruling on file is that the credit is raised **on the account,
  not against the bill**: a 25.00 concession against a 247.30 bill produces a credit note for −25.00
  **and the bill still reads 247.30.**
* **A third door is drawn and disabled:** an *Issue credit* action on the account itself, refused with a
  reason saying the accounting question behind it is unanswered. **That question was answered on
  12 August 2026** — a goodwill credit debits a separate write-off account — **and the code that needed
  the answer was written. Only the refusal was left behind.**
* **The row** (`credit_notes`, owned by billing): `account_id` · `original_invoice_id` · `amount`
  (−100.000000 for the restatement, −25.000000 for the concession) · `currency` · `reason` (the
  correction's reason code) · `issued_at` (the correction's business date) · **`credit_note_no` — null,
  because nothing writes it.** It **references** the invoice rather than modifying it, which is the
  whole point: an issued bill is immutable, so a credit is a new row beside it.
* **Three things the database guarantees.** The amount is **never positive** — a check constraint
  (`BR-BIL-074`, added 2026-08-15 **after two writers stored opposite signs and a sign-off panel read
  272.30 where the customer owed 222.30**). The row **freezes once issued**: amount, currency, account
  and source cannot change. And a number, if one is ever written, is **unique per utility**.
* **THE NUMBER IS THE THING TO NOTICE.** Every credit note in the product carries `credit_note_no:
  null`. **That is not for want of machinery** — the utility's numbering settings already carry a
  *Credit memo #* series with a default format of `CM-0001`, seeded and ready, **and no code has ever
  asked it for a number.** *(`06-backend/apps/billing/models.py:1334` the nullable column with no
  writer · `core/numbering.py:101 CREDIT_MEMO`, defined and never allocated from, with its default
  format at `:317` · `apps/billing/release.py:845` the id fallback.)*
* **AND IT HAS A VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE.** The bill-run sign-off panel names the credit notes in a run,
  and when the number is missing **it falls back to the row's database id** — so **a finance user
  signing off a run reads a sentence with a raw UUID in it**, which **B14 rule 31 forbids outright: no
  database id is ever the visible value of a field.**
* **The six readers, and the one nobody can do.**

  | Reader | What it does with the credit note | Scope | State |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | The ledger posting | **The one place a credit note does real work.** A restatement debits the original bill's revenue buckets and credits receivables; a concession debits write-off and credits the customer credit balance. | the row | Built |
  | Bill detail screen | Lists the credit notes raised against that **one** bill, with amount, reason and date. **The only screen a person can read a credit note on.** | one bill | Built |
  | The correction chain | The same list again, on the chain view that walks original → rebill. | one bill | Built |
  | Bill-run sign-off | Nets the credit magnitudes into the run total and names up to five of them — **by database id, because they have no number.** | one bill run | Built, **names ids** |
  | Ledger reports | Counted as an adjustment in the GL reports, **by the posting's source type rather than by reading the table.** | the books | Built |
  | A letter to the customer | A goodwill concession queues a *"credit issued"* email. **A restatement sends no credit note — it sends the rebill, which is the right document.** | concessions only | Built |
  | The account balance | **Nothing.** Outstanding is bill totals less payment allocations; account credit is payments less allocations less refunds. **Neither reads this table.** | — | **Not read** |
  | **All credit notes for an account** | **Nothing. No query, no route, no screen, no export.** | — | **Absent** |

* **THE DIRECT ANSWER TO *"where can a user view all the credit notes for an account?"* — NOWHERE.** To
  find every credit note Ajinkya has ever been given, somebody must **open each of his bills one at a
  time** and read the panel on each. There is no list, no filter, no account tab and no report — **and
  the database index built for exactly that lookup, on utility plus account, has never had a query run
  against it.**
* **AND A CREDIT NOTE CHANGES NO NUMBER THE CUSTOMER SEES.** The worked case: a goodwill credit on a
  247.30 bill posts **DR write-off 25.00 / CR customer credit balance 25.00** — balanced, through the
  ledger service, and right. **The agreed answer is that the customer owes 222.30**, and that figure is
  **frozen in the signed test fixtures — it is not in dispute anywhere.** What the account screen says:
  **outstanding 247.30** (bill totals − payment allocations) and **account credit 0.00** (payments −
  allocations − refunds). **Neither one mentions credit notes.** So the concession is real in the
  ledger and **invisible to the customer, the clerk, the balance, the next bill and the collection
  ladder** — and **a letter does go out saying they have been given 25.00, and then they are chased for
  the full 247.30 they were told they no longer owe.**
* **For a RESTATEMENT this does not bite**, because the rebill carries the corrected total and the
  customer's balance follows the rebill — **provided CS-36's missing step is built.** **For a
  CONCESSION it bites hard, and it is worse than a silent gap: the customer is told.**

### CR-059 · 7b · CREDIT NOTES — CURRENT PROCESS AGAINST PROPOSED PROCESS

| | Current process | Proposed process |
|---|---|---|
| **Creating one** | Two writers, both inside the bill-correction workflow. The account-level *Issue credit* action is disabled **for a reason that expired on 12 August.** | Unchanged for corrections. **The account action is enabled**, since the accounting it was waiting for is ruled and built. |
| **Numbering** | `credit_note_no` is null on every row. The sign-off panel **prints database ids to a finance user.** | Allocated from the **Credit memo #** series the utility already has, **at creation, in the same transaction.** The panel prints `CM-0001`. |
| **Seeing one** | Only on the detail screen of the bill it was raised against. | **Also on the account:** a Credits tab listing every credit note with its number, date, amount, reason and the bill it came from. |
| **Effect on what is owed** | **None.** A concession leaves the balance untouched **while the letter says otherwise.** | A concession **raises visible account credit**, so the balance, the next bill and the collection ladder all agree with the letter. |
| **Reporting** | Present in the general ledger as adjustments; **no operational report at all.** | A credit-note report over a date range, by reason, **alongside the write-off report** — the two together answer *"what did we give away, and what did we fail to collect"*. |

### CR-059 · 8 · THE THIRTY-SEVEN CHANGE SPECIFICATIONS, IN FULL

Every one carries: why · the new rules **as SENTENCES** (ids allocated at write time, §0c) · the
backend work · exactly which screens change and how · data · proof · dependencies · what is already
ruled.

---

#### CS-1 · Take money from a card / ACH gateway — **v2 scope, costed not asked**
* **Why.** Rails are the only way money arrives without a clerk touching it, and they are the
  precondition for autopay ever charging anybody (CS-9). The dedupe namespace
  `webhook|<gateway>:<event>` and the database uniqueness that makes a redelivery harmless are already
  built — **nothing listens.**
* **New rules (3).** A gateway payment is recorded by the same service as a counter payment; **a second
  write path for money is forbidden.** · An unverified signature is refused **before any row is
  written**, and the attempt is recorded as a security event. · An event naming an account this utility
  does not hold is **quarantined for a person, never matched by guesswork.**
* **Backend.** `apps/payments/webhooks.py` (one docstring line today) gains signature verification,
  event→account resolution and a single call to
  `services.record_payment(idempotency_source="webhook", …)`. A new **unauthenticated** route outside
  the tenant-path scheme, keyed by the gateway's own tenant identifier. Per-utility gateway credentials
  in settings.
* **Screens (3).** **S8 Settings** — gateway credentials + the webhook URL to paste into the gateway ·
  **S33 Payments · Record payments** — a source column and filter so gateway money is distinguishable
  from counter money · **S35 Payment modals** — a quarantine review modal for events that matched no
  account.
* **Data.** New table `payment_webhook_events` (raw payload, signature result, resolution state) + its
  RLS policy. **No change to `payments`** — the key column and its index already exist.
* **Proof.** A redelivered event writes one row; a tampered signature writes none; a full round trip
  against the gateway's sandbox.
* **Scope, already ruled.** Card rails are **not in this version** (2026-08-08: no Stripe,
  provision-only for v1). **This is a v2 build, not a v1 decision waiting on anybody.**
* **Then needs a ruling, when picked up.** What happens to money whose account cannot be matched — hold
  it in quarantine, or refuse it back to the gateway.

#### CS-2 · Import a lockbox or CSV remittance file — **buildable now**
* **Why.** A utility on a bank lockbox receives one file a day carrying hundreds of cheques. Today
  every one is typed by hand, and the story covering it has been a draft since W4.
* **New rules (2).** A remittance import is **staged**: upload → validate → preview → commit;
  **nothing is applied on upload** (the same shape the meter-read import already uses). · A row that
  cannot be matched to an account **with certainty** is left unmatched for a person; **a
  name-and-amount heuristic never commits on its own.**
* **Backend.** `apps/payments/lockbox.py` already holds the pure bank-file kernel and the file + tags
  idempotency — it gains the **remittance parser beside the statement one**. A staged-import service;
  commit calls `record_payment` per row with `idempotency_source="import"`.
* **Screens (2).** **S35** — the Lockbox modal the prototype already draws, built as upload → preview
  and match → commit · **S33** — a batch filter and a link back to the batch that created each row.
* **Data.** Two new tables — `payment_import_batches`, `payment_import_rows` — plus RLS. Both are
  already named in the schema brief.
* **⚠ NOT BLOCKED — an earlier draft said otherwise and was wrong.** Ruled 2026-08-11: lateness is
  judged by **the actual date the money arrived**, never by the posting or import date, and an imported
  row takes its date from the file. Where a row carries no arrival date at all, the fallback to the
  recorded date was ruled the following day. **Both halves are settled.**

#### CS-3 · Let a customer pay online — **v2 scope, costed honestly**
* **Why.** The single largest reduction in counter work — and the furthest from what exists.
* **The real cost.** **It is not a payments change.** The product has no customer-facing authentication
  at all: the three roles are staff roles and every screen ID in the inventory is a staff screen. A
  portal needs customer identity, customer-facing screen IDs minted in the spec, and CS-1's gateway
  before a single payment can be taken.
* **New rules (2).** A customer-initiated payment is recorded by the same service, **with the customer
  recorded as the actor.** · A self-service session may **never** see or pay another account unless the
  customer link says they hold it.
* **Screens.** New IDs required — none exist. **A product decision before an engineering one.**
* **Scope, already ruled.** Out of v1 on 2026-08-08, in the same batch that removed card rails.
* *Not an intake channel — the other direction:* the bank statement import reads a file too and is easy
  to mistake for a payment source. **It is not:** it imports what the bank says happened so money
  already recorded can be tied out. It **creates no payment and touches no customer balance.**

#### CS-4 · Publish what each bill still owes — **the cheapest unblocking change in the module**
* **Why.** Two of the four allocation choices ship **disabled with their reason printed on screen**.
  The calculation exists and is correct — it just has no endpoint in front of it. **This one read is
  also what CS-11 and CS-12 both wait on.**
* **New rules.** **None.** `BR-PAY-001`'s four choices are already CONFIRMED. **This is a missing READ,
  not a missing rule** — worth saying, because **no sign-off is needed to build it.**
* **Backend.** Publish `GET /accounts/{id}/open-bills` over `billing_seam.open_invoices_for_account`,
  which already returns the number, the issue date, the total, what has been allocated and the
  four-class composition. **No money logic moves and the allocator is untouched.**
* **Screens (2).** **S22 · S35 Record payment** — enable *"A specific bill"* and *"Split across
  bills"*; a picker listing each open bill with what it still owes, and a **running remainder** ·
  **S21 Account detail** — the same figures on the Bills tab, which today can only show the issued
  total.
* **Data.** None.
* **Proof.** The two disabled options become enabled **and the on-screen reason text is deleted with
  them**; a split whose parts do not sum to the payment is refused; **the frozen allocation figure is
  unchanged.**

#### CS-5 · Open the door on a bounced payment — **the highest-value gap; also fixes a defect**
* **Why.** A returned cheque is a routine weekly event, the whole machine is finished and tested, and
  **no person can reach it.** Today it is a support call and a hand-written journal entry.
* **New rules (1).** None for the behaviour — `BR-PAY-013`, `BR-PAY-011` and `BR-PAY-002` are CONFIRMED
  and implemented. One new: **reversing a payment is Admin-only**, matching the refund gate; **the
  service carries no role gate today.**
* **Backend.** `POST /payments/{id}/reverse` calling `reversal.reverse_payment`, with the Admin gate
  added **in the service as well as on the route**. **AND A DEFECT TO FIX IN THE SAME CHANGE:**
  `resume_collections` is accepted (`reversal.py:681`), documented in detail (`:705`) and **never read
  anywhere in the function body**, so `ladder.restart_after_bounce` has no caller. Either wire it or
  remove the parameter — **and either way `ladder.py:83`, which states that the reversal calls it,
  stops being true and must change.**
* **Screens (3).** **S33** — a Reverse row action, which the prototype draws and this screen does not
  have · **S35** — the Reverse modal: **ONE reason — the bounce** — because the service refuses the
  other three by name (see CS-31); the bank's return date, an optional bank fee, and the
  resume-collections choice; **the locked-batch refusal shown BEFORE the button, not as an error after
  it** · **S21** — the reversing row on the Payments tab, already renderable, nothing to build.
* **Data.** **None.** Every column, index and trigger this needs already exists.
* **Proof.** The full bounce chain against a live database; the refusal when the payment sits in a
  reconciled batch; **one reversal per payment under a race.**
* **The collections side, for the record.** A bounce is meant to pause the ladder and let a person
  resume it, and the ruling on file is that it then **restarts at rung 1 rather than by age** —
  otherwise a customer whose cheque bounced gets a certified 48-hour disconnection notice as their
  first contact about a bill they believed they had paid.

#### CS-6 · Route the three missing refund steps
* **Why.** A refund can be approved and voided from a screen but **not raised, paid out or cleared.**
  The services are complete; only the demo seeder calls them. **So the approval queue that IS routed
  can never have anything in it.**
* **New rules.** None — `BR-PAY-014` and `BR-PAY-037` are CONFIRMED and implemented. **⚠ But a real
  hole:** `issue_refund` (`refunds.py:732`) and `clear_refund` (`:802`) carry **no role gate at all**,
  which is why the no-door gate never listed them — **so the gate must be added in the service, not
  only on the new route.**
* **Backend.** Three routes in the existing `refunds_api.py`: `POST /accounts/{id}/refunds` (raise —
  Admin or Clerk; the credit test runs in the service) · `POST /refunds/{id}/issue` (Admin) ·
  `POST /refunds/{id}/clear` (Admin or Executive — **it is a bank fact, not an approval**).
* **Screens (2).** **S58 Record refund** — raise and issue, showing the credit position and the payments
  behind it · **S39 Batch detail** — clear, beside the bank line that paid it (or on S58 if CS-15 is
  not built yet).
* **Proof.** The credit tested at request **and again at issue**; the over-refund and zero-credit
  refusals; both halves of a self-approval on the row.
* **⚠ Watch for.** The screen must **not cache the credit figure between request and issue** — a credit
  real on Tuesday can be gone by Thursday, **and the money moves on Thursday.**

#### CS-7 · Refund a credit built from several payments — **RULED 2026-09-01**
* **Why.** An account that overpaid twice holds one real credit and cannot get it back. The customer
  rings and the answer is no, **for a reason that has nothing to do with them.**
* **New rules.** None — the rule already exists and is CONFIRMED. `BR-PAY-014` was amended 2026-08-12
  in the PO's own words: the clerk chooses refund or credit, and a refund may be raised against the
  **credit balance**. **The law is ahead of the schema here, which is the unusual case.**
* **Backend.** **RULED 2026-09-01 — a refund belongs to the ACCOUNT, not to one payment.** So
  `refunds.payment_id` becomes **nullable** and a **NOT NULL `account_id`** sits beside it. The two
  alternatives are declined and recorded as declined (§6 Q6). It is still a change to a **signed
  schema**, so it goes through the contracts side rather than a payments lane — **but which shape is no
  longer the question.**
* **Screens (1).** **S58** — raise against the account's credit rather than against one payment,
  **listing the payments that built it.**
* **Worked case.** $40.00 in June + $17.13 in July, refunded as **one $57.13 cheque** against the
  account.

#### CS-8 · Move money between two accounts of one customer — **build it ONCE; four things land on it**
* **Why.** *"Offset first"* is CONFIRMED law — a customer holding a credit on one account and an arrear
  on another has the credit applied to the debt before any refund is paid. The product **computes both
  figures and moves nothing**, so a refund is refused rather than offset.
* **New rules (1).** A transfer between two accounts of the same customer is **one balanced movement
  recorded on both**, never a refund on one plus a payment on the other.
* **Backend.** The one reviewed writer for money crossing accounts is billing's balance-transfer path in
  `apps/billing/final_bill.py`; **extend it to a general customer-scoped transfer rather than minting a
  second writer.** `refunds.offset_before_refund` already computes what would move, and the customer
  link it needs is already published.
* **Screens (2).** **S21** — a Transfer action showing the sibling accounts and their balances ·
  **S58** — an offset-first step: what will be moved, and what is actually left to pay out.
* **Needs a ruling — OURS to decide and write down, not to ask.** Whether the offset may apply
  automatically when a refund is raised, or always needs a person to confirm it.
* **⚠ THIS IS THE SHARED DEPENDENCY OF FOUR THINGS:** CS-20's closing excess, CS-22's deposit
  carry-forward, CS-28's landlord residue and CS-32's payment move. **Build the transfer once.**

#### CS-9 · Actually draft the money when rails exist — **v2, and the ORDER is the point**
* **Why.** The intent rows were designed as the contract a real dispatcher would consume. Until then a
  customer who signed up for autopay still gets chased by a person.
* **Depends on.** CS-1. There is nothing to charge through until a gateway exists — **and that ordering
  is the point of the current design, not an accident.**
* **New rules (2).** An intent is executed **once and only once**, keyed on the intent itself. · A
  failed capture is a **recorded failure carrying its reason**, never a silent retry.
* **Backend.** A scheduled dispatcher reading `autopay_capture_intents` due today and calling the
  gateway; success records an ordinary payment through the same service. The intent status set grows
  beyond `awaiting_rails`.
* **⚠ ORDER OF WORK.** **Do not widen the status set before the rails land.** The single status is a
  deliberate guard — a status that can express a charge is one some path eventually gets written
  against, **and there is no charging path to write against yet.**
* **Screens (3).** **S32 Summary** — the autopay chip becomes a real queue of what will draft and when
  · **S33** — a failed-capture panel that routes to recording the money by hand · **S21** — enrolment
  and the next scheduled draft.

#### CS-10 · Run the collection ladder on a schedule
* **Why.** The ladder only advances when a person opens Outstandings and presses the bulk action.
  **Every result the engine returns already carries the words `no_scheduled_caller` — the code has been
  saying this about itself since it shipped.** For a utility with one or two staff, a chase that
  depends on somebody remembering is a chase that stops.
* **New rules (1).** The scheduled run is **per-utility and runs on that utility's business day, not on
  UTC.**
* **Backend.** Register a job in the existing job runner calling `ladder.run_ladder` per tenant. **The
  idempotence it needs already holds** — one step per account per pass is enforced in the engine, so a
  double run cannot double-notice anybody.
* **Screens (2).** **S70 Collections & notices rules** — a schedule switch and the hour it runs ·
  **S34 Outstandings** — when it last ran, what it did and when it runs next, **replacing the panel
  that currently says nothing runs it.**
* **Depends on.** The tenant business day — the same open question as the drawer day in reconciliation.
  **⚠ Running it on UTC would send a 48-hour certified notice a day early for a utility west of UTC.**

#### CS-11 · Reapply a payment to a different bill
* **Why.** A clerk who applies money to the wrong bill has no correction today except reversing the
  whole payment and taking it again. **The schema was built for this** — a reapply is reversing
  allocation rows plus new ones, and both tables are append-only — **and no service writes one.**
* **New rules.** None. `BR-PAY-031` is CONFIRMED and states the mechanism exactly; it has simply never
  been implemented.
* **Backend.** A `reapply_payment` service writing negative allocation rows and new ones in one
  transaction, with a reason and an audit row. **⚠ IT MUST POST NOTHING TO THE LEDGER.** The cash total
  has not changed — only which bill it met — so a reapply that posted would **double-count the money**.
  Saying so here is what stops the next lane adding a posting call **because every other write path has
  one.**
* **Screens (2).** **S33** — a Reapply row action · **S35** — the Reapply modal the prototype draws:
  the bills this payment met, and where to move it. Reuses CS-4's open-bill list.
* **Depends on.** CS-4.

#### CS-12 · One payment covering several accounts — **the multi-property tender**
* **Why.** A customer with three properties hands over one cheque; the clerk records three payments,
  splits the money on paper, and **gets three receipts printed for one cheque.** Nothing checks the
  split adds up, and a leftover is stranded on whichever account it was parked on.
* **New rules (3).** One tender may settle several accounts of one customer, recorded as **one tender
  row and N payments**, never as N unrelated payments. · The parts must **sum to the tender exactly**,
  or the whole submission is refused; **nothing partial commits.** · **Each account's payment carries
  its own duplicate-guard key.** Reusing one key across accounts silently records one payment and
  reports success.
* **New story.** One new story under one new epic — the multi-account tender. **Numbers taken from the
  live register at write time** (§0c); the document's `US-PAY-026` / `EP-PAY-08` are next-free reads as
  of 2.109.0 and are **not** allocations.
* **Backend.** A `payment_tenders` table (amount, method, reference, both dates) that each payment
  points at. A `record_multi_account_payment` service wrapping the existing per-account path in **one
  transaction — all or nothing** — plus a customer roll-up read over CS-4's open-bill position. New
  route `POST /customers/{id}/payments`.
* **Screens (3).** **S22 · S35** — extended: search the customer, list their properties with what each
  owes, type the amounts against a running remainder · **S21** — the tender shown on the Payments tab
  so one cheque reads as one cheque · **S33** — group the rows of one tender rather than showing three
  unrelated payments.
* **Data.** One new table plus RLS, and a **nullable** tender link on `payments`. The payment row is
  otherwise untouched — same immutability, same audit, same batch behaviour.
* **Depends on.** CS-4 for the open-bill list. CS-8 if a leftover should reach a sibling property.
* **⚠ THE TRAP, AND IT IS SILENT.** The duplicate guard is keyed on **tenant + token, NOT on the
  account.** A multi-account form that minted one token and reused it would have payments two and three
  treated as replays: the server returns payment one, **reports success, and writes nothing.** Worked
  case: **in the drawer 520.00, recorded 184.20, errors raised none.** The fix is one line of design —
  a distinct token per account, or widen the key — **but if it is missed, the failure is invisible.**
* **Needs a ruling — for the AUTOMATIC version only.** Whose property goes short when the cheque does
  not cover everything: oldest bill across all properties, the largest debt, the one closest to
  disconnection, or the clerk's choice each time. **Manual entry against three visible bills sidesteps
  the question entirely, which is why it is the right version one.**
* **The worked scenario, for the fixture.** Cheque **#8842 for $520.00**, 8 August: `ACC-1042` 12 Oak
  St Unit 1 owes 184.20 · `ACC-1043` Unit 2 owes 156.90 · `ACC-1044` 40 Cedar Ave owes 178.90. Today it
  fans into three independent recordings and re-joins only at the bank — **and nothing checks the
  split: type 184.20 / 156.90 / 179.90 and the product accepts all three happily.** Overpay at 600.00
  and the 80.00 remainder parks on ONE account and auto-applies to that account's next bill,
  **unreachable by a sibling in arrears.** Underpay at 400.00 against 520.00 and the clerk decides which
  property goes short, **nothing records the decision or its reason**, and whichever account is left
  behind walks up the collection ladder on its own. **What is already right and must not be rebuilt:**
  three balanced journal entries are not an error (each settled a different account's receivable), and
  matching compares batch totals to bank lines, **so the three-way split is invisible to reconciliation
  and ties cleanly.**

#### CS-13 · Let the month close see reconciliation — **cheapest item, largest monthly payoff**
* **Why.** Two of the close checklist's five items are ours — *batches reconciled* and *bank rec
  current* — and **neither can be computed**, so both report `unknown`, count as incomplete, and a
  utility closes **every** month over an explanation it has to type. The close module **deliberately
  reports `unknown` rather than a green tick it cannot justify** — the honesty is already there; the
  answer is not.
* **New rules.** None. `BR-LED-006` already names all five items. **This is two missing reads.**
* **Backend.** Publish the two callables the close module already names **by exact signature**:
  `apps.payments.selectors.unreconciled_batch_count(start, end)` and
  `apps.payments.selectors.unmatched_bank_line_count(start, end)` — named at
  `apps/ledger/close.py:153` and `:156`, resolved at `:479` and `:481`. **⚠ `selectors.py` already
  exists** (§0c finding 3), so this is two functions in an existing module and one line changing in the
  close module for each.
* **Screens (1).** **S42 Finance · month close** — two items stop saying `unknown` and start saying how
  many batches or lines are outstanding.

#### CS-14 · Store the statement balances and produce a reconciliation statement
* **Why.** A reconciliation is only proved when **the books plus the reconciling items equal the bank's
  own closing figure.** Today no closing balance is stored anywhere, so the two totals are never
  compared **as totals** — only batch by batch.
* **New rules (1).** A statement import captures the bank's **opening and closing balance**, and a
  period is reconciled **only when book + reconciling items = the closing balance.**
* **Backend.** Two columns on `bank_statement_imports`; a period read that assembles the statement from
  rows that **already exist** — deposits in transit (already a KPI), explained differences (already
  rows), unmatched lines (already queryable).
* **Screens (2).** **S38 Bank import wizard** — step 1 captures the two balances alongside the account
  and period it already asks for · **S37 Finance · Deposits & Bank** — the reconciliation statement
  itself, and the difference resolving to zero.
* **Data.** Two **nullable** columns, backfilled by nobody — an import made before the change simply has
  no balances **and says so.**
* **The statement shape.** Bank's closing balance 48,112.40 · less deposits in transit −1,122.78 · add
  outstanding refund cheques +44.50 · less unexplained lines −88.00 → adjusted bank balance
  **46,946.12**; cash per the books **46,946.12**; **difference 0.00** — the tie-out that cannot be
  done today.

#### CS-15 · Reconcile the money going out
* **Why.** Reconciliation only looks at deposits. Refund cheques, the bank's own charges and returned
  items are never matched, so **the bank account is half-proved: everything coming in ties and
  everything going out is taken on trust.**
* **New rules (2).** An outgoing item is matched to a bank line **by the same rule as a deposit**: equal
  amount, date within tolerance, one to one, no forcing. · **A refund is cleared by the bank line that
  paid it, not by a person typing a date.**
* **Backend.** Extend matching to negative lines; add a bank-line link to refunds; route the clearing
  step (CS-6) so it can be driven from the matched line.
* **Screens (2).** **S38** — outgoing lines appear in the review rather than being ignored ·
  **S39 Batch detail** — a cleared refund shown against the line that cleared it.
* **Depends on.** CS-6 — the clearing step has no route today.

#### CS-16 · Let an unmatched line be explained
* **Why.** A resolution row can only hang off a **batch**. A line that is genuinely not a deposit — a
  customer paying the bank directly, an interest credit, a bank error — can only be left alone, **and it
  sits there forever with nothing said about it.**
* **New rules (1).** Every bank line ends the period **either matched or explained**, with a reason and
  a GL account. **Silence is not a state.**
* **Backend.** Allow `bank_rec_resolutions` to hang off a **line** as well as a batch. The row already
  carries the signed amount, the reason, the GL account, the note and the author — **only its parent is
  fixed.**
* **Screens (1).** **S40 Finance reconcile modal** — the same modal, opened from a line instead of a
  batch.

#### CS-17 · Match many lines to one batch, and one to many — **ALREADY RULED TO BUILD**
* **Why.** A bank that combines two of our deposits into one credit, or splits one across two, **cannot
  be reconciled at all.** Every response already carries the gap, so a clerk is told before they open a
  batch that can never tie.
* **New rules.** A match may be a **set**; the set's totals must be equal and every member's date within
  tolerance. **The three existing refusals are unchanged: this widens what can tie, never what can be
  guessed.**
* **Backend.** Replace the single line-to-batch link with a match set.
* **⚠ THIS IS RULED, NOT OPEN.** The PO ruled on **2026-08-12** to build many-to-one matching, on a
  worked case of two deposits posted as one bank credit. **It is confirmed law and unbuilt code.**
* **Screens (2).** **S38** — select several lines for one batch · **S39** — show all the lines that make
  up the match.

#### CS-18 · Give difference reasons a real list
* **Why.** The reason on a resolution is **free text**, so no two clerks describe the same difference
  the same way and nobody can report on cause — *how much was processor fees this quarter, how much was
  error.*
* **New rules (1).** Reconciliation difference reasons are a **seeded, tenant-extensible list**,
  deactivated and never deleted, like every other reference list.
* **Backend.** One lookup table and a seed; the resolution keeps its free-text note for the detail. A
  report grouping differences by reason and GL account.
* **Screens (2).** **S8 Settings · Reference data** — **no new screen ID**: a reference list is data, so
  it is a card on the existing grid, exactly as bank accounts were ruled to be · **S40** — the free-text
  box becomes a picker plus a note.

#### CS-19 · Satisfy the deposit line on the first bill — **one missing call**
* **Why.** The rule is CONFIRMED and half-built: a deposit-purpose payment is supposed to satisfy the
  deposit line the first bill carries. **Payments publishes the figure; billing never asks for it.** So
  a customer who paid their deposit at the counter **is billed for it again on their first bill.**
* **New rules.** None. `BR-PAY-012` and `BR-BIL-012` both already say this.
* **Backend.** Billing's issue path calls `apps.payments.credit.deposit_payments_for_account` — already
  published, tenant-scoped and tested — and reduces the deposit line by what has been paid. **Payments
  changes nothing; this is billing's line to write.**
* **Screens (1).** **S21** — the first bill shows the deposit line already satisfied, rather than
  charging it twice.
* **Proof.** Take a deposit, issue the first bill, and the deposit line reads zero owing — **the case
  the test suite already describes and cannot exercise end to end.**

#### CS-20 · Accrue deposit interest — **blocks closing ANY account that holds a deposit**
* **Why.** It blocks closing any account that holds a deposit — **which is every residential account at
  a utility that takes deposits.** The rate is a confirmed rule and a real setting on a real screen;
  **nothing computes with it.**
* **New rules.** None. `BR-CUS-057` is CONFIRMED: a **per-utility simple annual rate, default 0%,
  accruing monthly, from the original receipt date, paid at refund or closure.** A frozen worked figure
  for it is still to be allocated.
* **Backend.** An accrual engine in `customers` publishing `deposit_interest_accrued(account_id,
  as_of)`, which the move-out settlement and the refund path both already want **by name**. **Interest
  is a liability movement, so it posts like the deposit itself — never as revenue.**
* **Screens (3).** **S21** — deposit held, interest accrued to date, total owed back *(worked: held
  150.00 received 02 Feb · interest accrued 3.50 · **owed back 153.50**)* · **S20 Move-Out wizard** —
  the settlement showing principal and interest **separately** · **S66 Billing defaults** — the rate
  field, which already exists, **gains the effect it describes.**
* **Where the excess goes — RULED 2026-09-01.** Holding $153.50 against $88.00 owed leaves **$65.50**:
  it **moves to their new account if they have one, and is refunded if they do not.** So the settlement
  needs CS-8's cross-account transfer and falls back to the refund path when there is no destination.
* **⚠ WATCH FOR.** The accrual must run **from the original receipt date, not from the account's
  opening** — a deposit taken late in a tenancy has accrued less, and **a single wrong start date is
  wrong on every account at once.**
* **⚠ AND PAYING OUT PRINCIPAL ONLY IS NOT A WORKAROUND** — it keeps the customer's own interest, on a
  bill that foots correctly.

#### CS-21 · The three deposit elections at move-in — **ALL RULED 2026-09-01, buildable**
* **Why.** Every utility does one of three things at move-in: take the deposit now, put it on the first
  bill, or waive it. **Only the first has a path today**, and the amount lookup that decides how much is
  unbuilt, **so the figure has no source on screen.**
* **New rules.** **RULED 2026-09-01 — all three elections stand** (take it now · add it to the first
  bill · waive it with a reason); the rule that carried them as *proposed* can be **CONFIRMED**. ·
  **RULED 2026-09-01 — the waiver reason is a short fixed list the utility sets, not free text**, seeded
  with *good payment history · landlord guarantee · assistance programme · manager's discretion*. · One
  new sentence: **an add-to-first-bill election creates NO payment** — it is a billing line, and
  **payments records nothing until money actually arrives.**
* **Backend.** The plan deposit-schedule read (rating), so the wizard can show the right figure; a
  waive-reason lookup; the election recorded on the account. **⚠ NOTE THE GUARD THAT ALREADY EXISTS:**
  how much the utility actually holds is **derived from cleared money** and is refused on every door a
  person types into — **the elections must not become a second way to set it.**
* **Screens (2).** **S19 Move-In wizard step 5** — the amount from the schedule, the three elections,
  and the reason box when waiving · **S8 Settings · Reference data** — the waive-reason list, a card on
  the existing grid, **no new screen ID.**

#### CS-22 · Carry a deposit forward to a new account — **RULED 2026-09-01**
* **Why.** A customer who closes one account and opens another should not be asked for a second deposit.
  The customer link that proves it is the same person is confirmed and built; **the mechanics of moving
  the held money are not.**
* **New rules.** **RULED 2026-09-01 — the deposit is OFFERED FORWARD, not refunded and re-collected.**
  The move-in screen states that $150 is held on the old account and the clerk accepts it. So it moves
  as a **liability transfer between two accounts**; the rule that carried this as proposed on mechanics
  can be CONFIRMED.
* **Backend.** The **same single writer as CS-8** — money crossing two accounts is one balanced movement
  recorded on both, **never a refund plus a fresh deposit.**
* **Screens (2).** **S19 step 4** — offering the prior deposit instead of collecting · **S21** — where
  the carried deposit came from.
* **Depends on.** **CS-8.** This is now the shared dependency of two rulings — the carry-forward and the
  closing excess — **so build the transfer once.**

#### CS-23 · Link an instalment payment to its instalment — **⛔ A DEFECT, AND IT UNDOES THE WHOLE FEATURE**
* **Why.** **Nothing links a payment to its instalment on the running product.** The one function that
  stamps an instalment as paid (`plans.py:336 record_installment_payment`) is called by tests and the
  demo seeder (`sample_data.py:679`) **and by nothing else.** The ordinary record path links a payment
  to the PLAN; **it never touches the instalment row.** **The consequences chain, and every one is
  customer-facing:**
  1. every instalment stays unmarked, so **from the day after the first one falls due the plan reads as
     behind**;
  2. the dunning pause therefore **never applies** — **a customer paying perfectly on time is chased up
     the collection ladder**;
  3. **missed-instalment notices go out to customers who missed nothing**;
  4. and **the plan never closes**, because completion is detected in the very function nothing calls.

  *Everything else about plans is built and correct. **This one link is what makes it work.*** **This is
  the highest-severity item in this CR after the bounced cheque, and unlike that one it is a DEFECT
  rather than an unbuilt feature — so it gets a defect row, not just a task.**
* **New rules.** None for the behaviour — `BR-PAY-021` and `BR-CUS-043` already define on-time-ness and
  closure exactly as the function implements them. **The routing is already ruled**: on 2026-08-12 an
  instalment payment was ruled to reach the plan first, as a **named exception** to
  oldest-invoice-first. **What is missing is the code that does it.** One new sentence: which instalment,
  when the amount is not an exact match — **the earliest unmet one, with the clerk able to move it.**
* **Backend.** `services.record_payment` resolves the account's live plan (**the read exists**) and
  calls `plans.record_installment_payment` **inside the same transaction.** Two questions must be
  answered **in code, not left implicit**: which instalment a payment satisfies when it is not an exact
  match, and what happens when one payment covers two instalments.
* **Screens (3).** **S22 · S35** — when the account has a live plan, show the schedule and which
  instalment this payment is meeting, **with the option to change it** · **S21** — the plan tab showing
  each instalment as paid or outstanding with its payment · **S24 Payment Plan wizard** — the plan's own
  progress, **which today cannot be true.**
* **Data.** None — the columns exist and are indexed. **Only the writer is missing a caller.**
* **Proof.** Pay every instalment on its due date: **the pause holds throughout, no notice is sent, and
  the plan closes on the last one. That test cannot pass today.**
* **Needs a ruling — a detail only, and OURS to decide.** The plan-first routing is ruled; what is not
  is whether a payment that does not match an instalment exactly meets the earliest one anyway, and
  whether an overpayment rolls onto the next.

#### CS-24 · A grace period before the pause lifts — **⛔ WITHDRAWN, AND KEPT ON PURPOSE**
* **Withdrawn.** This was already decided, and decided **the other way**. On **2026-08-12** the ruling
  was that a missed instalment **lifts the dunning pause immediately, with no grace period** — worked on
  the frozen $36.22 instalment. **The behaviour in the product today is the ruled behaviour.**
* **Kept, not deleted.** The row stays so the next reader **meets the answer rather than proposing it
  again** (law 13). **Nothing here needs building.**

#### CS-25 · Reject a request, and correct an approved write-off
* **Why.** A clerk raises a write-off for the wrong account. Today an approver can only approve it or
  ignore it, and the queue fills with requests nobody will action. **Worse: once approved, receivables
  have been permanently reduced and there is no path back** — while the append-only rule explicitly says
  an erroneous write-off is corrected by a **new row.**
* **New rules (2).** A request may be **rejected with a reason** by an approver; **rejection moves no
  money and is not a deletion.** · An approved write-off is corrected by a **reversing write-off row and
  a mirrored ledger entry**, never by editing or deleting the original — **and the debt comes back at
  its ORIGINAL age**, exactly as a bounced payment reinstates arrears at the original due date.
* **Backend.** Two states added to the closed set (`rejected`, `reversed`) with the check constraint
  widened; a `reject_write_off` service; a `reverse_write_off` service **asking the ledger for its own
  mirror — never composing a compensating entry.** Both Admin-gated, both audited.
* **Screens (2).** **S36 Finance · write-off queue** — a Reject action with its reason, and a Reverse
  action on an approved row · **S34 Outstandings** — an account whose write-off was reversed reappears
  **with its original age.**
* **Data.** No new table. The status check constraint widens and two nullable columns record who
  reversed it and why.
* **⚠ WATCH FOR — this is why it is ONE change and not two.** A reversal **must reopen the payment plan
  the approval closed**, or the customer is left with a debt and no schedule.

#### CS-26 · Report what was written off, and why
* **Why.** The rule splits this deliberately — payments owns the transaction, the ledger posts it,
  **finance reports it.** The first two exist. **Bad debt by reason, by month and by service is what a
  utility's board actually asks for, and nothing assembles it.**
* **New rules.** None. `BR-PAY-020` already names reporting as finance's third of the split.
* **Backend.** A read over `write_offs` grouped by reason and period. **The write-off entry already
  carries its own source type in the ledger**, so *what did we write off this year?* can be answered
  without joining through payments at all.
* **Screens (1).** **S36 Finance · Revenue & AR** — bad debt by reason and by month, tying to the
  ledger's write-off account. *(Worked shape: uncollectible 120 days 2,840.00 · 72% · deceased, no
  estate 712.40 · 18% · bankruptcy 387.60 · 10%.)*

#### CS-27 · Let a master pay its units' bills — **the sub-metering core case**
* **Why.** Sub-metered buildings are **this product's core market**, and a landlord paying one cheque
  for a block is the ordinary case there. Today it is **four hand-typed payments on four strangers'
  accounts**, with a landlord's overpayment landing as **a tenant's credit.**
* **Not the same as CS-12.** CS-12 groups **by customer**, and the customer link does not join a
  landlord to their tenants. **This groups by PREMISES** — unit → premises → owner → master account —
  which is a different key and a different authority question. **Build CS-12 first; this extends it
  rather than repeating it.**
* **THE THREE SHAPES PEOPLE MEAN BY "the master pays", and only one is built.**
  **A · the master's own bill** — the owner is billed for the hallway light and the car-park meter; one
  account, several units, one bill, one payment. **WORKS** — a master account is an ordinary account
  marked `kind=master` holding service agreements over the building's common-area units. *It is not a
  parent of the others.*
  **B · the owner holds every unit account** — several accounts, several bills, one cheque. **Three
  payments by hand** — and this is exactly CS-12's problem, **so CS-12 covers it.**
  **C · the master pays its TENANTS' bills** — several accounts held by different people, one cheque
  from a fourth. **NO CONCEPT AT ALL.** *Be careful: C looks like B and behaves quite differently,
  because the landlord and the tenants are not the same customer, so nothing joins their accounts, and
  the money is being paid by somebody who does not hold them.*
* **What goes wrong in shape C today, in order of severity.** Nobody checks the payer may pay — **there
  is no bill-to and no responsible party anywhere.** **An overpayment becomes a TENANT's credit** — the
  landlord's money, on a different person's account, and it will auto-apply to their next bill. Nothing
  ties the four together except the cheque number typed four times. And **a bounce is four separate
  acts on four ladders, against four tenants who paid nothing wrong.**
* **WHERE THE PAYMENT ENTRY LANDS — NOT A MATTER OF TASTE; THREE SIGNED RULES FORCE IT.**
  **Model 1 is correct:** a real payment entry on **each unit account**, allocated against that unit's
  bill and **annotated with the payer**; the **master carries the TENDER record and NO payment entry**,
  except for money deliberately parked as its own credit. Why: (i) a payment row carries exactly one
  mandatory account and money meets a bill only through an allocation against that bill's invoice, so
  settling a unit's bill **requires** a payment row on the unit's account; (ii) a cleared payment
  credits accounts receivable and **the receivable being reduced is the UNIT's** — put the payment on
  the master and you credit a debt the master never had while four bills stay open; (iii) the master
  genuinely does not owe this money — no consolidated bill exists, so a payment there would **create a
  credit balance beside four unpaid bills.**
  **What each place then shows.** *The tenant's account* — a real payment entry against their bill,
  **annotated with who paid it**, which is exactly what a tenant asking *"has my landlord paid my
  water?"* needs to see; balance 0.00. *The master's account* — the tender: the cheque, the date, the
  total and **the list of what it settled**; **no payment entry and no balance change**, because the
  master never owed these bills. *The master, exception* — **one payment entry only for money
  deliberately left over, carried as the master's own credit**, because a leftover has to live
  somewhere and **the only lawful home is the payer's account. It must never settle on a tenant's.**
  *The general ledger* — ONE balanced entry per tender: DR undeposited 742.60 / CR AR `ACC-1042` 184.20
  + `ACC-1043` 156.90 + `ACC-1044` 212.60 + `ACC-1045` 188.90. **The receivables that fall are the
  UNITS' — never the master's.** *The deposit batch* — **nothing new**; the parts join the day's batch
  by tender exactly as they do today.
  **Model 2** (bill the master, then recharge the units by transfer) becomes right **only** if a utility
  wants the landlord invoiced for the whole building — **that is consolidated billing, a much larger
  change**: billing, delivery, taxes and the plan snapshot all assume one bill per account. *Paying once
  and billing once are separate builds, and only the first is cheap.*
* **New rules (3).** A master account **may pay a bill on a unit of its own premises, and the authority
  is recorded on the payment**; a payer who is not the account holder is never assumed. · Money a master
  pays that no unit bill absorbs **returns to the MASTER's credit, never to a unit account's** — **a
  tenant must not end up holding their landlord's money.** · Reversing a master tender **reverses every
  unit payment it made** — and ⚠ **the rest of this sentence is SUPERSEDED.** It read *"and the
  collection consequence falls on the master, not on the tenants who paid nothing wrong"*, and the PO
  ruled the opposite on **2026-09-01**: *"If acocunt is will Utility , utility will chase it and apply
  penalty"* — **the TENANT's own account is chased and carries the penalty.** The superseded words are
  kept rather than edited away, so the change is visible and not just the conclusion. **What that
  ruling does NOT settle: whether the master ALSO carries a consequence.** It speaks to the tenant side
  only. Decide that and write it down before building this rule.
* **Backend.** CS-12's tender row gains a **payer that need not hold the accounts it settles.** A
  premises-scoped read: the units of a premises, their occupying accounts and what each owes. An
  authority resolver walking **unit → premises → owner → master**. **⚠ The join to build carefully:
  there is no account-to-master column today, and the owner link is NULLABLE — an unowned premises has
  nobody to authorise.**
* **Screens (4).** **S22 · S35** — pay by premises: the building, its units, what each owes, a running
  remainder, and a **may pay?** column · **S21** — on a master, the units it may pay for and what they
  owe; on a unit, **that this bill was paid by the master** · **S33** — group a master tender's rows ·
  **S17 Accounts list** — find the master **by building**, not only by name.
* **Data.** The tender row (CS-12) plus a payer column and an authority reference. **No new
  master-to-sub column is needed if the owner link is used** — a direct edge would be a schema decision,
  not a payments one.
* **RULED 2026-09-01 — two of the three settled.** A master **may always** pay a unit's bill (anyone may
  pay any bill; the tenant's agreement is not required), **and** paying it **does** give the master
  sight of that bill, including its usage. **So the authority check becomes a RELATIONSHIP check — is
  this unit on this master's premises? — not a consent check**, which is simpler than first drawn.
* **⚠ FOLLOWS FROM Q4b, AND IT IS OWED TO A PERSON.** A tenant's consumption becomes visible to their
  landlord. **Tell the tenant it happens** — at sign-up or on the bill — so it is a policy rather than a
  discovery.
* **What the rules already say about master and sub, and it runs the OTHER way.** When a sub-account
  closes still owing after its deposit has been applied, **the residue moves to the master** — qualified
  2026-08-27 to be **clerk-initiated**, and **the close-out path says in its own words that it collects
  no such consent and therefore transfers nothing.** Who gets chased is settled (2026-08-27: the
  sub-account is closed the moment the debt transfers, so **the ladder follows the master**).
* **~~Still open — ONE.~~ CLOSED, RULED 2026-09-01.** *"If acocunt is will Utility , utility will chase
  it and apply penalty"* — the tenant's bill is simply unpaid again, **the tenant's own account is
  chased, and the returned-cheque penalty applies to it. CS-27 now waits on nothing from the PO.**
* **Worked scenario for the fixture.** Owner's cheque **#9931 for $742.60** over `ACC-1042` J. Ilori
  184.20 · `ACC-1043` M. Okonjo 156.90 · `ACC-1044` R. Vance 212.60 · `ACC-1045` D. Chaudhry 188.90,
  with the master `ACC-9001` A. Rowe holding its own hallway bill of **69.60** (41.20 + 28.40).

#### CS-28 · Build the residue tie-back that is already ruled — **needs a record the product does not hold**
* **Why.** A tenant leaves owing more than their deposit covers, and the rule says that residue moves to
  the master. **The rule is CONFIRMED and qualified; the code says plainly that it transfers nothing and
  explains why.** So a landlord who agreed to stand behind their tenants' debts **cannot be made to.**
* **New rules.** The residue rule is already CONFIRMED, and its **2026-08-27** qualification settles that
  the tie-back is **clerk-initiated** — a deliberate act at move-out with an actor recorded; **it never
  fires on its own.** · **RULED 2026-09-01 — it moves only if the landlord agreed IN ADVANCE**, as a
  standing arrangement recorded on the building; **a clerk's tie-back CHECKS that arrangement, it does
  not create the obligation.** · **RULED 2026-09-01 — where there is no master account, the debt stays on
  the closed tenant account and is chased there**, which is already how a closed account with a balance
  behaves.
* **Backend.** The move-out settlement gains the tie-back step: resolve the master through the owner
  link, move the residue as **one balanced movement recorded on both accounts (the CS-8 writer)**, close
  the sub-account, and open the collections case **against the master.**
* **Screens (3).** **S20 Move-Out wizard** — the tie-back step: the residue, the master it would move to,
  whether a standing arrangement exists, and the clerk's explicit act · **S21** — on the master, residues
  transferred in and where each came from · **premises (new surface)** — **the standing arrangement
  itself: who agreed, when, and whether it still stands.**
* **Depends on.** **CS-8** (money crossing two accounts) and **CS-20** (a settlement cannot even be
  computed until deposit interest accrues).
* **⚠ THE NEW FACT THIS NEEDS, AND IT IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THE CHANGE RATHER THAN A DETAIL OF IT.**
  *"This landlord agreed to stand behind their tenants' debts"* **is not a fact the product holds.** The
  ruling requires a standing arrangement on the building — who agreed, when, and whether it is still in
  force — plus a place to set it and a check at move-out. **Without that record the ruling cannot be
  honoured, because there is nothing to consult.**
* **Still open — ONE.** The identifier that names the transfer's target is recorded as **ambiguous**, and
  **a transfer cannot be built against an ambiguous target.**

#### CS-29 · Charge the customer's returned-cheque fee
* **Why.** A utility that takes a bounced cheque is **out of pocket twice** — its own bank charges it,
  and the customer's fee that should recover that is never billed. On the frozen case the customer's
  balance comes back as **292.87 where it should be 322.87.**
* **New rules.** None. `BR-PAY-013` already says the NSF charge code is added automatically, and
  `BR-BIL-007` already puts the line write in billing priced from the charge catalogue. **Both halves are
  ruled; the read between them is missing.**
* **Backend.** Rating publishes a **charge-code read** (the same gap billing's late-fee path already
  refuses on), and **billing** writes the fee line on the bounce. **Payments writes nothing** — it never
  writes a charge line, **and typing the amount here is exactly the hand-keyed figure the rules forbid.**
* **Screens (2).** **S8 Settings · Reference data** — the NSF charge code and its amount, where the
  utility sets it · **S21** — the fee visible on the account as a charge, with the bounce it came from.
* **Depends on.** The same missing charge-code read blocks the late-fee path, **so fixing it once fixes
  both.**

#### CS-30 · Give a cheque a state of its own — **RULED 2026-09-01**
* **Why.** **There is no cheque in this system.** A cheque is an ordinary payment whose tender is `check`
  and whose number is typed into a **free-text reference field.** It has no table, no status of its own
  and no identity. Everything below follows from that:
  * **A cheque is not a thing** — the number has no format, no uniqueness and no index. **Two cheques
    can carry the same number; a typo is invisible;** *"find cheque 8842"* is a text search, not a
    lookup.
  * **No re-presentment** — banks routinely present a returned cheque a second time, and there is no way
    to say *"this is the same cheque, presented again"*; **the link to the bounce is lost.**
  * **No stop-payment or void-before-banking** — a cheque taken in error and torn up before the deposit
    is cut has no state to move to. The only correction is a reversal, **which is a bank event, not a
    counter event.**
  * **No post-dated handling** — a cheque dated three weeks out can be recorded with no clearing date,
    which is right, but **nothing knows it must not be banked until then** and nothing surfaces it when
    the day arrives.
  * **No "uncleared cheques" view** — the pieces exist (a `processing` filter, an *in transit* tile) but
    neither is a list of cheques awaiting clearance, **which is the thing a bookkeeper actually asks
    for.**
  * **And the receipt already sent** — a receipt was queued when the cheque was recorded. **Nothing
    withdraws or corrects it, and no rule covers what should happen to it.**
* **New rules (4).** A cheque carries its **number, its date and its drawer bank as structured fields,
  unique per utility**, not free text. · **RULED 2026-09-01 — a returned cheque presented again is the
  SAME cheque, carrying its history: presented → returned → re-presented → cleared.** Not a new payment,
  and not an unlinked one. · A cheque **not yet banked may be voided at the counter without a bank
  reversal**; once it is in a cut batch, only the reversal path applies. · A cheque **dated in the future
  is held out of the batch cut until its date**, and **named on the day it becomes bankable.**
* **Backend.** Structured cheque fields on the payment (or a small cheque table the payment points at), a
  **bankable-from** date consulted by the batch cut, and a void-before-banking path **distinct from the
  reversal**. **The lock and the reversal stay exactly as they are.**
* **Screens (4).** **S22 · S35** — cheque number, cheque date and drawer bank as real fields when the
  tender is a cheque · **S33** — an **uncleared cheques view** (uncleared · post-dated · returned) and a
  Void action while the cheque is still unbanked, plus **Re-present** on a returned one · **S37** —
  post-dated cheques becoming bankable today · **S21** — the cheque's own history.
* **Depends on.** **CS-5** — there is no point giving a cheque states nobody can move it through.
* **Ruled — nothing outstanding.** Lateness reads the actual date the money arrived (2026-08-11), so a
  re-presented cheque is judged on the day it finally cleared; and the record keeps one cheque with its
  history (2026-09-01). *(An earlier draft asked whether a re-presented cheque keeps the original posting
  date; the 2026-08-11 ruling already answers it and it is not re-asked.)*

#### CS-31 · A staff-initiated reversal — the general Reverse — **the single largest hole**
* **Why.** A wrong amount, a duplicate, a chargeback and a disputed payment are **all routine, and none
  of them has any lawful path.** The engine that would do the work is finished; **what is missing is the
  rule around it** — and the service is **right** to refuse until that rule exists, because running a
  staff correction through the bounce machine would **count an NSF against a customer who did nothing
  wrong and could move them to cash-only.**
* **The case, in full, because it is what a two-person office hits in week one.** A customer hands over a
  cheque for **100.00**. The clerk types **1,000.00** and presses Record. Two minutes later they see it.
  **Four doors, all shut:** *reverse it* — the engine exists and would do exactly this, but only for a
  bounce and only via no route · *edit the amount* — there is no PUT, PATCH or DELETE on any payment
  path; **the router answers 405** · *post −900.00* — a negative amount is refused; it would be **a
  second, invisible way to express a reversal** · *delete the row* — financial rows are immutable.
  **So what actually happens:** the account is **900.00 in credit** — money the customer never paid,
  which will be auto-applied to their next bill and the one after, **silently and correctly, because the
  product believes the row**; the books are **900.00 out** — receivables relieved by money that does not
  exist, and only a **hand-written journal entry outside the posting service, unaudited**, can put it
  back; **and after tonight it is worse**, because once the batch is cut and tied to a bank line the
  deposit total carries the wrong figure too, **and a reconciled batch LOCKS.**
  **Nothing in that picture is a bug.** Every single refusal is a rule doing its job. **The gap is that
  the one lawful way out was never given a door.**
* **New rules (2), and the four clauses being BUILT rather than written.** **None invented** —
  `BR-PAY-011` is CONFIRMED and already states all four clauses; **three simply are not implemented.**
  New: a staff reversal **never increments the NSF count, never sets the cash-only flag and never queues
  the bounce letter** — the engine already branches on the reason for exactly this, **and the rule should
  say so out loud so nobody removes the branch.** · The three staff reasons **require Admin or
  Executive**; the bounce does not, **because the bank decided it and no staff judgment is involved.**
* **Backend.** Widen `SUPPORTED_REASONS` (`reversal.py:450`) to all four, and implement `BR-PAY-011`'s
  three unbuilt clauses behind it:
  * **Windows** — a **server-computed** check per tender: **ACH 60 days · card 120 days · cheque
    unlimited.** Measured from the clearing date where there is one, otherwise the posting date, and
    **returned to the screen as a reason rather than a boolean** so it can be shown.
  * **Approval** — required when the payment is already applied to an issued bill, **or falls in a closed
    accounting period.** **The write-off queue is the pattern to copy; do not invent a second approval
    shape.**
  * **Consequence message** — **server-composed**, listing every bill that re-opens and by how much, plus
    any credit that goes negative. **It must be computed by the service, not assembled on the screen, or
    the warning and the outcome can disagree.**
* **Screens (3).** **S35** — the Reverse modal grows from one reason to four; a window state (*"this ACH
  cleared 74 days ago — outside the 60-day window"*); the consequence panel; and an approval step when
  the server asks for one · **S33** — the Reverse row action becomes available on more than bounced
  cheques, and the list needs a **reversal-reason column** so a bounce and a correction are told apart at
  a glance · **S36 Finance approvals** — reversals awaiting approval **join the write-off queue rather
  than getting a queue of their own.**
* **Data.** **None.** All four reasons are already in the column and its check constraint.
* **Proof.** Each reason end to end **on PostgreSQL**; a reversal outside its window refused **with the
  window in the message**; an applied payment refused without approval and accepted with it; and **the
  NSF count and cash-only flag proved unchanged after a data-entry reversal.**
* **⚠ THIS CORRECTS CS-5 AND THE TWO MUST NOT BE MERGED.** CS-5 opens a route to the bounce engine and
  its first draft described a Reverse modal offering *"one of four reasons"*. **Three of those four would
  be refused by the service.** Until CS-31 lands, that modal offers **ONE** reason. **CS-5 is a route
  over a finished engine; CS-31 is a rule to be implemented.**

#### CS-32 · Move a payment to the account it belonged to
* **Why.** Two accounts named Patel, adjacent unit numbers, one cheque. **Today this cannot be repaired
  even in two steps:** reversing on the wrong account and re-recording on the right one leaves two
  unrelated records, **a payment number the customer never saw**, and no way for anyone later to see they
  are the same money. It is also **the third change in this CR that needs money to move between two
  accounts** — the same dependency as carrying a deposit forward and refunding a leftover. **Building it
  once settles all three.**
* **New rules (3).** A payment moved between accounts is **a reversal on the source and a new payment on
  the destination, linked, sharing the original's posting and clearing dates.** **The dates must not be
  rewritten to today, or the customer becomes late on a bill they paid on time.** · The destination
  **re-allocates under its own rules**, which may land the money on entirely different bills — **that is
  correct and must be shown before confirming.** · A move is **refused once the payment sits in a
  reconciled batch**, exactly as a bounce is, until the batch is unreconciled — **the bank has already
  agreed that total.**
* **Backend.** One service function inside **one transaction** — a reversal, a new payment, and the link
  between them — plus a column recording that the destination payment came from another. **It shares
  CS-8's transfer mechanics; build the two together or the second will be a near-copy of the first.**
  Both legs post through the ledger service; **neither writes a journal line directly.**
* **Screens (2).** **S35** — a *"Move to another account"* modal: the account picker, a **required
  reason**, and a preview showing what re-opens on the source and what the money will meet on the
  destination · **S21** — **both** accounts' Payments tabs must show the move **as a move** — *"moved to
  2608-0155"*, *"moved from 2608-0141"* — rather than as an unexplained reversal on one screen and an
  unexplained payment on the other.
* **Data.** One **nullable** column on `payments` linking a moved payment to the one it came from. **No
  change to any signed contract.**
* **Proof.** The move on PostgreSQL with both accounts' balances checked; **the original dates proved
  intact on the destination**; refusal while the batch is reconciled; and the ledger tie-out —
  **receivables net to zero across the pair.**

#### CS-33 · Reverse part of a payment — **a schema and concurrency change on a money path**
* **Why.** Today a reversal is **all or nothing.** When only part of a payment fails — a partial
  chargeback, or a cheque where the words and the figures disagree and the bank honours the lower — the
  office must reverse the whole thing and record a second payment for the part that stood. **The
  customer's history then shows a payment that bounced when it did not**, and if it was a cheque **an NSF
  count and a cash-only flag can follow from it.**
* **New rules (2).** A partial reversal **may not exceed what the payment still stands for**, and the
  **sum of all reversals against one payment may never exceed it.** · A partial reversal **unwinds
  allocations in the reverse of the order they were made, newest bill first**, unless the clerk names
  which bill to re-open.
* **Backend.** **⚠ THE BLOCKER IS NOT THE ARITHMETIC, IT IS THE INDEX.** A unique constraint
  (`uq_payments_reverses`) permits **exactly one reversal per payment.** Partial reversal needs many,
  which means **replacing that guarantee with a summed check** — **and the unique index is what currently
  makes a retried request and a lost race indistinguishable, so the idempotency guard has to be
  re-established a different way.** This is a **schema and concurrency change on a money path**, not a
  feature toggle.
* **Screens (1).** **S35** — the Reverse modal gains an amount field defaulting to the full amount, and a
  line showing what will still stand afterwards.
* **Data.** Drop or narrow `uq_payments_reverses`; add the summed constraint. **A signed-schema change —
  contracts lane, not payments.**
* **Proof.** Two partial reversals summing to the original; a third refused; **and concurrent identical
  requests proved to write ONE row on PostgreSQL, since the index that used to guarantee it is gone.**

#### CS-34 · Correct what is not money
* **Why.** A mistyped cheque number changes nothing financial and cannot be fixed. **It is the smallest
  item here and it has a real cost: the reference is what a bank line is matched on, so a wrong one is an
  unmatched line and a reconciliation nobody can finish.** The same applies to a memo, and to a payment
  recorded under the wrong tender.
* **New rules (2).** The **reference and memo may be amended**; the amount, the account, both dates and
  the allocations **may never** be. **Every amendment writes an audit row carrying the old value and the
  new.** · The **tender may not be amended once the payment has been swept into a deposit batch**,
  because batches group by day and tender: **changing it would move the payment between two batches, one
  of which may be reconciled and locked.**
* **Backend.** **Deliberately NOT a PATCH on the payment resource.** The rule that there is no edit verb
  on a payment path is **load-bearing and should stay absolute** — a route that accepts a partial body
  invites the next field to be added to it. Instead **a named endpoint that accepts only these fields and
  nothing else, so what can be amended is visible in the route rather than enforced inside it.**
* **Screens (2).** **S35** — a small *"Correct reference"* modal: reference, memo, tender where still
  allowed, and a **required note** · **S21** — a corrected reference shows **as corrected**, with the
  previous value on hover, **so a customer quoting the old number can still be found.**
* **Data.** None. The audit trail already carries before-and-after.
* **Proof.** Amendment permitted and audited; **every money field refused by name**; the tender refused
  once batched; and **a bank line proved to match after a reference is corrected.**

#### CS-35 · A manual credit or adjustment, told apart from cash
* **Why.** A goodwill credit, a billing correction, a regulator-ordered adjustment — **none of these is
  money received, and today the only way to put one on an account is to record a fake payment.** **The
  database already knows this:** the payment `type` column carries `payment`, `credit` and `adjustment`,
  the screens already know how to render a signed row, and the frontend already publishes all three.
  **Nothing writes anything but `payment`. The recording function does not even accept the type.**
* **New rules (3).** A credit or adjustment row is **never swept into a deposit batch and never appears
  on bank reconciliation.** It is not cash and it will never appear on a statement; **batching one would
  make the day's takings permanently un-tieable.** · It **posts to its own ledger account, not to
  undeposited funds**, and requires **Admin approval above a tenant-set threshold**, matching write-offs.
  · It carries **a reason from a tenant-maintained list**, so *"how much did we give away last year, and
  why"* is a question with an answer.
* **Backend.** Accept the type on the recording path and **branch three things on it**: skip batching ·
  choose the ledger account · apply the approval gate. **The allocation engine needs no change** — a
  credit meets open bills exactly as a payment does. **⚠ The BATCHING branch is the one that matters;
  without it every adjustment silently corrupts the deposit total.**
* **Screens (3).** **S22** — a type selector (payment · credit · adjustment) which **hides the tender and
  reference fields for the latter two**, because there is no cheque and no bank line · **S33** — a type
  column and a filter; **the day's cash total must EXCLUDE credits and adjustments, or it will not tie to
  the drawer** · **S66 Billing defaults** — the adjustment-reason list and the approval threshold.
* **Data.** None on payments. One reason lookup, seeded, in the tenant lookup set — **the same shape as
  the deposit-waiver list.**
* **Proof.** An adjustment **proved absent from that day's batch and from bank reconciliation**; the
  ledger tie-out with a mixed day of cash and credits; and **the approval gate driven RED first.**
* **⚠ CS-38 DEPENDS ON THIS ONE.** The credit-type row is how a goodwill concession becomes visible.

#### CS-36 · Re-allocate the payment when a bill is corrected — **⛔ LIVE TODAY, AND A WRONG NUMBER REACHES THE CUSTOMER**
