* **Why — and this is the most damaging item in the CR**, because it is the **only one that is fully
  wired and reachable today** and produces a wrong number that reaches the customer. Every other
  correction gap ends in a clerk being unable to act; **this one ends in a paying customer being invoiced
  and chased for money they do not owe, while the books quietly say the opposite.** It also **silently
  breaks the month-end tie-out between the receivables ledger and the customer subledger, by exactly the
  amount that was paid.**
* **The worked case, in full.** Ajinkya pays **100.00** for a **100.00** bill (`2608-0141`, issued 8 Aug,
  due 22 Aug; paid in full 15 Aug, **on time**). On 28 Aug the read turns out to be wrong and staff
  correct the bill to **80.00**. **Executing the correction writes four things, and all four are
  correct:** a credit note for −100.00 (DR revenue / CR receivable) · a rebill `2608-0166` at 80.00
  **inheriting the ORIGINAL 22 Aug due date** · the original moves to `corrected` (**the one column that
  may move after a bill is issued**) · an audit row with before, after, delta and the rebill link.
  **AND A FIFTH THING IT DOES NOT DO: THE PAYMENT IS NEVER TOUCHED.** The 100.00 allocation still points
  at `2608-0141` — **a bill that is now invisible to payments, because only `issued` and `paid` bills are
  read** (`apps/payments/billing_seam.py:140 OPEN_INVOICE_STATUSES`).
  **So the two halves of the product now disagree:**
  * **his account screen says** — outstanding **80.00** (the rebill, with nothing allocated to it) ·
    account credit **0.00** (his 100.00 is fully applied, **to a bill nobody reads**) · **days late 6**
    (the rebill inherited 22 Aug, so it is **overdue on arrival**);
  * **the ledger says, and it is right** — +100.00 −100.00 +80.00 −100.00 = **receivable −20.00**, the
    utility owes him 20.00;
  * **the gap is 100.00 and nothing anywhere reports it.**

  **Two further consequences reach the customer.** He goes into the collection ladder and **the first
  notice is for a bill he overpaid.** And **his own money cannot help him**: issuing a bill already draws
  down account credit automatically and that machinery works, but Ajinkya has no credit — his 100.00 is
  still recorded as fully applied. **The one mechanism that would have rescued this is present, correct,
  and starved of the input it needs.**
* **Why it happens: a seam that was designed and half built.** `BR-BIL-014` names the re-allocation
  explicitly, and the code composes one on every preview — **and what it composes is a SENTENCE.** The
  plan is a list of one English sentence, verbatim: *"payments allocated to the original re-allocate to
  the rebill; any excess becomes a carried account credit. Billing emits this plan; payments executes it
  — no allocation row is ever edited."* **No invoice id. No amount. Nothing a program could act on.**
  Every word of it is the right design; it is displayed to the clerk on the preview, **and then nobody
  does it.** (`apps/billing/corrections.py:620` the plan sentence · `:1141 execute_restatement`.)
  **And the gap was seen at the time:** `WARN_PAID_IN_FULL = "bill_already_paid_in_full"` is defined at
  `corrections.py:202` **and never raised.** The clerk correcting Ajinkya's bill is shown warnings about
  upward corrections and closed periods, **and nothing at all about the fact that the bill in front of
  them has already been paid.**
* **What should happen — ONE inserted step, and the rest already works.** Between the credit note and the
  rebill: **release the allocations** — one negative row per row the payment wrote against the original,
  −100.00. **That is the only new work.** Then: the credit position rises **on its own** (100.00 paid −
  0.00 applied = 100.00, computed from rows) and **the rebill draws it down** (issuing a bill already
  applies account credit; it takes 80.00). **Result:** outstanding **0.00** · account credit **20.00**,
  visible and refundable · **days late 0** · **the ledger is unchanged at −20.00, and the two now agree.**
  **The same one step handles all three directions with no extra rule.** Correct **UP** to 120.00: the
  100.00 is released, the rebill's issue draws all 100.00 down, **20.00 is left owing — on the rebill, at
  the original due date, which is exactly right.** **Partly paid** (60.00 against 100.00, corrected to
  80.00): 60.00 released, the rebill draws all 60.00, **20.00 owing** — no special case. **A goodwill
  credit** needs nothing at all, **because no bill changed and no payment moved.**
* **Two details that make this cheaper than it looks.** **The release is not a new mechanism** — it is
  precisely what a bounced cheque already does: one negative allocation row mirroring each original row,
  hung off the payment, **editing nothing.** That code is written, tested and correct — *it is the
  reversal engine's own second step.* And **the draw-down is not new either.** **⚠ THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE
  TRICK: release BEFORE the rebill issues, inside the same transaction**, or the rebill issues against a
  credit balance that does not exist yet.
* **New rules (3).** **None invented for the behaviour** — `BR-BIL-014` is CONFIRMED and already says
  *"payment re-allocation plan … plan emitted to payments; execution payments-owned"*. **This builds a
  signed rule, and the existing plan sentence is a correct specification of it.** New: releasing an
  allocation is **append-only** — negative mirror rows, never an edit, exactly as a bounce re-opens a
  bill; **it posts NO journal line, because no money moves.** · **The release runs for a RESTATEMENT
  only** — a goodwill credit and a document-only correction release nothing, because no bill changed. ·
  **The release happens BEFORE the rebill is issued, inside the correction's one transaction**, so the
  rebill's existing credit draw-down can consume it. **Stated as a rule because it is invisible in the
  code and will otherwise be "tidied" into the wrong order.**
* **Backend.** One new payments service — **release every allocation against a named invoice, returning
  what it released** — published on the seam billing already resolves payments callables through. **One
  call added to the restatement, between the credit note and the rebill.** Nothing else changes: the
  credit position is computed from rows and rises on its own, and the rebill's draw-down already exists
  and is already called.
  **Two things to get right:** the release must be **idempotent against a replayed execution** — the case
  already holds one row per bill and only moves `queued` to `done`, **so the guard exists and must be
  relied on rather than reinvented**; and it **must be proved on PostgreSQL, not the default suite** —
  this is a multi-statement write inside a transaction that also posts to the ledger (**hard-won law
  14**).
* **Screens (3).** **S30 Fix a bill** — the **settlement panel** on the preview: paid to date · what the
  rebill takes · what returns to credit · what is still owed — **and the `bill_already_paid_in_full`
  warning that the code defines and never raises** · **S21** — the Payments tab must show the release **as
  a release**: *"re-allocated — bill 2608-0141 corrected"*, not as an unexplained negative row · **S33** —
  the same on the payments ledger, so the day's totals are readable when a correction ran.
* **Data.** **None.** Allocation rows already carry everything needed, and a negative one is already
  lawful — **it is what a bounce writes.**
* **Proof.** The full case on PostgreSQL at **each of the three shapes — down, up and partly paid** —
  asserting the outstanding, the credit and the receivable balance after each. **The tie-out is the real
  test: subledger equals ledger, which is the assertion that would have caught this.** Plus a replayed
  execution proved to release **once**, and a goodwill credit proved to release **nothing.**
* **⚠ WORTH DOING BEFORE THE FIX SHIPS, BECAUSE IT IS SMALL.** **Raise the `bill_already_paid_in_full`
  warning now, on its own.** It changes no money and no schema — the constant exists, the preview already
  renders a warning list, and the screen already displays it. It will not fix anything, **but it puts the
  fact in front of the clerk who is about to correct a paid bill, which is the person best placed to
  notice that the number afterwards is wrong.**

#### CS-37 · Give credit notes a number and a place to be seen — **⛔ contains a live B14 rule-31 breach**
* **Why.** **Two problems with one cause:** a credit note has **no identity a person can quote**, and
  **no home a person can find it in.** A customer ringing to ask about a credit they were given **cannot
  be helped without opening their bills one by one**, and the finance user signing off a run **is shown a
  database id — which the repository's own UI rules forbid on any screen.**
* **New rules (2).** A credit note **takes its number from the tenant's Credit memo series at creation,
  in the same transaction as the row, and never afterwards.** The series, its default format (`CM-0001`)
  and its settings screen **already exist.** · A credit note is **never displayed by its database id.**
  Where the number is genuinely absent on historic rows, **the screen shows the bill it was raised
  against and the date, never the id.**
* **Backend.** **One numbering call in each of the two writers.** **One account-scoped read — the index
  it needs exists and is unused — and one route to serve it.** **Historic rows keep a null number; they
  are NOT back-filled**, because the row freezes at issue and **a migration that rewrote history would be
  exactly the thing the freeze is there to prevent.**
* **Screens (3).** **S21 Account detail** — **a Credits tab**: number, date, amount, reason, and a link to
  the bill it came from — *the answer to "show me every credit note on this account"* · **S28 Bill
  detail** — the existing panel shows the number instead of a dash · **S31 Bill run release** — the
  sign-off sentence names credit notes **by number**, and **the id fallback is REMOVED rather than left
  as a safety net.**
* **Data.** **None.** The column, its unique index and the account index all exist.
* **Proof.** Two credit notes in one run proved to take **consecutive** numbers; the account tab proved to
  list credit notes **from several different bills**; and **the sign-off panel proved to contain no id —
  the check that would have caught this one.**
* **⚠ FILE THE DEFECT SEPARATELY.** The raw UUID on the sign-off panel (`release.py:845`) is a **breach of
  B14 rule 31**, ratified 2026-08-31 in the PO's words *"no Databse ID on screen - that is a rule"*. It
  gets its own defect row with an `escape_reason` — **no gate in this repo reads rendered output**, which
  is why a ratified UI rule went unenforced.

#### CS-38 · Make a goodwill credit reduce what the customer owes — **⛔ THE CUSTOMER WAS TOLD IN WRITING**
* **Why.** The utility decides to give a customer **25.00**, posts it correctly to the books, **and writes
  to tell them.** The customer's balance does not move, their next bill is calculated without it, and the
  collection ladder chases them for the full amount. **The agreed figure is 222.30 and the product says
  247.30.** *Of everything in this document this is the one where the customer has been told something in
  writing that the system then contradicts.*
* **New rules (1).** A goodwill concession **must leave visible account credit of the same amount.** **The
  ledger entry alone does not discharge the obligation; the balance a customer and a clerk read must move
  too.**
* **NO FIGURE CHANGES.** The 25.00, the 222.30 and the posting accounts are **all signed and stay exactly
  as they are** — **this makes the product agree with them.**
* **Backend.** The concession needs to raise a credit **the payments side can see**, and the cleanest
  route is **CS-35's credit-type row**: the correction asks payments to record a credit row for 25.00,
  which the credit position picks up **with no change**, and **the next bill's existing draw-down consumes
  it. Build CS-35 first.**
  **⚠ THE ONE THING TO SETTLE IN THE BUILD: THERE MUST BE EXACTLY ONE POSTING.** Today **billing** posts
  the concession. If payments records the credit row **it must not post a second time** — so **either**
  payments' row is marked non-posting, **or** the concession moves to posting through payments entirely
  and billing's credit note stays as the document. **Decide it once, write it in the docstring, and
  assert the ledger totals either way; a double post here is a real 25.00 of invented money.**
  **⚠ AND THE SMALLER ALTERNATIVE IS WRONG.** Teaching the credit position to read `credit_notes` directly
  is less code **but gives the account balance two sources of truth in two modules, which is how the
  outstanding figure and the credit figure start to disagree.**
* **Screens (2).** **S21 Account detail** — the concession appears on the Payments tab as a **signed credit
  row, described as a concession and not as money received** · **S33 Record payments** — the same, and
  **the day's cash total must exclude it** — a concession is not takings and would not tie to the drawer.
* **Data.** None beyond CS-35's reason lookup.
* **Proof.** The frozen case end to end: **a 25.00 concession on a 247.30 bill leaves the account owing
  222.30 ON THE SCREEN, not only in the books.** The ledger proved to carry the concession **exactly
  once.** And **the collection ladder proved not to chase the 25.00.**
* **⚠ ONE THING THAT IS FREE, AND SHOULD GO FIRST.** **Enable the account-level *Issue credit* action, or
  restate why it is blocked.** It is disabled with a reason saying the accounting behind it is undecided;
  **that was decided on 12 August, and the code implementing the decision was written and works.** The
  same expired reason is quoted in **two other places in the correction code, describing a path that
  executes.** Nothing is at risk in correcting the words — **but a blocked button explaining itself with a
  question that has been answered is how the next person concludes the feature is further away than it
  is.**

### CR-059 · 9 · THE FIFTEEN PAYMENT SURFACES THAT EXIST TODAY

Counted from the built frontend, not the specification — a screen is here only if a route or a component
actually renders it. **Recorded so a later lane does not rebuild one.**

| # | Screen | ID | Route | Kind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Payments · Summary | S32 | `/payments` | tab |
| 2 | Payments · Record payments | S33 | `/payments/record` | tab |
| 3 | Payments · Outstandings | S34 | `/payments/outstandings` | tab |
| 4 | Payments · Collections | **no S-ID** | `/payments/collections` | tab |
| 5 | Finance · Deposits & Bank | S37 | `/finance/deposits` | page |
| 6 | Bank import wizard | S38 | `/finance/deposits/import` | page |
| 7 | Deposit batch detail | S39 | `/finance/deposits/:id` | page |
| 8 | Finance · Write-off queue | S36 part | `/finance/write-offs` | page |
| 9 | Account detail · Payments tab | S21 | customers | tab |
| 10 | Record payment modal + result panel | S22 · S35 | from 2 and 9 | modal |
| 11 | Write-off modal + result panel | S35 | on 3 | modal |
| 12 | Collections run panel | S34 bulk | on 3 | panel |
| 13 | Explain-the-difference modal | S40 | on 7 | modal |
| 14 | Bulk mark returned-mail modal | **no S-ID** | on 1 | modal |
| 15 | Payment plan wizard | S24 | customers | wizard |

**Behaviours on those screens that a later lane must not "fix":**
* **S32 Summary** — every figure is **served, none computed in the browser.** Average, a bucket share and
  DSO can each come back as **nothing**, and **nothing renders `$0.00` in their place** — *a day with no
  payments has no average, which is a different statement from zero.* Method-mix shares are added **as
  decimals, never re-rounded.** **There is no retry-autopay action anywhere.**
* **S33 Record payments** — fourteen columns, **two of them always empty on purpose**: Batch and Receipt
  are typed and served as blanks rather than dropped, **so the screen states the absence instead of the
  cell reading as a failed load.** **No bulk toolbar and no row-action menu** — every action the prototype
  draws there (Reverse, Reapply, Send receipts, Refund) has no endpoint, **and a checkbox column selecting
  rows for nothing is worse than none.** The date-range filters the server accepts are not rendered
  either — **an empty date select narrows nothing while looking as though it had.**
* **S34 Outstandings** — **four of the six bulk actions render DISABLED with their reason on the button**,
  rather than being hidden. The selected total is summed in the browser on the decimal grid because no
  endpoint totals a selection, **and it returns nothing rather than skipping a value it cannot parse.**
* **Collections tab** — a fourth tab with **no ratified screen ID**, built because the ladder engine could
  previously only be driven and never read. *(Third row of its worked example: `ACC-1301`, balance 2.40,
  62 days — **under the floor**, and that is the floor doing its job.)*
* **S37 Deposits & Bank** — **a batch the bank has not shown serves its difference as NOTHING, never as
  `0.00`** — *a figure nobody filled must not read as one somebody counted.* *In transit* is its own tile
  for the same reason. **The reconciled row is locked by a database trigger and Unreconcile is the only
  way back.**
* **S38 wizard** — **no "Force match anyway".** The two tags are also the idempotency key.
* **S39 batch detail** — once reconciled, Reconcile **disappears** and Unreconcile takes its place — *the
  screen follows the service rather than guessing*; **the reconcile button refuses while any part of the
  gap is unexplained, and there is no override.**
* **S21 Payments tab** — **not a second implementation**: the same payments table scoped by account, **so
  the two views can never drift on what a payment is, what it settled, or how the two dates read.**
* **S22/S35 Record payment** — **two dates, never one**; the posting date is pre-filled from the browser's
  day and always visible. **No account balance is shown where the prototype prints one** — it is a cached
  figure this payment does not update, **so it would be stale in the one moment it mattered.** The result
  panel **states what did NOT happen as plainly as what did** (*"the account's cached balance was not
  updated"*).
* **S35 Write off** — **the amount is not typed**; it is the account's computed balance, **so a clerk
  cannot write off a figure they invented.**
* **Collections run panel** — **reports skips as loudly as sends.**
* **S24 plan wizard** — the schedule is computed **once**, in the wizard, and only re-checked on save.

**Specified, and with no screen at all — five:** **S58 Record refund** (the queue, approve and void
endpoints exist and **nothing in the frontend renders a refund**, so the only doors that exist cannot be
reached) · **Reverse a payment** (S35 part — the prototype draws the modal; there is no endpoint behind
it) · **Reapply a payment** (S35 part — same) · **Import lockbox** (S35 part — the staging tables do not
exist) · **Send receipts · issue credit · post adjustment** (S35 part). *Four of the five are the same
story: the prototype drew a modal for an action that has no endpoint, and the screen was **correctly not
built** rather than shipped as a button that does nothing.* **S42 Export to accounting** exists but is the
ledger's screen, not a payments one.

### CR-059 · 12 · IF YOU SEQUENCE IT — the short answer

1. **Fix the three defects first** (tasks 5–8). CS-23 is chasing customers who are paying on time and
   stopping any plan from ever closing; the dead ladder parameter means a bounced cheque never restarts
   collections; the sign-off panel is printing raw UUIDs at a finance user in breach of a ratified UI
   rule. **None needs a rule, a schema change or a decision from the PO.** Task 8 — un-blocking *Issue
   credit* — is free and belongs with them.
2. **Then the cheap unblockers** (tasks 9–14). CS-13 stops the month close reporting `unknown` every
   month · CS-4 turns on two buttons already sitting disabled on screen **and unblocks three other
   specs** · CS-19 stops a customer being billed twice for a deposit they have already paid.
3. **Then the two places the product tells the customer a wrong number** — **CS-36** (a corrected bill
   says 80.00 owed and six days late when the customer has already paid 100.00) and **CS-38** (a 25.00
   concession that the customer was told about in writing and is then chased for). **These two are the
   only gaps that are live, reachable and customer-facing today.** CS-38 needs CS-35 first.
4. **Then credit-note identity** (CS-37) — small, no schema, and it closes the rule-31 breach.
5. **Then the doors** — CS-5 for a bounced cheque, CS-6 for a refund.
6. **Then CS-20**, because until deposit interest accrues **no account holding a deposit can be closed at
   all.**
7. **Then the deposit thread, which the 1 September rulings unlocked in one go:** build the
   account-to-account transfer **once** (CS-8) and it carries the carry-forward, the closing excess, the
   landlord residue **and** the payment move between them.
8. **Everything else either waits on those, or is v2.**

**If you fix ONE thing:** the reversal path. Every other gap is either a deliberate deferral or a
convenience. A bounced cheque is a routine weekly event for a small utility, the machinery to handle it
correctly is finished and tested — the reversing row, the reinstated arrears at the original due date,
the ledger mirror, the NSF count, the customer's letter — **and none of it can be reached from the
running product.**

### CR-059 · 13 · WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN SCOPE

* **Consolidated billing** — one bill per customer or per building. Much larger: billing, delivery, taxes
  and the plan snapshot all assume one bill per account. **Named here so it is not confused with the
  payment problem: paying once and billing once are separate builds, and only the first is cheap.**
* **Card rails and the customer portal** (CS-1, CS-3, CS-9) — **v2 by the 2026-08-08 ruling.** Costed
  above, **not proposed for this release.**
* **A bank feed** replacing the hand-uploaded statement — *fine for a utility with one or two staff. A
  later convenience, not a correctness gap.*
* **`GET /payments/{id}` and a payment detail page** — deliberately absent and staying absent.
* **Bulk actions on the payments list** — deliberately not rendered while the endpoints do not exist.
* **Back-filling `credit_note_no` on historic rows** — the row freezes at issue, and **a migration that
  rewrote history would be exactly the thing the freeze is there to prevent.** Historic rows show the
  bill and the date instead.
* **A second source of truth for the account balance.** CS-38 explicitly declines teaching the credit
  position to read `credit_notes` directly, **because that gives the balance two sources in two
  modules.**
* **Anything that would move a ❄️ FROZEN `B4`/`B5` figure.** If a task finds itself moving one, it
  **STOPS** and goes to a finance re-sign through `HUMAN-GUIDE §6`.

### CR-059 · 14 · VERSION (change-process §7)

Nothing has shipped under this CR, so **no version has moved.** The product is at **`2.123.0`** (§0b).
Each wave that lands bumps the **change** digit — `2.124.0`, `2.125.0`, … — and each fix on top of a
landed wave bumps the **fix** digit. **Every task row in §11 gets its landing version written into it
when it closes**, and **the CR cannot be marked done with no version.**

### CR-059 · 15 · ROLLBACK

* **Tasks 1–4 (W0) are documentation** and carry no runtime risk. **They are also the tasks that must not
  be skipped:** the nine rulings exist in one place today, **and that place is not the repository.**
* **W1–W3 are additive doors and missing callers.** Backing them out is removing a route and a call site;
  no data written under them is invalid afterwards, because every row they create is a lawful payments
  row.
* **CS-36 (W4) is the one to be careful with in the other direction:** it changes what a correction
  writes. Rolling it back leaves the released allocations in place — **which is correct**, because a
  released allocation is a negative mirror row and the arithmetic that reads it is unchanged. **What must
  not happen is shipping the release AFTER the rebill issues**; that ordering is a rule for exactly this
  reason.
* **CS-38 (W4) has a specific double-post risk.** Until the one-posting question is settled and asserted,
  **a concession could post twice — a real 25.00 of invented money.** The ledger-total assertion is the
  rollback guard, not a nice-to-have.
* **CS-37 (W5) is additive and safe to back out**, because historic rows keep a null number either way.
  **The one thing not to do on rollback is restore the id fallback** — it is a rule breach, not a safety
  net.
* **CS-7 (task 60) and CS-33 (task 66) change signed schema and are NOT rollback-cheap.** CS-33 in
  particular **removes the index that currently guarantees one reversal per payment**; **it must not ship
  until the replacement idempotency guard is proved on PostgreSQL under concurrent identical requests.**
* **CS-9 (task 71) must not widen the autopay status set before the rails exist.** **Rolling back a
  widened status set does not roll back the rows written against it.**

The dash is the problem: it is honest, it is correct, and in a 73-row table it is
invisible. Meanwhile "landed" was reported up the chain and heard as "done".

⚠ **AND THE REGISTER UNDERSTATES WHAT EXISTS WHILE THE SCREENS OVERSTATE WHAT WORKS.**
Several rows marked as never started have live, mounted endpoints; several rows marked

was wrong by twenty-six rows, and it is corrected here.

read from code at `2.109.0`, commit `ddde9e3b` — carries two kinds of content in one
voice: DESCRIPTIONS of what the code did (including honest statements of what was
missing) and SPECIFICATIONS of what to build. Its change register listed the second kind.

absent stayed absent, because it was never a task — and nobody was wrong at any single

sentences in the descriptive half (no payment detail page, no date-range filter, no row
selection on Record payments) and were never change specs. The fourth, a broken account
search, is in neither: a genuine regression, now fixed (`DEF-3506`).

**THE DOCUMENT HAS SINCE BEEN AMENDED TO CLOSE THAT SEAM**, at the PO's instruction. It
now resolves **63 stated absences** to one of exactly two outcomes — a specification
number, or OUT OF SCOPE with its reason. **There is no third outcome**, and the document
says so in its own words: an absence with neither is a defect in the table, not a
judgement call. Result: **46 already specified · 6 newly specified · 11 out of scope.**
Every register row now also carries **an on-screen acceptance line** — *what done looks

Two corrections were made to this analysis mid-flight and both are worth knowing: an
initial claim that the bank-reconciliation routes were missing was WRONG (they are
mounted in files the first probe did not cover), and an initial reading of this CR's
dashes overstated how much was unstarted. **A proxy that returns a plausible answer is
more dangerous than one that returns none.**

**THE RULE THAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED ALL OF THIS, stated so the next CR inherits it:**
*a task is not reportable until a person has used it on screen, and any absence a source
document describes gets a specification number or an explicit out-of-scope reason.* This
CR wrote the first half for itself in 34 of its own rows and never enforced it.

> "Can you also read - The Money Path - artifacts and write next CR - in very details"

### CR-060 · 0c · STEP 0 — WHAT MOVED UNDER THE DOCUMENT, RE-READ FROM CODE AT 2.123.0

**FINDING 1 — `accounting_method` IS NOT DEAD DATA. IT HAS A READER, AND THE READER IS BROKEN.**
The document's **C6** proposes retiring the column on the grounds that it *"sits in the settings table
with no reader"*. **That is no longer true at 2.123.0**, and the correction matters because C6 as
written would delete a column something depends on:

* `06-backend/apps/tenancy/selectors.py:470` reads it — the **`fiscal_billing` onboarding-checklist
  item** is complete only when `fy_start_month` **and `accounting_method`** and `close_cadence` are
  all set.
* `06-backend/apps/tenancy/services.py:879` **deliberately leaves it unset at provisioning**, with the
  comment saying so: *"`accounting_method` is deliberately ABSENT: the PO removed that control
  (CR-008 ruling 1 — it had zero readers), so seeding a value would revive a claim the product does
  not honour."*
* `services.py:2449` and `:2497` still accept and validate it on a settings save, so it is settable
  by API — **but the control that set it was removed, so no screen can set it.**

**Put together, that is a latent defect, not a tidy-up:** the `fiscal_billing` checklist item, which
points a new tenant at `settings/regional`, **can never go green for any tenant provisioned since
CR-008**, because it waits on a value nothing seeds and no screen offers. **C6 must therefore fix the
checklist condition in the same change as it retires the column**, and a defect row is owed either
way. *(The demo seeder at `seed_demo.py:134` still writes `"accrual"`, which is why the demo tenant
does not show the symptom.)*

**FINDING 2 — THREE OF THE FIVE JOURNAL-LINE DIMENSIONS ARE UNINDEXED, NOT ONE.** The document says
`unit_id` *"is stamped but has no index — the other four dimensions do"*. **Read from the migrations
and the model, `journal_lines` carries exactly five indexes:** `ix_journal_lines_entry`
(tenant, journal_entry) · `ix_journal_lines_gl` (tenant, ledger_account) · `ix_journal_lines_account`
(tenant, account) · `ix_journal_lines_premises` (tenant, premises) · `ix_journal_lines_source`
(tenant, source_type, source_id). **So `unit_id`, `service_id` AND `tax_authority_id` have none.**
The account-level and premises-level statements are indexed; **the unit, service and tax-authority
statements are all sequential scans.** The document's own scale task (T8) should add **three**
indexes, not one — and the service dimension is the one it elsewhere calls *"the segment most
utilities report on"*.

⚠ **AND FINDING 2 IS ITSELF CORRECTED, 2026-09-01, BY THE LANE THAT BUILT IT — MEASURED AGAINST A
REAL POSTGRESQL RATHER THAN READ OFF THE MIGRATIONS.** The five `ix_journal_lines_*` indexes named
above are correct and the three missing composites are correct. **What is NOT correct is the sentence
*"the unit, service and tax-authority statements are all sequential scans"*.** They are not, and never
were: **Django puts a single-column index on every ForeignKey**, so `journal_lines_unit_id_*`,
`journal_lines_service_id_*` and `journal_lines_tax_authority_id_*` have existed since `ledger/0001`.
A dimension statement index-scanned ONE of its two columns and applied the other as a filter. Measured
on **6,098 real journal lines across 14 tenants**, PostgreSQL 16.13, before `ledger/0010` and after:

| The service statement — one tenant, one service | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| plan | Index Scan on `(tenant_id)`, `Filter: service_id` | **Index Only Scan** on `(tenant_id, service_id)` |
| rows discarded by the filter | **496** | 0 |
| rows read to return 194 | 690 | **194** |
| shared buffers | 21 | **3** |

**The gain is real and smaller than this finding implies**, and the waste it removes scales with how
much the tenant has rather than with the size of the answer. ⚠ **AND AN INDEX IS NOT PARTITION
PRUNING:** both plans still touch the empty `journal_lines_2027`, because the query carries no
predicate on `created_at`. That is `OQ-193` and it is untouched.

⚠ **THE `tax_authority` INDEX INDEXES NOTHING TODAY, AND THAT IS A STATED ABSENCE RATHER THAN A
DEFECT.** `0 of 6,098` lines carry a `tax_authority_id`, because rating publishes no
`tax_authority_id_for_tax` — `apps/ledger/reporting.py` already carries that absence in its own words
and the collected-tax read refuses with it. It is laid now because it is free now and locks a
twelve-million-row table later, and it starts earning the day **C19 / T7d** fills the column.

⚠ **AND WHAT THE GRANULARITY HALF OF T8 ACTUALLY COSTS, MEASURED THE SAME DAY ON THE SAME DATABASE —
FOUR FIGURES FOR THE PO, BECAUSE `2 · WHAT SIGNED STATEMENT IS BEING REVERSED` NEVER LISTED THIS ONE.**

1. **What a partition holds today — and monthly buys NOTHING today.** The whole product's books are
   **6,136 journal lines in ONE yearly partition, `journal_lines_2026`**. Every one of them was
   written on the same day, so a monthly partition would hold **the identical 6,136**. The case for
   monthly is entirely a projection, not an observation.
2. **Partitions are NOT tenant-scoped — CONFIRMED from the DDL, not from this document.** Both tables
   are `PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)` (`ledger/0005` line 146, `billing/0016` line 128, and
   `pg_get_partkeydef` on the live database agrees). **There is no `tenant_id` in the partition key**,
   so one partition holds every tenant's lines for that period: today `journal_lines_2026` carries
   **15 tenants**. At the disputed 80,000-account ceiling (T1) that is 12 M lines per tenant per year
   **multiplied by every tenant in the box**.
3. **`audit_log` and `meter_reads` really are MONTHLY — CONFIRMED, not repeated.** Live catalog:
   `audit_log` has 4 monthly partitions (`audit_log_2026_09` … `_12`), `meter_reads` has **28**
   (`meter_reads_2024_09` … `_2026_12`), and both migrations declare `PARTITION BY RANGE` on a
   monthly grammar. `invoice_lines` and `journal_lines` have **2 each** (`_2026`, `_2027`). **So yes —
   the two largest financial tables carry the coarsest partitions in the product.**
4. **What it costs a tenant that already has posted lines: the rows are COPIED, never rewritten, and
   it is fast at this size.** PostgreSQL has no `ALTER TABLE … PARTITION BY`, so the only route is a
   new parent plus a copy — which `core/partitioning._rebuild` already does and `ledger/0005` already
   proved once. **Run against a full copy of the development database: `journal_lines` 6,136 lines
   yearly → monthly in 0.73s; `invoice_lines` 4,239 lines in 0.52s.** Row count, amount total and the
   md5 digest over every row's full text were **identical before and after, both tables** — no line is
   UPDATEd or DELETEd, the old heap leaves by `DROP TABLE`, and the three ledger triggers, ten
   constraints and all eight `ix_*` indexes came back off the catalog. **0 unguarded partitions.**
   The transaction is all-or-nothing and that was seen rather than assumed: an earlier run refused on
   a foreign key and left the table at 6,098 rows, same total, same digest, still yearly.
   ⚠ **It holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the length of the copy**, so on a host with millions of
   lines this is a maintenance window, not a rolling deploy.

⚠ **TWO THINGS THAT MUST SHIP WITH THE GRANULARITY CHANGE IF IT IS RULED FOR, NEITHER OF WHICH THIS CR
MENTIONS.**

* **THE CREATE-AHEAD RUNWAY COLLAPSES FROM ~2 YEARS TO 4 MONTHS, AND THE JOB THAT RENEWS IT IS NOT
  SCHEDULED.** B2 §5's runway is *current + 1* for a yearly table and *current + 3* for a monthly one
  — so `journal_lines` goes from partitions reaching into **2027** to partitions reaching four months
  out. `manage.py maintain_partitions` renews them and **its celery-beat wiring has never landed
  (TD-17)**; `09-infra/02-aws-runbook.md` §9.4 already warns that `audit_log` INSERTs fail ≈3 months
  after deploy for exactly this reason. Applied to the books, the failure is *"no partition of
  relation journal_lines found for row"* — **posting and billing stop.** Yearly is currently
  absorbing that gap with a year of slack. **Monthly removes the slack, so TD-17 becomes a
  prerequisite rather than a backlog item.**
* **THE DEPLOY WINDOW ITSELF FAILS LOUDLY AND UNHELPFULLY.** Between the image roll (registry says
  MONTHLY) and `manage.py migrate` (table still YEARLY), `ensure_partitions` raises the raw
  PostgreSQL error — measured: `partition "journal_lines_2026_09" would overlap partition
  "journal_lines_2026"` — instead of `core/partitioning`'s own *"this host is behind on migrations"*
  message, because the guard checks whether the parent IS partitioned and never checks its
  GRANULARITY. One `if` in `ensure_partitions`, and it belongs in the same change.
